We are thrilled to kick off Cognition Workshop this quarter with a presentation by Dr. James Evans, Max Palevsky Professor of Sociology and Data Science. Please join us this Wednesday January 7 at 3:30p in BPSB room 122 (IMB conference room) for Dr. Evans’s talk (title and abstract below).
See you Wednesday, Monica, Akram, Cambria, and Huiqin
Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought James Evans, PhD

Large language models have achieved remarkable capabilities across domains, yet mechanisms underlying sophisticated reasoning continue to be explored. Recent reasoning-reinforced models, including OpenAI’s o-series and DeepSeek-R1, outperform other merely instruction-tuned models on complex cognitive tasks, attributed to extended test-time computation through longer chains of thought. Here we show that enhanced reasoning emerges not from extended computation alone, but from the systematic simulation of complex, multi-agent interactions—a society of thought—which enables the deliberate diversification and debate among internal cognitive perspectives characterized by distinct personality traits and domain expertise. Through quantitative analysis using classified outputs and mechanistic interpretability methods applied to reasoning traces, we find that reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B exhibit much greater perspective diversity than baseline and merely instruction-tuned models, activating broader and more conflict between heterogeneous personality- and expertise-related features during reasoning. This multi-agent structure manifests in conversational behaviors including question-answering sequences, perspective shifts, and reconciliation of conflicting views, as well as in socio-emotional roles that characterize back-and-forth conversation, which together account for the accuracy advantage in reasoning tasks through both direct and indirect facilitation of cognitive strategies. Controlled reinforcement learning experiments further reveal that base models spontaneously increase conversational behaviors when solely rewarded for reasoning accuracy, and fine-tuning base models spontaneously increase conversational behaviors when they are solely rewarded for reasoning accuracy, and fine-tuning models with conversational scaffolding substantially accelerates reasoning improvement compared to base models and models fine-tuned with monologue-like reasoning. These findings indicate that the social organization of thought enables effective exploration of solution spaces. We suggest that reasoning models establish a computational parallel to collective intelligence in human groups, where diversity enables superior problem-solving when systematically structured and suggest new

opportunities for agent organization to harness the wisdom of crowds. I further discuss other new findings on the number and structure of AI agent reasoners and societies.

This document compiles abstracts for publications listed on the Knowledge Lab publications page where the abstract text was retrievable at generation time. For a subset of items, the destination page could not be fetched; those items are listed at the end.
1. Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology
Lingfei Wu; Dashun Wang; James A. Evans Nature 566, 378-382 (2019) - Published 13 Feb 2019 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-0941-9

Abstract. One of the most universal trends in science and technology today is the growth of large teams in all areas, as solitary researchers and small teams diminish in prevalence. Increases in team size have been attributed to the specialization of scientific activities, improvements in communication technology, or the complexity of modern problems that require interdisciplinary solutions. This shift in team size raises the question of whether and how the character of the science and technology produced by large teams differs from that of small teams. Here we analyse more than 65 million papers, patents and software products (1954-2014) and demonstrate that smaller teams tend to disrupt science and technology with new ideas, whereas larger teams tend to develop existing ones. Work from larger teams builds on more-recent and popular developments and receives attention immediately; small-team contributions search more deeply into the past, are viewed as disruptive, and succeed further into the future. These results suggest science policy should support diversity in team sizes.

2. Science of science
Santo Fortunato et al. Science 359(6379): eaao0185 (2018) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29496846/

Abstract. Identifying fundamental drivers of science and developing predictive models to capture its evolution are instrumental for the design of policies that can improve the scientific enterprise - for example, through enhanced career paths for scientists, better performance evaluation for organizations hosting research, discovery of novel effective funding vehicles, and identification of promising regions along the scientific frontier. The science of science uses large-scale data on the production of science to search for universal and domain-specific patterns. Here, we review recent developments in this transdisciplinary field.

3. Quantifying the dynamics of failure across science, startups and security
Yian Yin; Yang Wang; James A. Evans; Dashun Wang Nature 575, 190-194 (2019) - Published 30 Oct 2019 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1725-y

Abstract. Human achievements are often preceded by repeated attempts that fail, but little is known about the mechanisms that govern the dynamics of failure. Here we develop a simple one-parameter model that mimics how successful future attempts build on past efforts. Analysis suggests a phase transition separates failure dynamics into regions of progression or stagnation. Above the critical point, agents exploit incremental refinements to advance toward success; below it, they explore disjoint opportunities without improvement. Using large-scale data on NIH grant applications, startup ventures, and terrorist attacks, the authors find consistent support for the model and identify early signals that distinguish failure dynamics leading to ultimate success versus failure.

4. Metaknowledge
James A. Evans; Jacob G. Foster Science 331(6018):721-725 (2011) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21311014/

Abstract. The growth of electronic publication and informatics archives makes it possible to harvest vast quantities of knowledge about knowledge, or 'metaknowledge.' We review the expanding scope of metaknowledge research, which uncovers regularities in scientific claims and infers the beliefs, preferences, research tools, and strategies behind those regularities. Metaknowledge research also investigates the effect of knowledge context on content. Teams and collaboration networks, institutional prestige, and new technologies all shape the substance and direction of research. As metaknowledge grows in breadth and quality, it may enable researchers to reshape science by identifying areas in need of reexamination and pointing out new paths across disciplinary boundaries.

5. Millions of online book co-purchases reveal partisan differences in the consumption of science Feng Shi; Yongren Shi; Fedor A. Dokshin; James A. Evans; Michael W. Macy Nature Human Behaviour 1, Article 0079 (2017) - Published 03 Apr 2017 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-017-0079

Abstract. Passionate disagreements about climate change, stem cell research and evolution raise concerns that science has become a new battlefield in the culture wars. Using data derived from millions of online co-purchases, the authors examine whether shared interest in science bridges political differences or reinforces divisions. They find partisan preferences within and across scientific disciplines: liberal consumers prefer basic science, while conservative consumers prefer applied and commercial science, and conservative-linked science books cluster more narrowly within disciplines. They conclude that the left and right share an interest in science in general, but not science in particular, motivating remedies to attenuate selective exposure.

6. Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence
Jamshid Sourati; James A. Evans Nature Human Behaviour 7, 1682-1696 (2023) - Published 13 Jul 2023 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-023-01648-z

Abstract. AI models trained on published scientific findings can invent valuable materials and therapies, but often ignore the human scientists who shape discovery. The authors show that incorporating the distribution of human expertise - by training models on simulated inferences that are cognitively accessible to experts - can dramatically improve prediction of future discoveries, especially when relevant literature is sparse. These models succeed by predicting human predictions and the scientists who will make them. By tuning human-aware AI to avoid the crowd, the approach can generate scientifically promising 'alien' hypotheses that are unlikely to be pursued without intervention, helping to probe blind spots and accelerate discovery.

7. Prediction of robust scientific facts from literature
Alexander V. Belikov; Andrey Rzhetsky; James Evans Nature Machine Intelligence 4, 445-454 (2022) - Published 28 Apr 2022 https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-022-00474-8

Abstract. Growth in published science makes it harder for humans and algorithms to reason over prior knowledge and select the next experiment, compounded by uncertainty about reproducibility. Using massive digital archives and automated tools, the authors demonstrate a Bayesian calculus to predict robust scientific claims from literature, weighting findings by scientific, social, and institutional factors associated with replicability. In gene regulatory interactions, the approach estimates and counteracts sources of bias and suggests that scientifically focused but socially and institutionally diverse research activity is most likely to replicate, updating certainty and guiding future experiments.

8. The wisdom of polarized crowds
Feng Shi; Misha Teplitskiy; Eamon Duede; James A. Evans (and coauthors) Nature Human Behaviour 3, 329-336 (2019) - Published 04 Mar 2019 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-019-0541-6

Abstract. As political polarization rises, it is unclear whether polarized individuals can cooperate effectively. Analyzing millions of edits to Wikipedia political, social issues, and science articles, the authors infer editors' ideological preferences from contribution patterns. They find that polarized teams with balanced ideological diversity produce higher-quality articles than homogeneous teams, with especially strong effects in political articles. Talk-page analysis suggests polarized teams engage in longer, more constructive, substantively focused but linguistically diverse debates, pointing to institutional design principles to harness polarization productively.

9. Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery
Andrey Rzhetsky; Jacob G. Foster; Ian T. Foster; James A. Evans PNAS 112(47):14569-14574 (2015) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26554009/

Abstract. A scientist's choice of research problem affects personal career trajectories, and aggregated choices affect the efficiency of discovery. The authors infer preferences shaping problem selection from patterns of published findings and represent problems as links between scientific entities in a knowledge network. A generative model suggests scientists tend to make conservative choices around important molecules, becoming more conservative over time. This strategy is efficient for initial network exploration and individual careers but inefficient for science as a whole. Simulation experiments suggest increased risk-taking and publishing failures could substantially improve discovery speed, motivating institutional shifts in funding, evaluation, and publication.

10. Flat teams drive scientific innovation
Fengli Xu; Lingfei Wu; James Evans PNAS 119(23):e2200927119 (2022) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35658076/

Abstract. With teams growing across research, the authors examine how team structure relates to the character of knowledge produced. Using 89,575 contribution statements, they identify leadership versus support roles and define a team's 'L ratio' (leaders to total size), extrapolated to millions of papers. Relative to flat teams, tall hierarchical teams produce less novelty and more development of existing ideas, increase productivity for those on top and decrease it for those beneath, and trade short-term citation gains for reduced long-term influence. Within-person comparisons suggest the same researcher is more likely to produce disruptive innovation in flatter, high-L-ratio teams.

11. Slowed canonical progress in large fields of science
Johan S. G. Chu; James A. Evans PNAS 118(41):e2021636118 (2021) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34607941/

Abstract. As the number of papers published each year increases, it is unclear whether knowledge advances proportionally. The authors argue that too many papers can lead to stagnation by depriving reviewers and readers of cognitive slack and preventing accumulation of attention on promising ideas. Using data consistent with these predictions, they show that in large fields citations concentrate on already well-cited papers, canonical lists ossify, new papers rarely become highly cited, and newly published papers are less likely to disrupt existing work. They call for policy measures that shift how scientific work is produced, disseminated, consumed, and rewarded.

12. The high-dimensional space of human diseases built from diagnosis records and mapped to genetic loci
(Multiple authors including James Evans and Andrey Rzhetsky) Nature Computational Science 3, 403-417 (2023) - Published 27 Apr 2023 https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-023-00453-y

Abstract. Human diseases are often studied as independent entities, limiting understanding of illnesses as dependent states in a complex system. Using time-stamped clinical records from over 151 million Americans, the authors represent diseases as points in a continuous high-dimensional space where similar diseases are nearby. They then use the UK Biobank to perform GWAS on traits corresponding to positions in disease space, discovering genetic associations that can be used to predict morbidities across disease constellations.

13. Human languages with greater information density have higher communication speed but lower conversation breadth Pedro Aceves; James A. Evans Nature Human Behaviour 8, 644-656 (2024) - Published 16 Feb 2024 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-024-01815-w

Abstract. Across ~1,000 languages, the authors measure how densely languages encode information into words and show broad variation. Language information density is associated with a denser configuration of semantic information. Denser languages tend toward faster communication but conceptually narrower conversations in which topics are discussed at greater depth, indicating that language structure shapes human engagement with consequences across levels of society.

14. Health ROI as a measure of misalignment of biomedical needs and resources Lixia Yao; Ying Li; Soumitra Ghosh; James A. Evans; Andrey Rzhetsky Nature Biotechnology 33, 807-811 (2015) - Published 07 Aug 2015 https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.3276

Abstract. With growing biomedical needs and finite resources, the authors propose a health research opportunity index (health ROI) to measure misalignment of biomedical needs and research attention. They liken investment in understanding disease and discovering remedies to trades in a financial market, where research attention and funding act like subjective prices, and argue health ROI can identify conditions where greater returns on health research might be achieved.

15. In Silico Sociology: Forecasting COVID-19 Polarization with Large Language Models Austin C. Kozlowski; Hyunku Kwon; James A. Evans arXiv (2024) - arXiv:2407.11190 https://ar5iv.org/abs/2407.11190
Abstract. By training deep neural networks on massive archives of digitized text, large language models (LLMs) learn complex linguistic patterns that constitute discourses. The authors argue LLMs

can enable sociological inquiry by simulating respondents from specific contexts. Using an LLM trained on texts through 2019, they simulate American liberals' and conservatives' responses to pandemic questions and find simulated respondents reproduce observed partisan differences in 84% of cases. Justifications suggest partisan gaps correspond to differing appeals to freedom, safety, and institutional trust, implying COVID-19 politicization was largely consistent with prior ideological landscape.

16. Issue alignment and partisanship in the American public: Revisiting the 'partisans without constraint' thesis Austin C. Kozlowski; James P. Murphy Social Science Research 94, 102498 (2021) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0049089X2030096X

Abstract. Prior studies suggested Americans sorted into partisan camps while remaining largely non-ideological. Using American National Election Studies issues, the authors find rapid growth in correlations between political attitudes from 2004 to 2016, especially in economic and civil rights domains. They also find accelerated growth in the association between partisanship and issue attitudes, portraying the electorate as not only highly partisan but increasingly ideologically organized.

17. Are economists overconfident? Ideology and uncertainty in expert opinion Austin C. Kozlowski; Tod S. Van Gunten British Journal of Sociology 74(3):476-500 (2023) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36792913/

Abstract. Economics often advises policymakers and is seen as a high-consensus discipline, but professional opinions are divided by ideological commitments. Using data from the IGM Economic Experts Panel (51 economists at seven elite U.S. universities), the authors examine how ideological commitments relate to certainty in expert opinions. Economists with ideologically patterned views report higher certainty than less ideologically consistent peers, but mainly on topics closely related to the free market versus interventionism divide.

18. Shifting power asymmetries in scientific teams reveal China's rising leadership in global science Renli Wu; Christopher Esposito; James Evans PNAS 122(44):e2414893122 (2025) - Epub 28 Oct 2025 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41150718/

Abstract. China's emergence as a top producer of high-quality science raises questions about its trajectory toward leadership. The authors introduce a framework to assess shifting power dynamics in international collaborations by tracking leadership positions in teams. Using nearly 6 million publications, they document a shift in team leadership from Western countries to China; in U.S.-China collaborations, the share of leaders affiliated with Chinese institutions rose from 30% (2010) to 45%

(2023). They forecast parity timelines across critical technology areas and consider effects of U.S.-China decoupling and China's investments in training scientists via the Belt and Road Initiative.

Overview

The Chicago Center for Computational Social Science (C3S2), informally known as “the Cube” (i.e., C3) arises from an intellectual imperative at the heart of the University of Chicago’s mission: to ensure that even as computation and artificial intelligence (AI) become central to society, the social sciences remain equally central to understanding and shaping the computational age. Computational social science (CSS) has been emerging as its own field, with its own degree programs and conferences. We are leaving the era where CSS is essentially data science for the social sciences, and entering a new era where a lot of traditional methodological work is trivially automated, and AI is rapidly making inroads into higher-level cognitive parts of science like project design.

What distinguishes C3S2 is its dual commitment to using computation to understand society and to examine computation as a social phenomenon in its own right. Thus, the Center situates computation as both an analytic and a reflexive enterprise. This dual orientation differentiates it from technical institutes that prioritize an engineering perspective. Its research spans the investigation of artificial intelligence in economic systems, including innovation, market dynamics, and regulatory policy; the use of computational approaches to human development, education, and cognition; the study of social networks and collective behavior, from polarization

and coordination to diffusion and mobilization; the development of scalable methods for causal inference across large and heterogeneous datasets; the analysis of human-AI collaboration and creativity; and the normative and institutional study of algorithmic governance and ethics.

More and more, AI and data-intensive methods define how knowledge is generated and used to power the world. Further, AI systems are inherently social: They are increasingly built on complex neurological and “agentic” social architectures. This opens up new opportunities to study the social basis of modern AI, such as analyzing reinforcement learning as conversations between agents — and improve these social agentic interactions by improving how agents govern each other. New AI models can surface new theories, with new forms and resolutions of data.

For the continued development of computation, and its ethical and efficient use in society, the social sciences must not simply adapt to these transformations but lead them. Social scientists need to engage computation and AI in order to explore what kinds of new data, questions and sciences emerge through this interaction. C3S2 asserts that computation, far from replacing interpretive reasoning, offers new ways to interrogate meaning, power, and human behavior; and to steer and protect them through effective policy. The Center positions UChicago as the institution where social theory and computational innovation converge to produce new insights into the systems that structure human life, intelligence, flourishing, and safety. CSS graduate students differentiate themselves from those in computer or data science through stronger computation-enabled social-science theory and rigorous experimentation, e.g., including a focus on social science in an AI-human coexistent society and a social science lens on AI.

C3S2 strategically consolidates the University’s diverse computational social science activities—integrating the MA Program in Computational Social Science (MACSS), the Computational Social Science Ph.D. certificate program, the Computational Social Science Undergraduate Minor, the educational functions of the Center for Spatial Data Science (CSDS), and the longstanding Computational Social Science Workshop. This unification creates a single intellectual and pedagogical hub that magnifies the University’s impact in this rapidly evolving domain. It also elevates these foundational assets through new synergistic activities in research (like highly visible lectures, colloquia and conferences, and annual capstone events), education (including a new CSS major, summer institutes, and AI instruction) and engagement (e.g. a unified web portal, external partnerships, shared computational resources, and shared office space). C3S2 embodies the conviction that the social sciences are indispensable for understanding how algorithms, data, and digital infrastructures interface with societies and that rigorous and critical social science inquiry must remain central to any computational revolution.

2
Mission and Intellectual Vision
Mission. C3S2 has a dual commitment of advancing the social sciences through computational reasoning, data-intensive research, and methodological innovation – while exploring computation and AI as social phenomena in their own right. Rooted in UChicago’s tradition of critical, theory-driven inquiry, the Center has the following three arms:
Research: Catalyzes cross-disciplinary research that unites computational and

quantitative methods with theoretical and interpretative work.
Education: Equips students (UGs, masters and Ph.D.) to critically engage with
computation and AI.
Engagement: Builds shared infrastructure and industrial and policy partnerships that
translate scholarship into societal opportunity and impact.

Vision. C3S2 envisions a future in which the social sciences lead rather than follow the computational revolution. It will establish the University as a premier hub for socially grounded computation—a place where technical expertise, theoretical depth, and ethical reflection converge to address the defining questions of the digital age.

C3S2 is grounded in the conviction that computation has transformed not only the methods of social inquiry but also its theoretical and ethical horizons. AI, large-scale data modeling, and simulation now make it possible to illuminate the structure of human behavior and social systems at scales previously unimaginable. And understanding human and collective intelligence at new resolutions yields novel designs for powerful AI systems. The Center insists that these tools must be mobilized in ways that preserve and deepen the interpretive and critical roles of the social sciences. Computation, in this vision, is not merely a technical instrument but a new form of social explanation, one that reveals both the possibilities and the constraints of human organization, belief, and decision-making in an algorithmically mediated world.

Rooted in the University’s distinctive tradition of theory-driven inquiry, C3S2 advances a mission that is at once theoretical, methodological, pedagogical, and civic. It catalyzes collaborative, cross-disciplinary research that unites computational and interpretive approaches; it equips students to use computation as a tool for explanation beyond prediction; and it builds partnerships that translate scholarship into societal impact.
Strategic Imperative

The establishment of C3S2 marks a pivotal moment for the social sciences, one that echoes, yet surpasses, the quantitative revolution in the twentieth century. Today, as artificial intelligence and data-driven modeling redefine the boundaries of knowledge, it is the social sciences that
3
must illuminate the human meanings, ethical stakes, and societal implications of these computational advances. The University of Chicago is uniquely positioned to lead this transformation.

For instance, in psychology, Wilma Bainbridge’s lab has created an AI model that can predict people’s memories, such as what artwork people will remember at a museum, and what photos will go viral. She also published a textbook on big data and psychological science that illustrates crossing boundaries between big data and AI. Xuechunzi Bai applies computational cognitive models and machine learning to understand how individual decision processes can lead to the emergence and persistence of social stereotypes. Howard Nusbaum’s lab is developing an avatar of a Catholic priest up for sainthood based on generative AI and thousands of his writings. In economics, Greg Kaplan develops large-scale computational methods to solve heterogeneous-agent macroeconomic models, linking micro-level behavior to aggregate outcomes. In political science, Molly Offer-Westort’s research integrated machine learning methods with experimental design to answer causal social questions about how people change their views and attitudes online. In sociology, Bernard Koch explores how the system of benchmarks that has catalyzed past growth in AI and computer science risks slowing future advance. These are only a few of many examples of computational social science work being conducted across the University of Chicago.

C3S2 harnesses the intellectual depth and methodological diversity of its scholars to build an interdisciplinary community where theorists, empiricists, and data scientists collaborate to interrogate how algorithms shape and reflect human life. In doing so, the Center consolidates the University’s existing strengths into a coherent, faculty-driven framework that amplifies inquiry, fosters innovation, and reinforces the social sciences as the interpretive core of the computational age—an arena in which Chicago’s rigor and integrative vision have no peer.

Activities: Research, Education & Engagement
To advance this work, C3S2 will sustain an ambitious program of scholarly, pedagogical, and institutional activity that integrates existing foundational assets with new synergistic activities summarized in Figure 1 and described in this section.
4
Figure 1. Existing Foundational Assets and New Synergistic Activities of C3S2
Foundational Assets

C3S2 builds on a substantial platform the Division already operates at scale. The MACSS program, which now exceeds one hundred students, anchors the graduate pipeline and provides a proven structure for research practice and placement that a center can amplify through shared advising, workshops, and external partnerships. The undergraduate minor extends this pipeline and gives students an earlier on-ramp into computation-forward social science as well as a clear ladder into MACSS and doctoral study.

The Center also crystallizes a growing faculty community working across Economics, Psychology, Sociology, Political Science, Comparative Human Development, Booth, Harris, and more—reducing duplication and making collaborations easier to discover. The Center also works closely with Social Sciences Computing Services and the RCC to coordinate high-performance computing needs and data security infrastructure.

Pedagogically, C3S2 embodies the principle that computation should deepen rather than displace social science inquiry. The Center’s integrated curriculum links undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral training through scaffolded coursework, research assistantships, and experiential learning.
5

Finally, C3S2 is situated to connect Social Sciences with Computer Science and the Data Science Institute through co-teaching, joint advising, and collaborative methods development in areas such as causal ML, interpretability, and secure data engineering. Faculty are already active within university-funded AI research pillars; the Center provides the social-science backbone that threads these efforts together.
New Synergistic Activities

A new series of workshops and masterclasses will encourage collaborative innovation, supporting the acquisition of novel datasets, research assistance, and cloud-based computation. These programs are designed to foster both methodological advancement and conceptual depth, culminating in publications, public symposia, and grant proposals to the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health, Department of Defense and major philanthropic foundations. Annual conferences and public events will showcase results while positioning the University as an international leader in computational social science.

Enhancing Visibility and Community. C3S2 will serve as a single, highly visible hub for people, projects, courses, datasets, and industry/civic partnerships. A unified brand and new web portal will reduce search friction for collaborators and students, while a coordinated events calendar, newsletter, and working-paper series elevate UChicago’s profile in computational social science. This approach complements the Center’s consolidation strategy and early emphasis on launching unified communications.

Fostering Research Innovation. The Center will run a continuous program of new workshops, masterclasses, and panels that bring together methods innovators and domain experts. Fundraising by the new Executive Director of C3S2 will enable financial support for direct research costs of new collaborations that supplement existing university investments (e.g., focused on RAships for Masters students and AI credits). Annual capstone activities will showcase the research results and feed directly into external proposals to NSF, NIH, DoD/DoE, and private foundations.

Problem-First Workshop Model. A central pillar of C3S2’s intellectual culture will be its problem-first workshop model, inspired by the collaborative ethos of the Santa Fe Institute. Each workshop will convene faculty and students around a specific social problem, such as misinformation, AI and labor, or climate migration, and sustains engagement over multiple quarters or years. Weekly meetings will serve as forums for collective critique and synthesis, while intersession work will focus on co-mentored projects, methodological clinics, and data sprints. Students will learn new ways to use AI for research, such as technical foundations of LLMs at an intuitive level, skillful prompting to augment theorization without ceding autonomy,

new ways to use LLMs in supervised learning, the resurgence of agent based modeling, mechanistic interpretability, and experiments on LLMs to both understand their behavior and human behavior. These series will culminate in public-facing outcomes including open datasets, articles, books, policy demonstrations, and teaching cases, ensuring that scholarship will remain both rigorous and accessible. Through this model, C3S2 will bind together training and research, fostering a culture of shared inquiry that will transcend disciplinary boundaries.

Providing Intellectual Leadership for Pedagogy. C3S2 will align and grow pedagogical programs across the pipeline: It will launch a new undergraduate major in Computational Social Science and become the new home of the GIScience Minor; it will strengthen the MACSS program through the addition of thematic tracks and capstone partnerships; and it will extend the SISRM program and inaugurate a Summer Institute that brings external participants to campus, providing a platform for both pedagogical and public engagement. This work deepens existing collaborations (e.g., KnowledgeLab; MACSS–CSDS initiatives) and ensures that curricular innovation keeps pace with research.

C3S2 will continue to coordinate cross-listing, scheduling, skills credentials, and research assistantships so that the undergraduate pathway feeds seamlessly into advanced training. The doctoral certificate in Computational Social Science will formalize advanced training for PhD students across departments, with greater integration between methods sequences, field seminars, and practicum experiences with center funding and mentorship. We plan to expand the certificate program with the launch of the Center.

Expanding Research Engagement Beyond the Academy. C3S2 will structure sponsored research and data sharing with industry, government, and nonprofit partners through standard MOUs that protect academic freedom, define publication windows, and clarify IP and data rights. Fellows-in-residence and co-developed field projects will translate methods advances into policy experiments, product evaluations, and platform audits, activities that will also serve as practica and thesis pipelines for students. These engagements extend the Center’s industry partnership program concept into a durable portfolio of sponsored projects.

Serving as an Expertise Hub for Partnerships and Research Infrastructure. The Center will advise Social Science Division and campus leadership on infrastructure investments and management, including compute access (HPC/GPU), cloud cost optimization, and secure enclaves; standardize data-use and privacy agreements; and support reproducible workflows with versioned data and DOIs for code and datasets. Close coordination with SSCS and campus computing partners will shorten time-to-compute and time-to-data, enabling higher-throughput sponsored research and faster translation from idea to result.

7
Leadership and Administration
Governance and Leadership

Governance at C3S2 reflects the University’s commitment to transparency and faculty self-direction. The Center is led by a Director or Co-Directors serving renewable three-year terms, supported by Associate Directors representing core departments. An Executive Director is responsible for running C3S2’s operations. An Executive Committee provides strategic oversight and approves annual priorities, while an External Advisory Board composed of leading scholars and industry experts guides partnerships and philanthropy. Every three years, an Evaluation Committee of core affiliates reviews leadership performance, assessing progress on strategic goals, fundraising, and program outcomes. This governance structure ensures accountability, faculty participation, and continuity of vision.
Figure 2. Examples of Departments, Centers and Labs Engaged in CSS Research

The Center’s leadership includes James Evans, Professor of Sociology and Director of Knowledge Lab, and Marc Berman, Professor of Psychology and Director of the Environmental Neuroscience Lab, serving as Faculty Co-Directors. They are supported by an Executive Committee drawn from Economics, Psychology, Sociology, Political Science, and Anthropology, and by an extensive network of core faculty affiliates whose expertise spans the social sciences, computer science, and data science. Their collective work exemplifies the intellectual breadth and collaborative potential that C3S2 is designed to sustain. See Appendix for details.

Pedagogical Oversight
Faculty leadership provides the intellectual anchor for C3S2’s pedagogical mission, ensuring that the Center’s teaching and training programs embody the distinctive values of the social sciences
8

at the University of Chicago. Their role is to guide the development of curricula and learning experiences that link computational innovation to the theoretical, interpretive, and ethical traditions of the disciplines. Through this faculty-led direction, C3S2 integrates instruction, from undergraduate coursework and graduate methods training to collaborative research labs and professional development, while maintaining coherence and rigor across programs.

The guiding philosophy of C3S2’s pedagogy is that computation should deepen, not replace, social science inquiry. Faculty oversight ensures that students learn to connect technical skills with questions of meaning, power, and human behavior. Courses and workshops emphasize theory-driven methods, ethical reflection, and experiential learning that connect classroom instruction to real-world research challenges. In this way, faculty leadership sustains C3S2’s commitment to producing researchers rather than technicians, advancing a model of computational social science that is analytically sophisticated, conceptually rich, and socially engaged.
Facilities and Physical Infrastructure

The Center’s physical home is proposed for the East Wing of 1155 East 60th Street, where it will join complementary programs such as Knowledge Lab, the Center for Spatial Data Science, and MACSS. The space will include flexible teaching labs, seminar and collaboration rooms, and a secure enclave for projects requiring controlled data environments. Co-location will promote informal exchange, interdisciplinary collaboration, and a visible identity for the Center’s cross-campus mission.
Financial Model and Sustainability

Financial sustainability is central to the Center’s design. By consolidating overlapping units, C3S2 achieves efficiency gains that reduce administrative overhead while expanding capacity. A portion of MACSS revenue, combined with external grants, and philanthropic gifts will provide a diversified base of support. Additional income streams will include sponsored research, industry partnerships, summer program fees, and indirect cost recovery from major awards. The goal is to achieve financial self-sufficiency within five years through a combination of tuition flows, external sponsorships, and endowment returns.

Implementation and Phased Growth
Implementation will proceed in three stages (Figure 3). The first year will establish governance, consolidate programs, host the Advanced Topics in AI Summer Institute for CSS (funded by the existing APTO NSF award), and finalize the space plan. The second year will launch the undergraduate major and extended SISRM Summer Institute, and formalize the partnership
9

program with industry and civic organizations. By the third year, the Center will operate at full capacity, with sustained funding, recurring events, and measurable gains in publication output, external awards, and visibility.

Conclusion

The Chicago Center for Computational Social Science represents a transformative opportunity for the University of Chicago. By unifying existing strengths under coherent leadership, it simplifies the institutional landscape while amplifying intellectual reach. The Center reaffirms the University’s role as a pioneer in theory-driven, ethically engaged computation—one that produces not only new knowledge about society but also new ways of imagining what social science can be in the computational age.

Submitted Proposals
Can AI Do Science? Wilma Bainbridge, Akram Bakkour, Yuan Chang Leong, Monica Rosenberg

Large language models (LLMs) could serve as groundbreaking contributors to scientific discovery—especially in fields such as psychology, where new data can be collected in fully digital closed loops via crowd-sourcing platforms. Here, we will test the degree to which artificial intelligence (AI) can generate end-to-end scientific discoveries, from hypothesis formation through data collection and interpretation (Aim 1), and then
2

examine what types of discoveries occur when a team of AIs work together to create a miniature “laboratory” conducting a sequence of science experiments (Aim 2).
Explainable AI through Modularity (XAIM): AI Reviewers to Vet AI-Driven Labs Marc Berman, Hank Hoffmann, and Alfred Chao

We propose an approach we call explainable AI through modularity, or XAIM as a research area. XAIM systems will have interpretability built into the system from model creation, which differs from other explainable AI or XAI approaches where interpretability is added posthoc after models have been built. XAIM systems will have known features that will be combined together to make predictions, and if those features are objective, they can be determined by a black-box model. Therefore, the XAIM approach combines aspects of feature engineering with select uninterpretable black-box components for known objective features. Because users and the system itself will know what features are being used, the model will be able to reason about its own behavior and report to users how and why it made its decisions. We specifically propose to use our XAIM approach and apply it to AI-driven or assisted hypothesis generation and automated experimentation.
Enhancing AI Scientists with Automated Research Platforms Chenhao Tan (computer science), Ari Holtzman (computer science), Austin Kozlowski (sociology), Xiaoyan Bai (computer science).

This project seeks to make large language models (LLMs) more capable scientific thinkers—able to generate creative hypotheses, critique ideas, and collaborate productively with humans in networks. Building on two prototype systems, Hypogenic AI for hypothesis generation and AutoInterp Framework for automated research pipelines, we aim to enhance AI’s creativity, diversity, and reasoning to accelerate real scientific discovery.
Harnessing the Economic Power of AI Forecasting: A Case Study through Prophet Arena James Evans, Alec Sun, Jibang Wu, Haifeng Xu

In a recent project [Yang et al., 2025], our lab introduced Prophet Arena, a systematic benchmark platform designed to evaluate frontier large language models (LLMs) on their ability to process real-time Internet data and forecast outcomes of real-world events drawn from the Kalshi prediction market. Prophet Arena has been well-received by both the academic community and the general public, recognized as a meaningful proxy for general intelligence—one that cannot be easily overfitted through training-data contamination. Through this platform, we have begun to systematically characterize the strengths and limitations of AI forecasting. While LLMs exhibit matured capabilities in certain procedures of forecasting, a key open question remains largely unexplored: how can we harness the economic value of AI forecasts? In other words, given both the AI’s prediction and the market consensus, how should one optimally place bets to maximize

3
returns while accounting for uncertainty and risk? This proposal aims to bridge the gap between forecasting and economic decision-making by developing a principled framework that translates AI forecasts into profitable trading strategies. By combining theoretical modeling with empirical back-testing on Prophet Arena data, we seek to uncover both the optimal aggregation of AI and market beliefs and the deeper behavioral models that govern how AI systems reason about future events.
Absence Blindness in LLMs: Understanding what LLMs don’t see and why Ari Holtzman (Computer Science), Chenhao Tan (Computer Science)

Large language models systematically fail at detecting conspicuously missing information, achieving only 35-70% accuracy on our AbsenceBench despite near-perfect performance finding present information. This "absence blindness" represents a fundamental socio-cognitive limitation—in human interaction, what is not said carries as much meaning as what is articulated. We investigate whether this stems from architectural constraints of Transformer attention (which requires tokens to attend to) or from trainable biases. Through automated test generation, mechanistic analysis, and targeted interventions, we determine if absence detection is architecturally unsolvable or if engineering solutions exist.
Exploring Persona Space Austin Kozlowski, James Evans, Ari Holtzman

We propose a set of studies to explore the social perspectives, or “personas,” that LLMs represent and adopt. We argue that persona research has implications for model capabilities, AI safety, and social scientific applications, and we outline three relevant research directions: (i) Mapping Persona Space asks whether social personas lie within an interpretable, low-dimensional subspace in the model’s hidden layers, (ii) Cultural Configurations of Concept Space challenges the dominant hypothesis that features are encoded as fixed directions in latent space and instead proposes that feature directions are conditional on the persona specified in context, and (iii) Countering Persona Collapse explores methods to bring out the diverse perspectives encoded in LLMs during pretraining to counteract the tendency of instruction-tuned models to converge on highly uniform perspectives.
Beyond Linear Probes: Characterizing the Geometry and Topology of Knowledge Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models James Evans, Shiyang Lai, Jerry Luo, Yijing Li, Weiyi Tian

Linear probes trained on hidden representations have been shown to recover semantically meaningful directions—such as political ideology, factuality, and sentiment—implying that large language models (LLMs) may organize knowledge along single-dimensional and linear axes (Kim et al., 2025). However, such linear properties are unlikely to be universal. Recent evidence suggests that the representational spaces
4

of LLMs, while parameterized in Euclidean coordinates, exhibit inherently non-Euclidean geometries. Studies report stratified boundaries, local curvature, and complex manifold structures within language models’ embedding spaces (Robinson et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). For example, Anthropic researchers have demonstrated that Claude models construct intricate activation manifolds to solve seemingly simple counting tasks (Anthropic 2025). Such findings indicate that Euclidean assumptions may oversimplify how semantic information is encoded and organized. As a result, widely used similarity metrics—such as L-p norms and cosine distance—could systematically misrepresent the true relational structure of model knowledge. This proposal seeks to rigorously characterize the non-Euclidean geometries and topological structures that underlie LLM representations, in order to elucidate how conceptual knowledge is distributed, organized, and characterized within high-dimensional model spaces. By uncovering these structural principles, the project aims to establish a foundation for future advances in AI interpretability, representation diagnostics, and activation-level interventions.
Toward Artificial Intelligence for Human Memory Nakwon Rim, Mina Lee, Marc Berman and Yuan Chang Leong

This project examines how different forms of artificial intelligence (AI) influence human memory during complex cognitive tasks such as writing and information synthesis. As AIs increasingly support intellectual work in education, research, and professional communication, it is essential to understand how they can enhance learning and retention, as well as the conditions under which their use may impede cognitive outcomes. The proposed study will investigate how variations in AI design and usage shape memory outcomes. Participants will complete writing tasks under different AI conditions, such as adversarial AI feedback. Memory will be assessed at short- and long-term intervals to identify patterns linking AI use and memory retention. The results will advance our understanding of how AI interacts with human cognition and inform the development of AI that promotes active learning and sustained cognitive performance.
Modeling Linguistic Surprise Across Humans and AI During Narrative Understanding Ziwei Zhang, Yuan Chang Leong, Monica D. Rosenberg

Both human and artificial intelligence rely on predictions about the world to guide learning and behavior. When expectations are violated, we experience surprise—a fundamental signal that shapes attention, memory, and belief updating. Large language models (LLMs) encode word-level surprise. Humans construct event expectations by integrating multiple words, and are surprised when new events contradict these expectations. Do LLMs encode event-level surprise in a similar way to humans? This project aims to test whether LLMs can provide a computational framework to reverse-engineer how people build and update event representations, with broad implications for narrative comprehension and social communications.

5
When Does a Gesture Become a Gesture? Toward Embodied AI That Teaches Through the Body Pedro Lopes, Susan-Goldin Meadow, Yun Ho, and Marine Wang

Human gestures are powerful cognitive tools. Work by Susan Goldin-Meadow and colleagues shows that when children move their hands during learning, these movements reveal transitional knowledge, reduce cognitive load, and can produce conceptual change. Movement is therefore not only a way of expressing thought. It is a way of shaping thought. Despite this, artificial intelligences (AI)—even those that inhabit robotic bodies—rarely use movement as a mechanism for reasoning. Most AIs work externally, and textually, by completing the tasks for the users, rather than serving as a route to understanding by walking through the movements with users. This project introduces a new form of socio-cognitive AI.

Our memo. Our central claim is that a gesture promotes reasoning, when it expresses conceptual relations and reorganizes the learner’s internal representation of the problem.
Our demo. Thus, our central deliverable is to create embodied AI systems that guide learners to perform movements that encode reasoning structure.
Sensory Evolution and Robot Ethnography James Evans, Pedro Lopes, Leslie Kay, Susan Goldin-Meadow, Junsol Kim, Austin Kozlowski

In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence research, we confront a fundamental question about the nature of intelligence: how do cognitive systems develop the sensory capacities needed to perceive and reason about unexplored domains? Project SENSUS addresses this question by pioneering an approach to AI sensory development inspired by evolutionary biology, cognitive science, and social practices of scientific observation.
Theory of Robot Mind: Modeling Mind Attribution in Human-Robot Interactions Yuan Chang Leong, Ren Calabro, Sarah Sebo and Tess Flanagan

Humans excel at inferring unseen mental states–beliefs, desires, intentions–from others’ behavior, a capacity known as theory of mind (ToM). While robots do not experience hunger, desire, or other attributes typically associated with human “mind”, people routinely respond to them as though they do. For example, participants treat cheating robots with indignation (“you dirty cheater!”) and malfunctioning devices with frustration, interpreting unexpected behaviors in mentalizing terms; remarkably, they also engage brain regions associated with human mentalizing when interpreting robot actions. Current theories posit that people use themselves as a reference point to

6
understand non-human agents,6 yet two key questions remain unanswered that are essential for developing a mechanistic account of our “theory of robot mind” (ToRM).
Debiasing Humans: AI-Mediated Language Interventions in Hiring Contexts Mina Lee and Xuechunzi Bai

This project examines persistent gender bias in hiring and explores how AI writing assistants can both amplify and mitigate such bias. In contrast to traditional awareness-based interventions, we propose to test whether real-time, language-level interventions through AI suggestions in writing assistants can subtly shift people’s cognitive representation and their decisions in hiring. Building on our preliminary findings, the research will conduct three sets of large-scale experiments to generate robust empirical findings, aiming for a submission to an interdisciplinary journal by early September 2026. Our results will provide implications for AI writing assistants and human resources (HR) technologies, while raising broader questions about the balance between empowering evaluators to identify their own biases and delegating corrective actions to automated systems.
Searching Beyond the Manifold Jason Salavon, James Evans, Yangyu Wang, Yangjing Li

Generative AI systems excel at recombining existing patterns but remain confined to interpolating within manifolds defined by their training data, unable to genuinely explore beyond known territory. This limitation reflects a broader gap in understanding creativity itself: we lack frameworks for studying how novel ideas emerge through exploration rather than mere remixing. Drawing on decades of social science research showing that creativity is fundamentally socio-cognitive—shaped by networks of influence and collaborative learning—we propose a project that investigates how social structures enable or constrain movements through conceptual space. Using artistic evolution as both methodological foundation and proof of concept, we will develop AI systems that learn to navigate conceptual space the way disruptive human creative movements do: through structured social learning that ventures into novel terrain. By representing artists as generative models that learn from each other within controlled network structures, we can rigorously test how social architecture shapes exploration beyond existing manifolds, providing both theoretical frameworks and practical methodologies for organizing creative systems—whether human, artificial, or both.

Discovering Optimal Structural Forms for Collective Exploration and Exploitation Xuechunzi Bai, James Evans, Haifeng Xu
This project investigates how hierarchical structures can emerge spontaneously in multi-agent systems as an adaptive solution to the collective exploration-exploitation dilemma. Rather than imposing hierarchy from above, we examine how it arises endogenously when agents face costly communication constraints and must decide
7

whether to explore independently or follow others who have aggregated broader information. Through a three-stage research pipeline—multi-agent reinforcement learning simulations, large language model-based agents, and human behavioral experiments—we test whether uncertainty in the environment drives both the emergence of hierarchy (measured by inequality in influence) and the fluidity of its structure (measured by how often agents switch leaders). This research offers a novel mechanism for hierarchy that differs from classical theories based on dominance, prestige, or functional efficiency, grounding leadership instead in rational information aggregation under uncertainty. Practically, understanding these dynamics enables us to design the conditions under which functional structures emerge in AI collectives for distributed scientific discovery or automated resource management. More ambitiously, by identifying and engineering the unlikely conditions that produce novel hierarchical forms, we can create new forms of socio-cognitive AI that self-organize without centralized control—opening pathways to fundamentally new modes of productive social and machine organization.

Vision

When we ask whether artificial intelligence will surpass human capabilities, we are asking the wrong question. Intelligence isn’t a ladder with humans perched somewhere between rocks and superintelligence—it’s a vast, multidimensional landscape where slime molds solve network problems we cannot, ant colonies exhibit distributed cognition beyond our grasp, and bats navigate through echolocation in ways our minds cannot fully comprehend. At the University of Chicago, we are pioneering a radical new approach to AI that places social and cognitive dimensions at its core. Rather than racing to automate human tasks or chase the phantom of “artificial general intelligence” or “superintelligence” we’re discovering entirely new forms of socio-cognitive AI—systems that don’t just process information but engage in genuine collective thinking, social reasoning, and collaborative discovery with humans. This initiative transforms UChicago’s century-old “life of the mind” tradition into a bold new vision: creating AI that participates in the social and cognitive fabric of human knowledge creation.

What makes this vision both urgent and uniquely achievable at UChicago is our distinctive intellectual DNA—the capacity to develop foundational theory that reshapes entire fields while maintaining deep commitment to understanding the social dimensions of knowledge. By uniting scholars from computer science, neuroscience, philosophy, psychology, sociology, and beyond, we are not just building AI as a tool, but discovering it as a new kind of social and cognitive partner in human endeavors. Our approach is both analytical and constructive: we’ll build “abduction machines” that collaborate with scientists to generate surprising hypotheses, design human-AI collectives that form emergent cognitive systems transcending individual capabilities, and develop AI that can sense social tension, navigate ethical ambiguity, and participate meaningfully in human institutions from classrooms to boardrooms. We are creating a “social and behavioral science of the artificial”—using AI as both subject and collaborator to understand cognition and society at previously impossible scales. This is not about making AI more human-like; it’s about discovering new forms of socio-cognitive systems where human and artificial minds think together in ways neither could alone. Through this initiative, UChicago will establish the definitive framework for socio-cognitive AI, ensuring that as these systems proliferate globally, they enhance rather than homogenize human thought, preserve cognitive diversity, and open entirely new frontiers for collaborative intelligence.
Executive Summary

New technologies have always enhanced and complemented human capabilities. Large language models are not unique in this sense, but the way they complement our strengths is qualitatively different from other tools. Trained on vast corpora of human communication, these systems have internalized patterns of conversation, reasoning, and meaning-making that reflect our social and cultural life. While much of the AI field focuses on benchmarking these models against tests of mathematical or coding ability, their distinctive strength lies elsewhere: in their capacity to represent and navigate diverse social perspectives and modes of thought. This insight motivates two complementary research directions. First, we must understand how AI

2
systems represent and adopt human perspectives, mapping the cognitive and cultural landscapes encoded within them. Second, we can leverage these socio-cognitive capacities for a particularly demanding testbed: automated scientific discovery, which requires creativity, critical reasoning, and collaboration.

This initiative will advance several projects examining how LLMs encode and express social viewpoints. One line of work maps the "persona space" within models, asking whether social perspectives occupy interpretable regions in the model's internal representations, and whether the meaning of concepts shifts depending on the persona a model adopts. Related work examines the geometry and topology of knowledge representation itself, moving beyond simple linear probes to characterize the complex manifold structures through which models organize semantic information. Another project targets a fundamental limitation: "absence blindness," or the systematic failure of models to detect what is conspicuously missing from a text—a socio-cognitive skill essential to human communication, where what remains unsaid often carries as much meaning as what is articulated. Together, these investigations aim to reveal both the capabilities and blind spots in how AI systems model human thought. A complementary project examines the reverse direction—how AI systems shape human cognition, particularly memory, during collaborative intellectual tasks like writing.

A second cluster of projects explores whether AI systems can be imbued with the perspective-taking, creativity, and reasoning required for scientific discovery. One project tests whether AI can generate end-to-end scientific contributions, from hypothesis formation through data collection to interpretation, and examines what emerges when multiple AI agents collaborate as a miniature research laboratory. A second project develops automated research platforms that enhance LLMs' capacity for creative hypothesis generation and productive critique, aiming to make AI a genuine intellectual partner in discovery. A third project focuses on forecasting, developing frameworks to translate AI predictions into actionable decisions under uncertainty. Cutting across these efforts is work on explainable AI through modularity, which builds interpretability into AI systems from the ground up, a critical requirement if AI-driven science is to be trustworthy and verifiable. These projects collectively push toward AI systems that can participate meaningfully in the scientific enterprise, and foregrounds the necessity of diverse perspective-taking in the social production of knowledge.

A.	Personal Statement

I am a sociologist and computational scientist whose research focuses on the emergence of social and natural science knowledge. I use Big Data techniques applied to the analysis of text, images, networks, demographic information, and other structured and unstructured data types to understand how social, biomedical and physical knowledge is produced and how the system of knowledge production could be improved and optimized. My recent career has built training institutions and environments that coach students through not only the process of learning new and emerging computational methods, but using them persuasively to influence social science and scholarship. I conceived of and founded the first computational social science Masters Degree of its kind. I routinely mentor students personally to explore, use and defend these methods at the PhD, Masters and Undergraduate levels. I also have experience mentoring former graduate students and postdocs who have finished their PhDs and begin their academic or industry careers. I help to grow the mentoring relationship into a long-lasting partnership that will serve students with advice and grants well into the future. Because my lab collaborates actively with researchers in technology, search and media companies (for data), as also science funding agencies including the NIH, where I am a special volunteer, NSF, and funding agencies in Asia and Europe, my students obtain exposure to other career pathways in addition to academia. In the last 15 years, I have created a research program focused on Computational Social Science that focuses on understanding how to use emerging techniques and precisely designed institutions to improve discovery, invention and innovation. Our work is routinely featured in top publishing outlets including Nature, Science, and PNAS. Upon graduation many of my recent students have taken up academic positions at institutions including UCLA, Harvard, University of Michigan, University of Pittsburgh, McGill University, etc.; and also private companies including Facebook, Amazon and LinkedIn, all of which are adding computational social science initiatives. I have also mentored international students and collaborators and have been awarded grants from the NIH, NSF, DOD, numerous philanthropies (e.g., Templeton, Sloan), and companies (e.g., IBM, Amazon, Facebook), and awards from both disciplinary and multidisciplinary bodies.

C.	Contributions to Science
1. Next generation computational methods. More of the medical and social world live within large text data than ever before, from collective activity on the web, social media, and instant messaging to online transactions, government intelligence, and digitized libraries. This supply of text has elicited demand for natural language processing and machine learning tools to filter, search, and translate text into valuable data. These papers survey and advance some of the most exciting computational approaches to text analysis and related unstructured data, highlighting both supervised methods that extend old theories to new data and unsupervised techniques that discover hidden regularities worth theorizing. We highlight biomedical and social questions for which these advances offer powerful new insight.

2. Drivers of societal innovation.  One of the most universal trends in science and technology today is the growth of large teams in all areas, as solitary researchers and small teams diminish in prevalence. Increases in team size have been attributed to the specialization of scientific activities, improvements in communication technology or the complexity of modern problems that require interdisciplinary solutions. This shift in team size raises the question of whether and how the character of the science and technology produced by large teams differs from that of small teams. In a recent cover article in Nature, we analyze more than 65 million papers, patents and software products that span the period 1954–2014, and demonstrate that across this period smaller teams have tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas and opportunities, whereas larger teams have tended to develop existing ones. In other papers published in high impact outlets we explore the impact of research disciplines, industry and nonprofit collaboration, and the Internet and its influence on the unfolding process of scientific advance and biomedical innovation.

3. Skills and Innovation. Rapid research progress in science and technology (S&T) and continuously shifting workforce needs exert pressure on each other and on the educational and training systems that link them. Higher education institutions aim to equip new generations of students with relevant biomedical skills and expertise relevant to health care needs for decades to come, but their offerings sometimes misalign with commercial needs and new techniques forged at the frontiers of research. Here, we analyze and visualize the dynamic skill (mis-)alignment between academic push, industry pull, and educational offerings, paying special attention to the rapidly emerging areas of data science and data engineering (DS/DE). In an increasingly data-driven economy, the demand for “soft” social skills, like teamwork and communication, increase with greater demand for “hard” technical skills and tools. We have also explore the role of contractors and their skills in innovation contexts.

4. Science of Social and Natural Science

The science of science (SciSci) is based on a transdisciplinary approach that uses large data sets to study the mechanisms underlying the doing of science—from the choice of a research problem to career trajectories and progress within a field. With these publications, I actively forward a research program to understand and amplify the precursors of impactful science. The increasing availability of digital data on scholarly inputs and outputs—from research funding, productivity, and collaboration to paper citations and scientist mobility—offers unprecedented opportunities to explore the structure and evolution of science. The science of science (SciSci) offers a quantitative understanding of the interactions among scientific agents across diverse geographic and temporal scales: It provides insights into the conditions underlying creativity and the genesis of scientific discovery, with the ultimate goal of developing tools and policies that have the potential to accelerate science. A.	Personal Statement
I am a sociologist and computational scientist whose research focuses on the emergence of social and natural science knowledge. I use Big Data techniques applied to the analysis of text, images, networks, demographic information, and other structured and unstructured data types to understand how social, biomedical and physical knowledge is produced and how the system of knowledge production could be improved and optimized. My recent career has built training institutions and environments that coach students through not only the process of learning new and emerging computational methods, but using them persuasively to influence social science and scholarship. I conceived of and founded the first computational social science Masters Degree of its kind. I routinely mentor students personally to explore, use and defend these methods at the PhD, Masters and Undergraduate levels. I also have experience mentoring former graduate students and postdocs who have finished their PhDs and begin their academic or industry careers. I help to grow the mentoring relationship into a long-lasting partnership that will serve students with advice and grants well into the future. Because my lab collaborates actively with researchers in technology, search and media companies (for data), as also science funding agencies including the NIH, where I am a special volunteer, NSF, and funding agencies in Asia and Europe, my students obtain exposure to other career pathways in addition to academia. In the last 15 years, I have created a research program focused on Computational Social Science that focuses on understanding how to use emerging techniques and precisely designed institutions to improve discovery, invention and innovation. Our work is routinely featured in top publishing outlets including Nature, Science, and PNAS. Upon graduation many of my recent students have taken up academic positions at institutions including UCLA, Harvard, University of Michigan, University of Pittsburgh, McGill University, etc.; and also private companies including Facebook, Amazon and LinkedIn, all of which are adding computational social science initiatives. C.	Contributions to Science
1. Next generation computational methods. More of the medical and social world live within large text data than ever before, from collective activity on the web, social media, and instant messaging to online transactions, government intelligence, and digitized libraries. This supply of text has elicited demand for natural language processing and machine learning tools to filter, search, and translate text into valuable data. These papers survey and advance some of the most exciting computational approaches to text analysis and related unstructured data, highlighting both supervised methods that extend old theories to new data and unsupervised techniques that discover hidden regularities worth theorizing. We highlight biomedical and social questions for which these advances offer powerful new insight.

2. Drivers of societal innovation.  One of the most universal trends in science and technology today is the growth of large teams in all areas, as solitary researchers and small teams diminish in prevalence. Increases in team size have been attributed to the specialization of scientific activities, improvements in communication technology or the complexity of modern problems that require interdisciplinary solutions. This shift in team size raises the question of whether and how the character of the science and technology produced by large teams differs from that of small teams. In a recent cover article in Nature, we analyze more than 65 million papers, patents and software products that span the period 1954–2014, and demonstrate that across this period smaller teams have tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas and opportunities, whereas larger teams have tended to develop existing ones. In other papers published in high impact outlets we explore the impact of research disciplines, industry and nonprofit collaboration, and the Internet and its influence on the unfolding process of scientific advance and biomedical innovation.

3. Skills and Innovation. Rapid research progress in science and technology (S&T) and continuously shifting workforce needs exert pressure on each other and on the educational and training systems that link them. Higher education institutions aim to equip new generations of students with relevant biomedical skills and expertise relevant to health care needs for decades to come, but their offerings sometimes misalign with commercial needs and new techniques forged at the frontiers of research. Here, we analyze and visualize the dynamic skill (mis-)alignment between academic push, industry pull, and educational offerings, paying special attention to the rapidly emerging areas of data science and data engineering (DS/DE). In an increasingly data-driven economy, the demand for “soft” social skills, like teamwork and communication, increase with greater demand for “hard” technical skills and tools. We have also explore the role of contractors and their skills in innovation contexts.

4. Science of Social and Natural Science

The science of science (SciSci) is based on a transdisciplinary approach that uses large data sets to study the mechanisms underlying the doing of science—from the choice of a research problem to career trajectories and progress within a field. With these publications, I actively forward a research program to understand and amplify the precursors of impactful science. The increasing availability of digital data on scholarly inputs and outputs—from research funding, productivity, and collaboration to paper citations and scientist mobility—offers unprecedented opportunities to explore the structure and evolution of science. The science of science (SciSci) offers a quantitative understanding of the interactions among scientific agents across diverse geographic and temporal scales: It provides insights into the conditions underlying creativity and the genesis of scientific discovery, with the ultimate goal of developing tools and policies that have the potential to accelerate science. This perspective frames science as a complex, self-organizing, and evolving network of scholars, projects, papers, and ideas.
