1. Introduction Over the past half-century, longstanding US dominance of the global geopolitical balance of scientific, economic, and production capabilities has shifted. China’s meteoric rise in scientific advancement and technological production, and the ascendance of new productive powers including Korea and India, have corresponded with a decline in US scientific and technological leadership, and a reduction in US industrial dynamism and labor productivity. Technological change drives economic activity, creating new jobs while making others more efficient, replacing industries in cycles of creative destruction and generating new goods and services that promote human productivity and prosperity. Technological leadership requires driving advances and setting standards that will catalyze the future of global productivity—surprising competitors and adversaries rather than being surprised by them. Understanding technological progress and global leadership is key to ensuring sustainable prosperity, security, and equity, and buffering against economic shocks. Nevertheless, little is understood about what pathways could ensure advance in US competitiveness in critical technology capacity, production, and use. Predicting Technology Outcomes” (APTO) represent a central effort to build a scientific basis for understanding the policy levers that will drive sustained US technology leadership. This effort will require improved situational awareness regarding the global techno-scientific environment, strengthened capacity to predict technological advance across that environment, and establishing causal linkages between specific policy levers of the US government and progress and leadership outcomes.

In response, we propose a project that seeks to answer the following crucial questions: how can the US effectively track and predict worldwide investment, production, position, and trajectory in science and technology (S&T)? Where are the next scientific discoveries and technological disruptions most likely to occur and how can we recognize them the moment they occur? What are the policy levers that will ensure US performance and leadership in existing and emerging categories of critical technology?
A. Overview of project

We propose to expand recent work directing the research and global and domestic situational awareness for the National Network of Critical Technology Assessment (NNCTA), a research network funded by NSF’s Technology and Innovation Partnerships (TIP) directorate, to identify and evaluate societal, national, and geostrategic challenges facing the US and investments in key technologies that could help address them. We will model and predict the global system of technological development to understand and shape national technological capabilities, production, and use. To enable holistic exploration, we will build a powerful large language model (LLM) atop precise data on global technology funding, research, intellectual property, products, and their mentions, linked by the people, regions, and organizations producing and consuming them, to dynamically account for complex and emergent interdependencies among diverse technological domains. This model will enable the prediction of performance advances within existing critical technologies and the identification of new and emerging critical technologies.

Modern LLMs rely on Google’s deep neural network transformer architecture1 to encode language, networks, and other unstructured data into powerful models that form “digital doubles” of the systems they represent. ChatGPT and other LLMs are digital doubles of the training data (human text from the internet) that can model and reproduce what humans would write given prompts. Here, we rethink this power of LLMs in two important ways. First, LLMs form high-dimensional, geometrically interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as global observatories of the systems they encode. Through these powerful macroscopes, entities (e.g., technologies, scientific concepts, researchers, companies, nations) are rendered in context to reflect precise distances between them based on complex linkages in the underlying data. Second, LLMs are generative models, and like ChatGPT, can function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of their represented system to experimental provocation (e.g., technical advances predicted to result from specific funding, educational, or organizational policies). LLMs learn latent functions capable of generating language and structure that efficiently optimize responses and predictions to language prompts based on the pre-learned contextual embeddings2. Our LLMs will also support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of funding on

B. Lines of Effort (LOEs)

Our project will enable the analysis of technology capabilities, production, and use by developing Data Sets and Tools and Technology Outcome Modeling synergistically. Our data on scientific papers, technology patents and products, their metadata, and downstream mentions will drive estimation of our S&T LLMs. Our LLMs will be constructed and fine-tuned to technological capacity, production, and use, thus understanding both the syntax and semantics of S&T documents like an expert in all relevant technological areas, similar to how GPT-4 acts as an expert on all topics well-represented in Wikipedia and web. Using our LLM, in concert with others (e.g., Open AI’s GPT-4+; AI2’s OLMo, Meta’s LLaMA and open-source, fine-turned derivatives; and we will help guide DOE’s AuroraGPT, running atop the world’s fastest computer) will improve our ability to flexibly extract and synthesize new and expanded data from structured, semi-, and unstructured information about technology advance. These datasets will facilitate further improvements in our model’s ability to curate and digest new technology-relevant data in a virtuous cycle. Because our approach to technology outcome modeling is central to our ongoing production of data sets and tools, we organize our proposal to first discuss our former, then the latter.

C. Response to Solicitation
Our proposed project will contribute directly both to the goals of the APTO program and to complementary tasks that will further accomplishment of APTO goals.
Our Technology Outcome Models, built atop powerful transformer technology, with AI2—a global

leader in natural language processing and S&T data provision—will be trained chronologically as a proper, powerful predictive model of technology outcomes. These models will simulate the results of US policy levers on techno-scientific advance, drive the development and estimation of causally-identified structural models, and enable the incorporation of policy objectives directly into our models that will optimize them through discovery of new policies.

Our Data Sets and Tools will be relevant to key technologies of interest, including artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning; high performance computing and semiconductors; quantum information S&T; robotics and automation; disaster prevention and mitigation technology; advanced communications and immersive technology; biotechnology, genomics, and synthetic biology; data storage, management, and cybersecurity; advanced energy generation and storage technologies; and advanced materials and manufacturing technologies. We will include technologies beyond the focal areas for three reasons. First, we can advance understanding about critical technology development from the historical invention and development of technologies no longer deemed critical. Second, the complex system of S&T is deeply interconnected, such that attention, incentives, and resources associated with one area influence their availability in linked areas. Finally, our approach to dynamic modeling and data generation is tuned to predict emerging technologies and immediately identify the strategic significance of unexpected new technologies, which may themselves be critical for US security and prosperity, or play a critical role in the supply of other technologies that are. We will integrate across LOEs within our project, while actively complementing the broader portfolio of research projects across the program. We plan for our research on Technology Outcome Models to leverage others’ advances under the Data Sets and Tools LOE. For example, we hope to benefit from the performance annotations and extraction produced by “Technology Outcome Modeling with SPEED: Scientific Publication and Event Extraction Data” (PI: D. 2. LOE- Technology Outcome Modeling Technology Outcome Models. Our approach links the predictive power of LLMs with structural models for causal identification. LLMs are an emerging general purpose technology, reconfiguring information search, data synthesis, and generative prediction across a wide range of areas that optimize their response to prompted text in-context by gradient descent2. We aim to unleash and validate their potential for technological advance, assessment and prediction. Our work is driven by four hypotheses that model data on technological advance as a digital double of the underlying complex systems3. Model Inputs. Our model inputs include research proposals and awards, scientific papers, technology patents, marketed product descriptions, formal and informal text (e.g., business news, social media) about technology uptake, and the rich metadata that interlink them (e.g., disambiguated researchers, funding sources and amounts, hosting universities, assignee and producing companies). We will calculate complex combinatorial features that shape both the process of and incentives for discovery, including the size, structure, and competition among teams and among firms. We will calibrate these data with technology performance information on rich samples of technology documents (e.g., papers, patents, fact- sheets, news) as annotated by our experts and in collaboration with Murdick team’s explicit extractions of facts.

Our raw document input for training LLMs will consist of selected text from the preprocessed Dolma
dataset4, a general and fully open LLM training corpus of three trillion tokens released by AI2 in 2023. For scientific text, we will use Dolma’s peS2o v2 corpus5 spanning 39 million documents and containing 42 billion tokens, which we will augment with patent data from the BigPatent dataset6.
Model Outputs. Our technology LLMs will yield three model outputs. First, LLMs natively produce

high-dimensional, geometrically interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as a global observatory of the techno-scientific system they encode. The embedding spaces we will evaluate range between 1024 and 4096 dimensions (the hidden state sizes of the LLMs we explore). We will serve this observatory through a rich set of Web applications and APIs based on the Semantic Scholar platform, through which Allen Institute for AI (AI2) receives more than 8 million distinct visitors monthly. We will also serve observatory views through easy-to-interpret dashboards of global technology leadership and advancement for each focal technology area and emerging areas, sustainably wired to these persistent APIs. Second, our LLMs are generative models that function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of their represented system to experimental provocation (e.g., technical advances predicted to result from specific policies). Our LLMs will propose and support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of funding on interlocking discoveries, overlapping supply chains, global networks of skilled labor, and industrial organizations that drive or impede international technology leadership. Specifically, we will use our generative LLMs with various “temperatures” (likelihood of picking lower-probability solutions) to produce a distribution of outcomes we will normalize as probability distributions over the likelihood of precise technology outcome related to capability, production, and use. Because LLMs are natively programmed by natural language, a capability prediction may have the following form when made to a time-stamped LLM from t=1: “A semiconductor prototype invented by person [or company] i from country j in year t+7 will have energy efficiency of [Predicted Value 0.0-1.0]” [ground truth from annotated papers/patents = .859]. A production prediction may have the following form: “On a scale from 0 to 1, my confidence that company [or country] i can deliver x chips in t+5” [ground truth from company estimates=.2]. A use prediction may have the following form: “Rank the following 5 semiconductor firms [or chips, or countries] a, b, c, d, and e, in terms of their market share in year t+6” [ground truth from the business press or online discourse = c, b,

Our LLMs will also have the capacity to produce more specific qualitative predictions, such as the emergence of new metrics of performance for a given technology, likely in response to prior success and failure, and new functions or applications to which the technology is applied. We will also use our LLMs to guide the construction of structural, causal models to make precise predictions based on mechanistic components beneath the level of language, such as the number of scientists active within a domain, the amount of resources devoted to it, and the rate of prior progress. We will incorporate most of these signals into the LLM, but structurally disentangle them for causal estimation7,8.
We are equally interested in creating models that can produce a precise and accurate surprise signal,

i.e., they are surprised at the same rate that the human techno-scientific system was surprised by actual events, and thus can immediately recognize the significance of an unexpected techno-scientific event9. This will allow our model to appreciate the disruptive implications of a new technology, achieved level of performance, or ascendant performer the moment such an unpredictable, black swan event occurs10 permitting federal funding to respond nimbly with respect to a new technological capacity. We will assess the ability of our model to anticipate surprise as expressed in its novelty claims within scientific articles, technology patents, news, and informal (e.g., web) discourse.

Accuracy Evaluation. Prediction accuracy will be tested using out-of-sample prediction based on chronologically trained models and quantified using metrics that describe the gap between predicted and actual values, such as the Wasserstein distance in terms of transport probability (i.e., how much must the probability distribution move between predicted and actual distribution of outcomes). LLMs also enable more precise qualitative predictions (e.g., the character of a future invention; the articulation of a new metric), which we will assess in terms of model perplexity. We will test our models through out-of- sample hindcasting, predicting the past from the more distant past, and also across domains, using our derived structural models to assess one technology’s advance based on the performance of another. We will also target specific historical event predictions. Finally, to avoid overfitting, we will develop a pre- registry of future predictions for ongoing evaluation against the actual, unfolding future of technological outcomes.

Benchmarks. We will develop benchmarks for technology outcome models that include extrapolation
models. We will also evaluate simpler LLMs trained across orders of magnitude of parameter densities (up to the 70B parameter model we will produce for optimal prediction) and with ablations of relevant data signals, such as the inclusion or removal of a co-authorship signal, which in our prior work has improved technology prediction by more than 100%3.

Time Scale and Horizon. Predictions and accuracy will be reported annually and by decades. Our
predictions will also be made at the level of individual and company performers. We will register predictions for the immediate future (next year), with an emphasis on 5 years into the future for hindcasts, and a focus on conditional and unconditional capability, production, and use predictions.
Granularity and Generalization. Our technology LLMs and structural models will enable precise,

flexible predictions for specific and broader classes of technologies. Our approach relies on the hypothesis that increased predictive accuracy for any key technology can be reliably improved by leveraging facts unique to that technology and facts relating to complements, substitutes, and those linked by other resource dependencies (e.g., studied by the same community or supported by the same funder). Because LLMs rely on deep context, they are less likely to generalize between technologies, but will hallucinate out-of-sample according to signals based on underlying dependencies. Our structural models that disentangle factors driving technology development will be tuned to generalize across technology areas, accounting not only for features of each technology, but the intensity of human and material resources devoted to development, and the incentives of actors engaged in that development. Prior work by PIs Evans, Akcigit, and Wang suggests that organization size, structure, and market-share dramatically influence the likelihood that a team or company will defend or threaten the status quo11–14.

LLMs, including Open AI’s GPT-4, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s BARD, are trained indiscriminately on large tranches of temporally unlabeled text, including the Common Crawl and Wikipedia. This limits their development as engines of S&T prediction by obscuring their ability to honestly predict any particular technological artifact (e.g., a patent, article, or product) from the past. B1. We will work with the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (AI2) to develop the first chronologically trained LLM to tune their ability to contextually predict past technological advances without the shadow of the future, poising them to anticipate global technological futures from the present. This work builds on AI2’s track record of creating language models for science15 and compiling and releasing new corpora for LLM training16. It will require us to predict the timestamps of textual inputs (e.g., web text) with temporally labeled research papers and news to predict each technological advance from the past with data available to researchers and producers in the immediately prior period. We will test our hypotheses by hindcasting technology events from the past using data from the more distant past9. We will analyze technological capacities and uses predicted correctly, and examine “wrong predictions” to systematically identify “gaps” that frame opportunities to rise in global technology leadership.

Recent findings lend credence to our chronological training approach. First, “curriculum training” has been shown to improve learning by sequencing data in time17. Second, neural networks tend to have a bias toward more recent training in predicting future science compared to the randomized approach. Neural networks are known to “catastrophically forget,” meaning they model more recent training data better than older training data. Because future scientific literature will tend to be distributionally more similar to recent science than science from the distant past, training chronologically should boost performance on future data. Third, recent work18 showed that training an LLM on related documents in the same context window outperformed the randomized approach. We will place excerpts of a paper’s and patent’s references, and their author’s or inventor’s prior work, in the context when training on the paper, using a notion of relatedness and subjective inference (e.g., that a particular person, institution, or country will conceive of an advance) critical for scientific and technological progress.

Nevertheless, LLM chronological training comes with challenges. First, standard learning rate schedules tend to decay learning rates gradually as training proceeds. If applied naively, this approach leads to smaller learning steps on the most recent and relevant training data. Our previous work on continued pretraining19 addressed this problem when adapting a model in a single step toward a given domain or task. We will explore a generalization of that approach for chronological training that executes multiple learning rate re-starts as the training progresses. Second, older papers often have distributional peculiarities simply because the pdf extractions are noisier, and starting training on these (in straightforward chronological training) may leave the model in a suboptimal state from which it is difficult to recover. To address this, we will explore different initialization strategies, training on a variety of background documents to seed the model properly before chronological training on scientific corpora. We will explore different model architectures with different efficiency/accuracy tradeoffs. First, to

explore the value of complete, from-scratch chronological training, we will use the 345M-parameter GPT-2 architecture20, which has a 1024-token context length and 24 layers, and produces embeddings of 1024 dimensions. We will also explore more limited chronological training in two larger models starting from pretrained checkpoints, the large Longformer Encoder-Decoder (16384 encoder/decoder context, 12 layers in encoder/decoder, 447M parameters, 1024 dimensions)21 and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in Llama2-7b (4096 context, 32 layers, 7B parameters, 4096 dimensions)22. These models’ longer context lengths allow us to explore reasoning across document boundaries and citation edges, and will we explore further context expansion via continued pretraining23. In addition to standard LM training objectives, we will train on cross-document objectives (e.g.24) and use contrastive embedding objectives we found to be critical for producing high-quality embeddings from LLMs25. When starting from pretrained checkpoints, we must only evaluate the chronological training on science that comes after the cutoff date of the initial model. Contingent on the success of the previous models, we will test our techniques on vastly larger models via collaborations with AI2’s upcoming Open Language Model (OLMo), the Trillion Parameter Consortium (TPC, which brings together groups training LLMs on HPC), the Texas Advanced Computing Center, other NSF-funded HPC facilities, and Argonne National Laboratory, which is

We will validate the second aspect of our hypothesis, i.e., that training in a holistic way across technologies improves predictions regarding performance within technologies. This will draw our work directing research in the National Network for Critical Technology Assessment (NNCTA), and our studies of China’s rising role in disruptive and prescient scientific advance, and their disproportionate presence in emerging technology areas, which manifested improved prediction by accounting for all technology fields. We will increase the precision of these models with our LLMs and evaluate the benefit of cross-domain modeling using (1) ablation studies that selectively exclude technological domains in the prediction of others, and (2) by predicting emerging technological domains that merit new consideration as critical technologies. Identification of these emerging areas will represent a policy-relevant by-product of our approach. We will also validate this hypothesis as we move from technological production to use. The diffusion of technologies unleash creative destruction whereby novel combinations of prior technologies clear the field by “destroying demand” for competing technologies 26. To anticipate these, we must be able to predictively model functional equivalence—e.g., electric vehicles supplanting gas ones. Such equivalences have historically been followed but not predicted by innovation scholars and policy: measured ex post with the diffusion of successful innovations and firms and the failure of alternative products and firms27. Our holistic, cross-technology approach should allow us to pinpoint the competition and replacement of some technologies by others for specific functions in the economy. We will validate this hypothesis by positively identifying functional equivalence through LLM-based similarities, and demonstrating improved prediction in the use of specific technologies based on rising and falling demand and discursive attention paid to other, more and less related technologies.

B2. We will build on our previous work on fine-tuning language models to learn embedding geometries useful for downstream tasks25,28–31. We showed that the language model (word2vec) trained with mobility trajectory data of people is mathematically equivalent to the optimization of the gravity law of mobility. So, we can create a model that embeds institutions into a vector space, where the locations of the institutions are optimized to reflect how researchers move among them (the more flux between two institutions, the closer they become).

We developed a method to use this training strategy in combination with LLMs. Using the data of trajectories, we can fine-tune a pre-trained LLM so that its embedding space is optimized to follow the gravity law of mobility. For instance, by using data on the sequence of papers written by individual scientists to fine-tune an LLM, we obtain a space where we can embed all sentences while being optimized to incorporate the information about how scientists (and their institutions and countries) move among topical areas. This embedding space allows us to predict future collaboration between scientists as well as the emergence of new scientific journals in the embedding space. Moreover, due to the nature of the embedding space that optimizes for the gravity law, we can estimate the “gravity potential” of each location, which roughly captures the topic’s strength of attraction. This metric is demonstrably correlated with new activities in the area and the emergence of new journals. We expect that the same will be true

regarding the emergence of new critical technologies.

The flipside of collaborating researchers facilitating flows of technological innovation is that their capacity to address novel inquiries, seize opportunities, and confront emerging challenges can be limited. In early work, we explored the degree to which a scientist departs

from their previous research trajectory in relation to a focal paper. Considering both the case study of research on COVID-19 and the broader scientific landscape, we uncovered a “pivot penalty,” characterized by a significant decline in the impact of new research as scientists deviate further from their previous body of work, suggesting a fundamental friction that governs science’s capacity to adapt 35. We employ the pivot measurement framework to investigate the adaptability of scientists as they transition toward all listed critical technological fields, from AI, high-performance computing, quantum information science, and semiconductors to energy-relevant materials, synthetic biology, and biotechnology. We seek answers to whether scientists from diverse backgrounds shift their focus toward these vital technological domains, and which fields feed such transitions. And when do pivoting strategies yield success and impact? A3. Hypothesis 3: Modeling (a) incentives to technologically innovate, (b) the structure of

technology innovation, and (c) a technology’s interlock with potential applications will improve our prediction of technology production and use. A3a. Technological progress unfolds through a process of “creative destruction” as innovative new entrepreneurs replace less productive old incumbents. Some incumbents address the resulting conflicts with productive strategies that center on innovation, leading to competitive advantage through better products or more efficient production, ultimately benefiting society. Broad and diverse participation and healthy technological competition involving more individuals, organizations, and regions that lie close within the embedding space of technological capability will predict greater increases in production efficiency, quantity and performance36. Other incumbents employ nonproductive strategies, which involve actions such as leveraging political connections37, unproductive patenting38, and anti-competitive acquisitions12, primarily aimed at impeding creative destruction and reallocating resources in favor of incumbent firms. One example of nonproductive strategy emerges from our recent study of more than 500,000 local politicians, showing that as firms become increasingly politically connected, they gain more market share and leadership but paradoxically exhibit reduced innovation in patents37.

B3a. We will link new technological advances with the research groups, firms, and incentives that follow from their competitive position to improve prediction of technology production and use. We will validate our hypothesis about diversity and competition by undertaking expert elicitation through an audit experiment that sources contracts for a broad sample of technologies from companies, incentivizing realistic estimates by imposing contractual penalties for missing supply deadlines. Through this, we will seek unbiased estimates of a company’s production potential by having a purchasing agent ask them the amount of money they would be willing to forfeit for missing their production obligations. A3b. Structures of innovation. Prominent innovation theories portray technology innovation as cumulative, where new breakthroughs build on past accomplishments, akin to Newton’s “standing on the shoulders of giants.” The development of knowledge is directly linked to a complex innovation network comprising scientists, research institutions, private sector entities, and governmental agencies, collectively driving the rate and trajectory of discoveries into technologies. Building on our prior work3,39–41, we anticipate that comprehensive examination of this network can enhance our ability to predict the journey from scientific exploration to technological advance, production, and use, but also the enduring stability, speed, and timing of knowledge dissemination across domains. This enhanced understanding will offer valuable insights for policymakers. For example, increasing reliance of growth in downstream technologies in medicine and defense on upstream research in biology and materials implies that lapses in research or subsidies for R&D in one period will have rippling repercussions in years that follow. We expect this line of reasoning will extend to regional and firm-level variations. This expanded perspective will provide policymakers with a nuanced understanding of the delayed causal impact of innovation policies on economic and business outcomes. B3b. We will link upstream research and technological capabilities with downstream production through networks induced through geographical proximity, the flux of transitioning researchers, and the assignment of intellectual property to trace causal impacts.

Data Set: People. We will use a range of sources to construct and share an open dataset of immigration and emigration among US and global technology talent. This will involve tracking the flow of international talent, using visa applications of immigrants in the US from Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Department of Labor, and the State Department, containing country of origin, occupation, and company of employment. We will couple this with data on employment- based visas (e.g., H-1B, L-1), green card applications, and J-1 and F-1 visas using FOIA requests. We will also incorporate LinkedIn data, which includes individuals’ unique identifier, name, predicted gender and ethnicity, education history, work experience, and location. We will link these with disambiguated publication and patent data from ORCID profiles. With these data, we can precisely track the cross-border, cross-company movements of technology innovators. It will also allow us to identify natural experiments to estimate the causal effect of people flows and training on progress.

Data Set: Funding. We will produce an open dataset that traces trends in funded technological
research from extracted detailed metadata on funding from awards, proposals, and article acknowledgement statements (see Figure 4). This will also draw on government grant data aggregated

from a variety of agency databases, FOIA requests, and specialized grant-tracking platforms. This rich dataset will include comprehensive details about each grant, including project abstracts, methodologies, financials, timelines, participating demographics, and final outputs. We will use our LLMs to synthesize information across the grant lifecycle, from initial calls for proposals to concluding reports. This will allow us to uncover strategic and thematic shifts in investment, correlated with technological advancement, offering a panoramic view of development dynamics across technological sectors. It will also allow us to use natural experiments for the estimation of causal effects of funding on progress.

Data Set: Concepts, Components, and Emerging Critical Technologies. We will generate an open dataset of S&T concepts and components in existing and emerging critical technology areas. These will be assembled into a directed acyclic graph that reflects the complex compositionality of research (e.g., papers and patents) and the technology products they produce. Drawing on our approach piloted in the NNCTA to predict emerging fields with LLMs trained on random walks across the hypergraph of research3, we will register an evolving list of new critical technologies, justification for their criticality (e.g., security, commerce, supply chain), and linked papers, patents, and products. Developing this dataset will involve a continuous process of extraction, disambiguation, compositional inference from context, and prediction, drawing on our LLMs. This will enable us to build LLMs atop research and technology components, rather than full-text, which we have demonstrated helps to improve discovery prediction3,9. Data Set: Products. We will develop an open dataset of technology products and their performance

properties that draws upon product fact sheets, barcode registries, and Wikipedia entries, which will enhance product descriptions and establish connections with patent filings, following51,52. These entries tend to incorporate terminology present in patent texts, offering comprehensive coverage of common product modules. Finally, we will incorporate dynamic data on technology usage from the presence and LLM-coded character of product mentions in business and popular press, the web and social media. We will validate and complement product mentions with Nielsen-Kilts scanner data housed at UChicago, obtained from retail point-of-sale systems, which will enhance our metrics or production and use. This provides comprehensive details on consumer goods (barcodes), including product attributes (e.g., formula, style, content), well-documented pricing and sales data. 4. Broader Impacts 4.1. Collaboration and Knowledge Transfer. We will provide policy makers and funding agencies with customized real-time dashboards to provide situational awareness, simulate policy impacts and discover optimal research policies. These dashboards, to be powered by AI2’s persistent application programming interfaces (APIs), which currently support over 8M unique monthly users, will link: 1) publication, patent, and product databases, 2) expert assessments of productive capacity that we will have created and synthesized, and 3) our generative models of the techno-scientific system. To maximize the relevance and impact of these dashboards, we will collaborate with the University of Illinois at Chicago’s Electronic Visualization Lab, with domain experts, and with key US government agencies, committees and directorates that support government functions including strategic planning and funding prioritization, technical horizon scanning, skilled talent availability and utilization analysis, partnership and alliance cultivation, research protection and counter-party risk analysis, and supply chain analysis. 4.2. Advancing Science and Technology. Our work will directly benefit scientific discovery and technological invention by helping to improve LLMs tuned to propose hypotheses and novel designs. Specifically, we will collaborate with the AuroraGPT project (see above) using our system as an intelligent assistant to support scientists and engineers. 4.3. Broadening Participation of Underrepresented Groups: Integrating Education & Research. We will partner with the Summer Institute in Computational Social Science (SICSS) to 1) directly broaden participation in our modeling and analysis, 2) to more deeply integrate this research with education, and 3) to share our LLMs for science materials. In contrast to computer science, social science has significantly more PhDs awarded annually (5k vs 2k) and higher participation by women (50% vs 23%) and underrepresented minorities53. SICSS successfully connects diverse early career scientists with advanced computational skills in a network of over 2,500 people from over 500 universities. Its 2-week intensive program expands access to those historically excluded, including 51% female and 18% African,

We will intentionally recruit graduate students and postdocs from this diverse network, and we will assess short and long-term impacts of this partnership with SICSS. 4.4. Education and Next Generation Workforce Development for Underrepresented Groups. We aim to broaden representation of underrepresented groups in the US S&T workforce by engaging them in the computational and statistical analysis of complex phenomena. To accomplish this, we will (1) pilot content in classes of Chicago Public Schools (CPS) high schoolers, (2) evaluate these pilots and refine the experience into instructional materials and on-line modules designed for national and global distribution, and (3) guide education policy to advocate for high school student training in the technologies that our models predict to become the most influential in the future.

1) We will partner with two UChicago-based programs to pilot new content on LLMs, advanced causal analysis, and processes of technological change and creative destruction: the College Readiness and Access Programs and Economics for Everyone (E4E). Both co-develop and serve content to hundreds of CPS high schoolers in AI, S&T, and economics. CPS high schools students are very diverse: 78% are economically disadvantaged, 36% African American, and 47% Latino. 2) We will evaluate these pilot experiences and refine content to create new modules for broader distribution with Skew the Script, a nonprofit that has dramatically increased passage rates among disadvantaged high schoolers on AP statistics and math tests nationwide; and Veritas AI, a nonprofit that extends AI technologies to middle and high school audiences. Specifically, we will add expertise about transformers, LLMs, digital doubles, and causal analysis integrated with AI prediction. 3) We will partner with Data Science for Everyone, a nonprofit engaged in education policymaking with 16+ US states to bring data science, AI, and other critical technologies to high schools. We will share our predictions of emerging technologies to strategically align opportunities for diverse youth with the future needs of the nation. 4.5. Public Engagement with Science and Technology. We will work with the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC) on a series of events that make AI less terrifying, exotic, or destabilizing for a broader public. A new UChicago/SAIC joint graduate course will explore predictions of future art and culture using models based on the LLMs guiding our research to produce provocative, public-facing art outputs. We will also host public lectures and an annual workshop on the dangers and opportunities surrounding AI prediction and society at SAIC’s McLean auditorium in downtown Chicago. Similar public events have drawn diverse audiences of 300-600 with a sizable contingent from the arts. The results of these cultural predictions and class projects will become digital exhibitions on SAIC’s high traffic website. Through quarterly Science Cafes held at the MapRoom, we will directly engage diverse audiences with forefront science, while gaining valuable insights into honing a popular narrative about APTO science. 4.6. Evaluation & Metrics We will track these efforts using a mixed methodology that combines quantitative and qualitative metrics. We will track direct usage of the research products (e.g., citations, data-set and dashboard usage), include measures of engagement (e.g., requests for customization), and results of usage (e.g., policy impacts). To evaluate the SCISS program, we will track participant statistics (numbers, demographics, fields, etc.), and administer pre, post, and follow-up surveys and focus groups to probe attitudinal changes, identify new collaborations or projects, and document research shifts. For high school programs, we will track quantitative measures including demographics, while local and longer programs will seek both formative and summative input from the students and instructors to facilitate co-design of the educational modules. We expect over the life of the project to work directly with hundreds of early career scientists and students and reach orders of magnitudes more via our partnerships.

Funding Ideas into Reality James Evans and Nadav Kunievsky January 31, 2025
1.
Introduction

Grants are widely regarded as the driving force behind scientific exploration, propelling advances in knowledge and expanding the frontiers of human understanding (e.g., Miao et al. [2023]). Among the primary funders of such exploration, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) plays a pivotal role in enabling groundbreaking research and fostering medical innovation. Studies consistently highlight the importance of NIH funding in shaping downstream research (Rosenbloom et al. [2015], Azoulay et al. [2019], Azoulay et al. [2011]) while also influencing the careers and productivity of researchers (Jacob and Lefgren [2011], Wang et al. [2019]). Together, these findings emphasize the central role of funding in advancing science and supporting the broader research ecosystem.

Despite this well-established impact, a critical question remains: Do funding agencies such as the NIH enable the exploration of entirely new ideas, or do they primarily subsidize research directions already gaining momentum in the scientific community? This distinction is crucial for understanding how science funding drives innovation and for determining how resources can be optimally allocated. In this proposal, we focus on NIH grants and propose a method to estimate whether their funding causally facilitates the publication of ideas that might not have been pursued without financial support.

Answering this question involves two major challenges. First, the outcomes of unfunded projects and ideas are difficult to observe. Specifically, it is not straightforward to link a grant application that was denied funding to subsequent research that may have independently addressed its proposal. To overcome this, we propose leveraging large language models (LLMs) to extract the core research questions and methodologies from grant proposals. These extracted elements can then be analyzed to determine whether similar questions were later addressed in published research.

Second, identifying the outcomes of ideas is not sufficient to establish the causal effect of funding. Funded ideas are likely to differ systematically from unfunded ones in terms of quality or feasibility, creating the potential for biased comparisons. To address this, we propose employing a Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD, e.g., Cattaneo and Titiunik [2022]), which takes advantage of the NIH’s scoring system and funding threshold. By focusing on proposals that score just above and just below the funding cutoff—proposals that are comparable in quality but differ in their funding status—we can more reliably isolate the causal effect of funding on the realization of ideas. This approach minimizes confounding factors and ensures that observed differences in outcomes can be attributed to the funding decision itself.

In what follows, we provide a detailed review of the data and methodology we will use in our analysis and conclude
with a discussion of the expected contributions and broader impacts of this research.
2. Data and Methodology
2.1. Methodology

Our empirical approach consists of two main steps. In the first step, we extract the main ideas from grant applications and scientific papers. In the second step, we use a Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) to identify the causal effect of approving a grant application on the outcomes and publication of the idea.

In the first step of our empirical approach, we utilize LLMs such as GPT-4o1 or LLaMA, to systematically extract specific components from grant applications (This approach has been used in other scientific setups, such as Zhang et al. [2024]). Our focus is on identifying research questions and methodologies within each proposal. This targeted extraction allows us to dissect the core elements that drive each research idea, providing a clear framework for subsequent analysis.

After extracting the research questions and methods, we aim to examine all future published papers to determine whether the research questions have been addressed and whether the methods have been used. However, analyzing the entire universe of published papers would be prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a two-step process: first, using a retrieval method to obtain a set of candidate papers, and second, employing LLMs to evaluate whether each of these retrieved papers addresses the questions posed in the grant application.

Specifically, we intend to utilize Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to identify and retrieve scientific publica- tions that are semantically aligned with the extracted research questions and methodologies from the grant proposals. RAG, as introduced by Lewis et al. [2020], combines the strengths of retrieval-based methods with generative models to enhance the relevance and accuracy of retrieved documents. By employing RAG, we can efficiently locate relevant publications that are semantically close to the research questions and methods outlined in the proposal. Next, we will use an LLM-based evaluator to assess the alignment between the grant application’s research questions and methods and the retrieved publications. This evaluator will determine whether the identified papers effectively address the research questions posed in the grants and whether they employ the same methodologies.

To ensure the validity and reliability of our methodology, we will conduct an evaluation using a subset of funded grant proposals and their corresponding publications. Funded proposals, which typically have a clear and traceable link to subsequent research outputs, provide a ground truth for assessing the accuracy of our extraction and matching processes. This evaluation will involve comparing the LLM-extracted research questions and methodologies against the content of the associated publications.

In the second step, we aim to understand the causal effect of providing funding to a research proposal. To estimate this, we build on the work of Wang et al. [2019] and others who leverage the fact that NIH funding decisions are primarily determined by thresholds and evaluation scores. This funding policy enables us to exploit the highly nonlinear relationship between funding success and evaluation scores around the funding threshold to estimate the causal effect of funding. Specifically, we compare the publication probability of ideas that scored just above and just below the threshold, thus examining proposals with similar quality ideas, where the only difference is that one received funding while the other did not. This approach allows us to isolate the causal effect of NIH funding on the realization and dissemination of ideas.

This method captures the local average treatment effect for research ideas near the funding threshold, assuming that potential outcomes changes smoothly around the cutoff and a distinct jump in funding probability at 𝑐.

2.2. Data Needed From the NIH
To evaluate whether NIH-funded projects foster the development of novel ideas, we require the following from the administrative NIH data:
Grant Application Texts: Full-text data from grant applications, including detailed descriptions of research questions, methodologies, and objectives. These texts will enable us to extract and analyze the core ideas and methods proposed in each application.

Grant Evaluation Scores: Detailed scoring data, including numeric evaluations and reviewer comments, to identify applications near the funding cutoff. These scores are critical for implementing the regression discontinuity design and estimating the causal effect of funding.
Funding Decisions: Binary indicators of whether a grant was funded or not.

Grant-Linked Publications: Records linking funded applications to subsequent scientific publications, if exists. This linkage is vital for validating our LLM model.

Additionally, we will integrate this NIH data with Clarivate’s Web of Science and PubMed: These databases will provide a comprehensive set of scientific publications to track the broader dissemination and impact of the ideas proposed in grant applications. Using these resources, we will assess whether NIH-supported research introduces novel contributions to the scientific literature.
3. Anticipated Impact

OurstudywouldevaluatetheNIH’sroleinfosteringinnovationandadvancingscientificknowledge. Thisprojectwould aim to quantify the unique contributions of NIH grants by developing and applying cutting-edge tools to measure the creation of new knowledge that would not arise without NIH support. This research would provide a critical framework for understanding the broader impact of NIH funding on scientific progress.

In addition to measuring these contributions, our work would seek to inform policy discussions by optimizing grant allocation strategies. By comparing the anticipated trajectories of funded versus unfunded research, we would aim to shed light on how funding decisions influence the direction and pace of scientific discovery. Our empirical strategy, which would leverage a RDD, would be particularly relevant to policy makers. Since changes in funding policies are often made at the margins rather than involving a complete reoptimization of funding approaches, our method would focus on the marginal effects of NIH funding, aligning closely with real-world decision-making concerns, and ensuring the applicability of our findings to policy.

To achieve these goals, we will leverage state-of-the-art large language models combined with robust causal inference techniques. Our novel approach will showcase a method for integrating LLMs with causal inference, potentially opening new avenues at the intersection of these fields and offering innovative methodologies for addressing complex questions in science policy and beyond.

1 Bartik Instrument Approach for Funding

I propose using the shift-share instrumental approach to address one of two causal questions. We could examine how funding to a scientific field impacts the production of non-funded papers in that field, or alternatively, how funding to a country affects the output of non-funded papers within that country. Given that the necessary assumptions for causal identification are unlikely to hold for both approaches simultaneously, it is needed to choose one framework for analysis.

This methodology draws on the use of Shift-Share instruments, originally developed to address the endogeneity between employment growth and economic development (Bartik [1991], Bartik [1994]). In particular, areas with higher growth rate tend to attract greater higher labor supply, making it difficult to isolate the causal effect of employment growth on economic growth. The Bartik approach addresses this issue by instrumenting local employment growth using the interaction between pre-treatment local employment shares by sector and national employment growth rates by sector, thereby isolating local employment changes driven by national labor demand shocks rather than local supply-side factors.

In our case, we seek to apply a similar strategy using ”large shocks” in funding, which we may argue are exogenous to the idiosyncratic shocks affecting individual countries or scientific fields outputs. The discussion builds on the work of Borusyak et al. [2022] and Goldsmith-Pinkham et al. [2020].

What was accomplished under these goals and objectives (you must provide information for at least one of the 4 categories below)? Major Activities: In this report, we detail our goals, progress, and plans to perform the following 3 key tasks for the nation. These 3 major tasks include the following.
(1) Assemble Technology Data that trace the causes and consequences of technological capabilities, production, and use,
(2) Building Models to Assess & Predict Technology Outcomes; and

(3) Broaden the Impacts of Innovation Intelligence
Specific Objectives:

Specific Objective 1 - Assemble Technology Data AI systems model the world and generate predictions based on the patterns learned from their training data. High quality data is therefore the “fossil fuel” powering the AI revolution, and having the best model for a given domain will often come down to having the best data. Hence, a primary objective of our project is to assemble the most extensive and highest quality database of critical technology capabilities, production, and use, with linkages to upstream scientific discoveries and patenting activities driving these trends.

Specific Objective 2 - Assess and Predict Technology Outcomes Modern LLMs use the recently developed “transformer” architecture to encode language, factual information, networks of association, and other unstructured data into powerful models that form “digital doubles” of the systems they represent. In this project, we rethink this power of LLMs in two important ways. First, LLMs form high-dimensional, probabilistically and geometrically interpretable knowledge representations available for detailed analysis, functioning as global observatories of the systems they encode. Through these powerful macroscopes, entities (e.g., technologies, scientific concepts, researchers, companies, nations) are rendered in context to reflect precise

Finally, our LLMs will also support the estimation of causal models that identify the impact of funding on interlocking discoveries, overlapping supply chains, global networks of skilled labor, and industrial organizations that drive or impede international technology leadership.

Significant Results:

Significant Results 1 - Assemble Technology Data - Progress & Accomplishments: Our collaboration with Syntropy has yielded a substantial corpus of product data. We have ingested and processed 1,135,810 products across critical technology domains including microelectronics, wireless devices, and high-performance computing. This includes 65+ subcategories such as microprocessors, microcontrollers (86,142), power management integrated circuits (117,809), memory integrated circuits (52,287), graphics processing units (3,301), and wireless & RF Integrated Circuits (16,412). Product data is accompanied by capabilities data and often includes unstructured data such as long-form product factsheets or technical specification documents, allowing us to characterize technology capabilities including computational throughput for GPUs, core count and instruction set architecture for microprocessors, efficiency metrics for power management ICs, and performance specifications for wireless components. Beyond commercial products, we have incorporated data from regulatory filings such as FCC equipment authorizations, which provide technical specifications beyond standard catalogs. We have also integrated global production data from the Semiconductor Industry Association spanning 1976-2023, capturing units shipped, billings, and average selling prices across 17 primary product categories. This integration of capabilities with production and pricing data enables us to understand how technical performance, supply constraints, and market dynamics shape technology outcomes. Our team has also assembled substantial product performance data on biomedical therapeutics (hundreds) and artificial intelligence models (thousands of large language models, large vision models, and related models). This data was assembled across commercial and government (e.g., U.S. FDA) biomedical databases, leaderboards, publication data, and U.S. patents.

We have also assembled and integrated extensive publication and patent databases, including Semantic Scholar (by our partner, the Allen Institute for AI); the Microsoft Academic Graph and its successor, Open Alex; Clarivate’s Web of Science, Digital Science’s Dimensions, the arXiv.org collection, and the US Patent & Trademark Office data.

Based on data artifacts (e.g., product factsheets, papers, patents) we have been building an automated system to handle the data extraction process. In this first year, our team successfully developed an initial prototype for automatically extracting structured Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) from unstructured scientific text using LLMs. We established preliminary KPIs for key technology areas including energy storage, superconductors, AI models, and pharmaceuticals, with other areas such as quantum and medical devices in development. We have used this system to evaluate data from over 1,000 papers.

Our current pipeline supports automated extraction of key performance indicators from raw text or PDFs, which can be collected from sources like the ArXiv API or local repositories. The system consists of four steps: (1) data acquisition from multiple sources, (2) data processing and metadata extraction using domain-specific prompts and calls to LLMs, (3) metadata storage in cloud databases, and (4) data analysis and visualization.

We have built a prototype web interface for tracking KPI extraction progress, other analyses, and summary statistics. The interface provides an interactive, real-time dashboard to inspect the data, enabling viewing of source papers for validation, plotting of quantitative KPIs, and tracking qualitative extraction results including hypothesis consensus over time. The pipeline was built with both scalability and accessibility in mind; we have already made these tools available to external

Significant Results 2 - Assess and Predict Technology Outcomes - Progress & Accomplishments: In this first year, we have heightened capacity to extract a variety of science and technology assessments from LLM representations. We have already achieved successful results in (i) Researcher movement and collaboration prediction, (ii) Paper and patent citation and impact prediction, (iii) Technological topological hole filling, and (iv) Embedding distance - performance correlation. Researcher Movement and Collaboration Prediction: We measure representation quality in terms of R2 and RMSE for predicted flow in the embedding space (based on similarity) and normalized data flow (targeting 0.6-0.9 for R2). We trained GRaM, a text embedding model fine-tuned to capture the movement of researchers across semantic space. Early analyses suggest that GRaM outperforms SPECTER (our prior model) and other Sentence-BERT-based models in predicting researcher movement within this latent science space. We also evaluated our models in terms of predicting new collaborations using only cosine similarity between pairs of authors without prior co- authorship. Preliminary results indicate the model slightly outperforms other text-based embedding models and substantially outperforms network-based approaches (see Fig. 2 in the attached Y1 PDF report).

Citation and Impact Prediction: As a baseline, log-error measurement |log(c(t)+1) - log(ĉ(t)+1)| was applied to science and patent citation networks. Our LLM representation-based model achieved better results in most cases with prediction error ranging from 1-2% (science) to ~20% (patent). Our current model (red) also achieved highest precision in predicting high impact scientific papers (left) and patents (right).

Topological Hole Filling: We have made strides in developing a novel method of predicting technological advance by identifying topological holes in the science and technology representation and predicting when and how they will be filled. In Fig. 4 (attached Y1 PDF report), the x-values are thresholds on the size of holes, and the y-values are the proportion of holes below that citation threshold. In year 1, we made the novel empirical discovery that top-cited papers tend to fill larger holes.

Embedding Distance and Performance Correlation: We analyzed machine vision papers from the Papers With Code platform, which provides metadata and benchmark results across AI advances. Using SPECTER embeddings, we calculated pairwise cosine similarities between papers using their titles and abstracts, revealing a significant negative correlation between semantic similarity and benchmark performance scores.

We also worked to identify which embedding dimensions most strongly correlate with specific performance metrics. Using the same embeddings, we applied the SemAxis method to state-of- the-art papers to derive a semantic axis correlated with improvements in benchmark scores. Preliminary results suggest a moderate correlation. Figure 5 in the attached Y1 PDF report illustrates the methodology and depicts the trajectory of state-of-the-art papers along the SemAxis and UMAP projections, with the background colored by research fields.

Science Data Integration: We successfully integrated three major publication datasets—OpenAlex (170+ million records), Dimensions, and Semantic Scholar (67 million records)—creating comprehensive science data infrastructure with metadata on authors, collaborations, universities, and funders.

AI Research Focus: We curated keyword lists, identified representative AI papers and patents, created synthetic CVs through name disambiguation for scientists transitioning into AI fields, and developed dual-timeframe methodologies to quantify research interest shifts and map researcher migration patterns.

Data Linkage Progress: We created concordance datasets linking 672 CPC subclasses with 1,228 HS codes and 308 NAICS codes using fine-tuned LLMs. Our funder disambiguation pipeline achieves 93% accuracy, and we developed methods for linking semiconductor products to firms and matching products to upstream patents using transformer-based embeddings.
Generative Modeling to Predict Technology Outcomes

Generative models simulate probable futures given the global science and technology system, enabling "deductive" imagination of how current conditions lead to technological outcomes and "abductive" recognition of unexpected discoveries' significance. This will allow our model to identify the disruptive implications of a new technology, achieved level of performance, or ascendant performer the moment such an unpredictable, "black swan" event occurs. This rapid identification system can empower federal funding to respond nimbly to the emergence of disruptive anomalies.

In year 1, we have (i) assessed generative model quality, predicting combined works, collaborations, advance content, and citation velocity using standard metrics; (ii) evaluated generative model reliability to understand how well automated assessments correlate with human judgments when evaluating S&T predictions; (iii) developed a generative model of evolution at the scientific frontier; and (iv) assessed how model perplexity predicts the variance of scientific, technological, and product success.

Predictive Model Quality: We developed a causal model of science and built an automated benchmark for predicting near-future scientific advances. Our generative model first predicts a set of collaborating scientists, then which prior work the group will draw from, then the content of the scientific advance itself and finally its potential impact. Our initial benchmark covers AI research and includes 70,000 examples and 630,000 companion papers covering key references and author histories.

Generative Model Reliability: In evaluating each component of our predictive models, we rely on established metrics (e.g. Spearman correlation). However no existing metrics performed well according to human judgements when evaluating proposed advances. We have therefore developed an automated metric using "LLM-as-a-Judge" that achieves performance comparable to inter-human agreement on identifying technological advances.

Developing Generative Model of Frontiers: We developed a generative model of the citation network based on the knowledge space embedding model. First, we developed a null model where the generation of the scientific "frontier" is randomly created around existing papers. As a refinement of this null frontier model, we developed a generative model inspired by the boids framework to explain how scientists shift their research over time through interactions with peers.

Model Surprise: We analyzed the model perplexity of research papers in relation to advancement indicators such as review rating, review confidence, and impact factor. Our analyses find that high perplexity (which we conceive as scientific surprise) is often associated with higher rating scores, greater uncertainty in the peer review process, and a greater likelihood of appearing in journals with either very high or very low impact factors.
Causal Modeling to Steer Technology Outcomes

Another key achievement has been developing causal modeling capabilities. Generative AI models may forecast the most likely immediate techno-scientific futures, or recognize surprises with strategic significance, but alone they cannot identify and isolate causal factors that can be leveraged by national science policy to steer towards sustained technological leadership. therefore complement our LLM-based models with causally identified structural models that describe the downstream technological implications of policy and funding decisions.
In Year 1, we focused on building structural models that would allow us to directly account for causal levers in technology policy, and to assess model alignment with macro indicators (e.g., GDP, productivity growth, and firm size distributions).

Dynamic General Equilibrium Framework Development: We successfully developed a comprehensive dynamic general equilibrium model that embeds firm-level innovation as the primary driver of long-run productivity growth. This foundational framework incorporates input- output linkages across industries, allowing firms' outputs to serve as intermediate inputs in other sectors' production processes. Unlike existing network-based growth models, our framework features fully endogenous productivity growth driven by strategic firm innovation decisions that shape both sectoral and aggregate economic outcomes.

Model Performance and Validation: We established analytical foundations showing that aggregate GDP is proportional to a weighted sum of sectoral productivity levels, with productivities evolving based on the distribution of firm-level innovation and investment behaviors. The model successfully calibrates to historical U.S. productivity growth trends, providing empirical grounding for our theoretical framework. Our model generates realistic endogenous firm size dynamics through heterogeneous productivity-enhancing investments, achieving strong calibration results matching critical empirical moments including the share of small firms by count and employment and the thick right tail of large firm distributions within sectors.

Sectoral Value-Added Alignment: We successfully targeted macro moments on sectoral GDP composition, with long-run sectoral shares shaped by endogenous technology accumulation and micro-level demand elasticities. Using estimated elasticities and observed value-added shares, the model infers relative sectoral technological advantages arising from firm innovation patterns.

Micro-Level Dynamics: Our model captures micro-level dynamics through firm-level heterogeneity. Firms differ in productivity, markups over marginal costs, profitability, entry/exit behavior, and innovation intensity. These differences emerge naturally from variations in each firm's production elasticities and technology, leading to misallocation of production inputs across firms. This misallocation provides a rationale for industrial and innovation policy interventions.

Policy Analysis Foundation: We established theoretical foundations for modeling indirect effects of public funding interventions by embedding input-output linkages and sectoral innovation in a general equilibrium setting. This enables identification of resource allocation strategies that yield highest total returns across full production chains, not just within directly funded sectors.
What opportunities for training and professional development has the project provided?

Developing the Next Generation Workforce has been an important aspect of our work. In order to transmit the skills associated with this work to the next generation, we have developed Innovative Academic Programming, such as the launch of a popular "Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth" course as collaboration between Principal Investigators Evans and Akcigit, that integrates computational, economic, and complex systems approaches to technology analysis to train next-generation researchers in capabilities essential for national technology strategy. We have also launched a new weekly “AI, Innovation and the Economy” seminar featuring international research leaders to create an intellectual focal point for advancing the field while building networks of expertise crucial for sustained American leadership in technology forecasting. This seminar is helping to form the basis for the World Bank’s 2026 report on AI and development. We have also broadened access to relevant skills by executing Summer Institutes in Computational Social Science (SICSS) at University of Florida and Clark Atlanta University, with expansion planned to Tuskegee University, Gustavus Adolphus College, and University of Rochester in 2025. These programs specifically target under-resourced institutions to broaden participation in computational social science and AI-driven research methods. We have also engaged in program evaluation by a dedicated evaluator tracking the efficacy of existing content and new LLM- based materials (with 233 contributors to the GitHub repository and more than .25M views over the program’s lifetime). We also engage in application pool analysis (institutional variety, disciplinary variety, career stage variety). Future years will involve the measurement of career outcome follow-ups with alumni, publication tracking, and network expansion. Finally, we have engaged in Workforce Pipeline Development by recruiting and training graduate students, postdoctoral scholars, and research specialists across partner institutions, creating a skilled workforce capable of sustained operation and expansion of predictive technology capabilities. This has resulted in program-supported postdocs and students entering professorships at institutions including UC Berkeley, Purdue University, Yonsei University (Korea).

What do you plan to do during the next reporting period to accomplish the goals?

In the next reporting period, we will focus on significant refinement and validation of our extraction systems. Key objectives include collaborating with domain experts to validate extracted data and refine KPI definitions, rigorously benchmarking the accuracy and efficiency of automated extraction across different LLM providers and expanding the system to include more diverse data sources. We will improve LLM prompts for better extraction accuracy, run large-scale extractions on Argonne's Aurora system to process 100s of thousands of papers and patents, and demonstrate quantifiable KPI relationships to corroborate expert insights. Additionally, we will work with Syntropy to obtain production and release dates for longitudinal tracking of product evolution, enabling us to study how product attributes evolve over time and interact with upstream innovations.

In the next reporting period, we will focus on significant scaling and refinement of our systems, expanding our data extraction pipeline to process hundreds of thousands of product fact sheets, patents, and scientific publications, eventually scaling to millions in subsequent years. Key technical objectives include running large-scale extractions on Argonne's Aurora system, improving LLM prompts for better extraction accuracy, and rigorously benchmarking performance across different LLM providers, while collaborating with domain experts to validate extracted data and refine KPI definitions across all technology domains. Working with Syntropy, we will obtain production and release dates to enable longitudinal tracking of product evolution, studying how product attributes evolve and interact with upstream innovations, and demonstrate quantifiable KPI relationships to corroborate expert insights and provide empirical validation of the innovation lifecycle model. Our linkage efforts will focus on completing the lifecycle tracking framework to trace products from research publications and grants through patents to market adoption, including finalizing the patent-to-product linking pipeline, expanding publication-to-patent connections beyond ArXiv to include patents and product fact sheets, and strengthening connections between academic research funding and downstream commercial outcomes, ultimately providing detailed insights into how public R&D investments translate into technological progress and economic value.

In the next reporting period, we will incorporate our newly acquired technology data into our successfully piloted representation models. We will further improve our technology distance-performance correlation across technology categories. Finally, we will begin to use embeddings to establish links between products and patents that are not as explicit as the citations that exist upstream in basic science and technology development. In future years, we will engage in transfer prediction-improving accuracy in predicting which performance attributes transfer between technologies and the effectiveness of embedding models in connecting scientific output directly to product innovation.

In the next reporting period, we will validate our models through comprehensive micro-moments matching by accurately replicating technology firm-level dynamics including entry/exit rates and innovation patterns, while demonstrating robust out-of-sample predictive power for untargeted patterns and reproducing observed network structures of industry-to-industry flows and shock propagation mechanisms. Our work will capture competition patterns by modeling market structure-innovation relationships, enabling rigorous impact assessment through policy experiment simulations that generate credible insights about funding interventions. We aim to discover novel feedback loops and spillover effects previously unmodeled in the literature, quantify their significance for policy effectiveness, and translate findings into specific, implementable policy levers that provide actionable recommendations for technology strategy and innovation policy.

What was the impact on teaching and educational experiences?

In order to transmit the skills associated with this work to the next generation, we have developed Innovative Academic Programming, such as the launch of a popular "Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth" course as collaboration between Principal Investigators Evans and Akcigit in Winter, 2025, that integrated computational, economic, and complex systems approaches to technology analysis to train next- generation researchers in capabilities essential for national technology strategy.

The course description follows: “Social and cultural innovation, alongside economic growth, are among the most compelling, critical and challenging phenomena in modern social science. Innovation has always been associated with unleashing transformative growth in art, science, and the economy, and in this class we explore these issues in the context of the contemporary emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI). AI represents a novel source of innovation in the economy and society, but also a powerful tool for understanding, modeling, and steering innovation in new ways. The primary purpose of this course is to enable students to understand innovation and growth in the age of AI, and with tools from AI alongside theoretical frameworks and methods from economics, sociology, evolution, and complex systems necessary to study them. The course strives to provide students with a background in dynamic analysis, data analysis, and modern AI requisite for studying innovation in the modern age. We will also consider a number of compelling theoretical and empirical challenges, ranging from the paradox of institutionalizing innovation to inequalities that emerging AI capacities could create or remove to advances it could unleash in science and technology to the spread of misinformation to consequences of AI tools and “agents” in all domains of modern life to existential risks associated with AI. We will cover theories and models at an abstract and advanced level. We recommend a degree of quantitative and computation maturity (e.g., basic calculus, matrix algebra, statistics, and programming). The course will involve a technical homework and mid-term, along with a final proposal and single or group project involving theoretical and data analysis that explores innovation and growth in the age of AI.”

The class has received accolades, exemplified by this unsolicited email just following the course midterm: “Dear Professor Ufuk and James, Before the midterm, I wanted to take a moment to send this note of appreciation. I know this is a bit random, but I just got off the phone with my parents, telling them how excited I am about this class, and I felt compelled to reach out. This has been the first course at UChicago that has truly sparked my curiosity and passion. I’ve never felt this engaged in a class before, and it has made me seriously consider pursuing a career in AI. While I’m not yet sure what that path will look like, I’m incredibly grateful for the inspiration and perspective you’ve provided. Thank you for creating such a thoughtful and engaging learning environment. Every lecture has been insightful, relevant, and genuinely exciting, and I really appreciate the effort you put into making this such a meaningful experience. Looking forward to the rest of the quarter! Best, Klaudia Barbarossa”(UChicago '26 Undergraduate Student).
