Changes/Problems
Changes in approach and reason for change

For a project of our size and distributed scale, there will necessarily be unexpected struggles, but also serendipity-happy accidents. For us, there were more of the latter than the former, and the two were coupled. Artificial Intelligence has witnessed rapid advances since the grant began in summer 2024. Consider the increased efficiency of LLM training in the context of reasoning models like those open-sourced by DeepSeek. These have influenced our project. They have made it harder to build chronological training models that outcompete contemporary models, as those “baseline” models are themselves improving at a rapid pace. Nevertheless, the field of models relevant to our program as a whole has undergone significant improvement, with the greatest recent advances in model pre-training and fine-tuning, which has accelerated our efforts to assess science and technology with representation learning. In short, AI developments have been more beneficial than detrimental to our program and bode well for our ability to pilot a National Innovation Intelligence Infrastructure (NI3) for critical technologies that increase American technology competitiveness, prosperity, and security.

About the picture on the cover

The image on the cover symbolizes our innovation policy initiatives and efforts related to scientific planning for science policy. The CHIPS and Science Act, along with related national, regional, and commercial efforts of 2022, seeks to build a foundational scientific understanding of the policy levers that will drive sustained technology leadership in an increasingly competitive global environment. The Innovation Policy Lab initiative in collaboration with our Global Science & Tech Observatory will construct a virtual laboratory to establish causal linkages between specific government, philanthropic, and corporate policy levers and S&T leadership. Through this initiative, we are designing AI systems to simulate outcomes of S&T policy perturbation, including targeted funding, educational competition, and organizational policies. We seek to use these policy simulations to support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of funding on interlocking discoveries, overlapping supply chains, global networks of skilled labor, and industrial organizations that drive or impede international technology leadership.

Introduction

The National Science Foundation (NSF) launched the NSF-APTO Program to enhance national capacity to assess and predict outcomes of research and development in critical technology areas. This Program will help decision makers identify specific investments and policies that enable the United States to accelerate development of critical technologies essential for long-term national security and economic prosperity. The program received funding in August of 2024 and work began in Q4 of 2024.

The University of Chicago NSF-APTO Program comprises scientists and engineers from the University of Chicago, Northwestern University, Indiana University, the Allen Intelligence, various corporate Institute for Artificial partners, and participants from Argonne National Laboratory. To catalyze collaborations between these participants and to kick-off the program, the University of Chicago organized a two-day workshop, on November 1 and 2 of 2024. During this two-day workshop, researchers across our partner institutions came together, gave lectures, engaged in focused discussions and forged effective working relationships. View the workshop newsletter here.

We have also developed a new course for undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Chicago, entitled “Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth”, designed as a new collaboration between the two Principal Investigators James Evans and Ufuk Akcigit. We have also begun a new weekly seminar on AI, Innovation and Growth at the intersection of the social and computational sciences with weekly visitors from around the world. Our Principal Investigators, postdocs, and students will interact with these research leaders to gain novel insights on our ongoing projects.

To provide structure to our organization, increase productivity, and maximize operational efficiency, we have organized ourselves into five distinct but fully integrated cross-disciplinary operational thrusts. Each thrust will work on core, cross-integrated aspects of the program and is led by a thrust leader who is also a co-principal investigator. We have organized regular weekly meetings for these thrusts. During these weekly meetings, team members gather to discuss recent efforts, report progress updates, exchange information and ignite the generation of new ideas relevant to our overall goal.

Overview and Importance of LLMs and Related LLM Applications

A “large language model” (LLM) is a form of artificial intelligence that uses deep learning algorithms to process and generate human-like text by analyzing massive amounts (i.e., webscale) of text data, allowing it to perform tasks like translation, summarization, question answering, creative writing, and drafting code, essentially mimicking human language and underlying reasoning patterns through a complex multi-layer neural network architecture called a “transformer.” The transformer architecture excels at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them.

In addition to teaching human languages to artificial intelligence (AI) applications, language models (LLMs) can also be trained to perform a variety of tasks like understanding protein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease. Like the human brain, large language models must be pre- trained and then fine-tuned so that they can solve a widening range of practical, business, and scientific problems. Large language models have large numbers of parameters, which represent the model’s complex knowledge bank. Their problem-solving capabilities are being applied to fields like entertainment, finance, and healthcare.

large
In the context of the NSF-APTO Program, and the mission of accomplishing the strategic objectives of the NSF’s Technology and Innovation Partnerships (TIP) directorate, LLMs are powerful because they can be trained with large- scale science, technology, and product data. This will enable us to predict and steer future technology advance, ensuring continued U.S. leadership in global technology advancement relevant to greater security and prosperity.

Our proposed technology LLMs will yield three key model outputs, and one key data output. First, LLMs natively produce interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as a global observatory of the techno-scientific system they encode, signposting how the U.S. can navigate toward greater global leadership. Second, our LLMs are generative models that function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of government and industrial policies to facilitate U.S. leadership. Third, our LLMs will propose and support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of government policies that drive or impede international technology leadership. Finally, our models will improve the extraction of product-level data that, in turn, will improve the success of the models themselves and the science of technology advance that they support.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used in molecular engineering, biochemistry and synthetic biology, allowing researchers to design new molecules and optimize existing ones by leveraging their ability to learn patterns from vast amounts of chemical data, predicting molecular structures and properties to accelerate drug discovery and materials science development.

MID-YEAR PROGRESS UPDATE - JANUARY 2025
1:
Construct an initial version of a science prediction benchmark, capable of assessing existing AI models’ capacity for predicting content of future scientific papers, technology patents, and products.

Predictive models of science could accelerate the identification of breakthroughs, help funding organizations prioritize investments, and begin to automate certain scientific workflows, but broad-coverage benchmarks for evaluating such models do not exist. In the past six months, we have built an initial version of a science prediction benchmark for LLMs and other science-domain models, consisting of 6 tasks (3 generation + 3 classification/regression), covering open computer-science-domain literature from Semantic Scholar’s paper corpus. These tasks include:

1)
Follow-up proposal prediction: Given a set of existing literature, predict the proposal of a paper that will cite this set.
2) Author collaboration prediction: Given a set of authors’ publication histories, predict the proposal of a paper that
they will go on to collaborate on.
3) Experiment prediction: Given a paper proposal and summaries of papers it cites, predict the list of experiments that
will be conducted to test/verify the proposal.
4)

Impact prediction: Given a paper proposal and summaries of the papers it cites, predict its citation velocity upon successful publication.
5)
Co-citation prediction: Given a set of existing papers, predict whether all of them will ever be simultaneously cited by a future paper.
6) Author Interest prediction: Given an author’s publication history and a new paper, predict if the author will go on
to cite the paper.

While the classification/regression tasks can be evaluated straightforwardly using accuracy and correlation metrics, the generation tasks pose a more difficult challenge for evaluation, since (a) many possible correct answers exist and (b) accurately measuring the extent to which an output paper proposal covers the essence of a given paper is challenging. We are exploring the use of multiple evaluation strategies for these tasks, including a novel retrieval-based metric, and other established LLM-based metrics/frameworks (BERTScore, RAGChecker, IdeaMatcher, etc). Our results so far indicate that these evaluation metrics are only mildly correlated with each other. We intend to collect human annotations to determine which of them correlate the best with human judgements and use that metric for the generation tasks in our benchmark.

2. Develop an early-stage chronologically-trained scientific language model, on scientific text. We have also been exploring ways to develop a science-domain language model that has been trained in a chronology- and/or citation-structure-aware manner, because we hypothesize that models trained this way would be better-equipped to perform science prediction tasks. Specifically, we have experimented with continually pretraining public 8B-scale LLaMA models on sets of scientific literature that have been serialized in different ways (BFS, DFS, publication date, by clustering semantically related papers together, etc.) to capture chronology and citation-structure. The models we train in this manner can then be further fine-tuned for use on downstream prediction tasks from our benchmark. Our efforts on this front have not yet yielded promising results. The models we have developed this way are often outperformed by non-science-domain LLMs like GPT4o and even by similarly sized LLaMA models fine-tuned directly on our benchmark tasks (without any additional pretraining). We believe that this may be because the highly-trained instruction-tuned LLaMA models that we work with undergo catastrophic forgetting and lose their robust instruction-following abilities during our continued pretraining phase. We intend to explore more training strategies and architectural choices for science-domain models after we finalize and release our science prediction benchmark. MID-YEAR PROGRESS UPDATE - JANUARY 2025

In the initial phase of our work, we developed an integrated approach designed to provide clear guidance on structuring and optimizing science funding across a range of high-impact research areas to promote technological leadership, general welfare and sustained economic growth.
1:

Construct an array of dynamic general equilibrium models to capture the behaviors of scientists and firms underfunded and unfunded scenarios as revealed in our LLMs, explicitly formulating the optimization problem faced by individual researchers.

One of our primary achievements was the development of a dynamic general equilibrium (DGE) model that spans multiple sectors, incorporates endogenous firm innovation processes, and captures knowledge spillovers from both basic science and academic publications. We have also embedded input-output linkages to reveal how advancements in one sector can cascade through the broader economy, impacting output across diverse industries. By detailing how researchers and firms optimize their innovation strategies and benefit from exogenous technological spillovers from outside of their fields, this flexible framework enables us to evaluate the heterogeneous macroeconomic impact of various government- funded research programs on both welfare and growth. As a theoretical laboratory, the model generates counterfactual predictions on the effectiveness of government funding given to different scientific and technology fields, highlighting the importance of cross-sectoral interactions and spillovers. Validating these predictions, however, requires precise estimation of key parameters—an endeavor that hinges on high-quality datasets capturing researchers, institutions, and product-level details, which we turn to in the following section.

One critical aspect of constructing high-quality datasets is curating the most recent and comprehensive records of publications and patents, which serve as the foundation for our measurement of knowledge spillovers among researchers and across technological fields. Accurate disambiguation of authors and institutions is paramount to capturing the pathways through which ideas diffuse. In this regard, support from partners such as AI2 is invaluable. Only reliably disambiguated publication and patent datasets allow us to minimize the bias in measuring spillover flows between researchers, institutions, and sectors. Building on our existing data infrastructure, we have updated our publication and patent repositories by incorporating the SemanticScholar dataset from AI2 and the latest version of the OpenAlex database. These updates are complemented by rigorous validation procedures, including the examination of key distributions such as annual publication counts, document classifications, and the detection of author lumping, where multiple publications are erroneously assigned to a single author. These evaluations allow us to assess the conservativeness of disambiguation algorithms provided to us and ensure the robustness of the datasets for downstream econometric and computational analyses.

A parallel component of our data acquisition strategy focuses on product- and firm-level data, particularly in strategic high-tech industries. This enables the precise estimation of production functions and elasticity parameters within the DGE-network model introduced earlier. These elasticity parameters guide how technological and scientific advancements ripple through the economy by shaping supplier-customer relationships and influencing input substitution patterns across sectors. By integrating firm-level data with aggregate input-output tables from the BEA, we aim to capture both upstream and downstream effects of technical change with unprecedented granularity. Our collaboration with contractor Syntropy ensures the acquisition of these highly detailed product-level datasets and their alignment with our modeling framework. Once integrated and combined with our existing data sources, this information will facilitate the estimation and calibration of the model, laying the groundwork for robust policy analysis.

3:
Pilot linking our model to data on the size, organizational structure, and industrial or field position of sponsored universities and businesses in targeted technical advance to predict how changes in strategic funding, training, and inter-country alliances will shape strategic technologies.

In summary, we have made considerable progress in developing our dynamic general equilibrium framework and establishing a solid foundation for comprehensive data collection that incorporates robust name disambiguation and firm- and product-level details. Building on these achievements, our next steps will focus on estimating the model’s key parameters (goal 3), performing counterfactual innovation and science policy analyses, including embedding LLM- based forecasts of scientific progress to evaluate their potential economic outcomes. As we advance, we are committed to strengthening collaborations with partners and stakeholders, refining our findings, and delivering a comprehensive blueprint for effective and impactful science and innovation policy.

3. Develop a generative model of NSF grants based on the scientific publications.

For generative modeling of grants and products, which can be pivotal for predictive modeling and causal inference of funding impact, we have finalized a preliminary study on a generative model of scientific citation systems. This approach models the evolution of the entire citation system, rather than individual publications, to more accurately predict future citation trajectories. Our model includes two components: (1) a publication generation model, currently a zero-knowledge null model that positions each new paper near a randomly chosen existing paper in the embedding space, and (2) an embedding-based citation model that generates new citations based on embedding distance (“relevance”), existing citations (preferential attachment), and fitness (“quality”). In evaluations of predicting future prominence (e.g., inclusion in the top x% of cited papers), this whole system-level approach outperforms traditional paper-level models. We aim to extend this foundation to develop generative models that also account for grants, patents, and products, enabling more comprehensive insights into the interplay between funding and scientific outcomes.

1. Begin expert elicitation to extract and share an open dataset of technology performance indicators from technical content in sampled papers, patents, and products to benchmark automatic extraction.

We have developed a pilot LLM extraction pipeline, overseen by technical experts from Argonne National Laboratory. In the next 6 months, we will use this to develop key information that is central to understanding research progress over time in two focus domains critical for both economic and national security. The two focus domains will be energy storage (including e.g., Li-ion, Na-ion, Fe-based batteries) and microchips; we also aspire to consider a third stretch domain of artificial intelligence (AI). The developed artifacts will include: 1) a set of proposed quantitative key performance indicators for each domain and 2) a set of proposed qualitative indicators for each domain. These quantitative and qualitative KPI will be validated with multiple domain experts to ensure they capture the most important information. For example, with energy storage, we imagine extracting metrics such as energy density, power density, and cycle life, and for microchips, node size, transistor density, and power efficiency among other important indicators.

We will work closely with the other teams to enable the creation of robust data pipelines capable of processing diverse document types (e.g., papers, patents, data sheets) across the domains of interest to collect the validated quantitative and qualitative KPI. We envision that such a system will increasingly employ advanced natural language processing techniques, leveraging large language models (LLMs - e.g., GPT, Claude, Llama) to identify and efficiently extract the identified metrics from unstructured text. We will also work to define the specifications of the LLMs needed to perform such extractions and investigate extraction evaluation metrics to ensure the system will perform reliably across many different textual contexts and scientific domains. We will also help to ensure that the system is designed with flexibility in mind allowing for the addition of new domains and metrics as needed.

2. Build and deliver an initial dump (~500k products) of product factsheets data for critical technology areas (e.g. Microelectronics and High-Performance Computing).

To date, we have collected and integrated over 219,000 product factsheets, representing 43.9% of our target. Our dataset includes comprehensive product documentation (some documents spanning 300 pages) with detailed metadata for essential microelectronics products: microcontrollers, memory chips, FPGAs, and RF transceivers. The data, sourced from major distributors like DigiKey and Mouser as well as directly from microelectronics vendors, provides valuable insights into product capabilities and their evolution. Through tracking technical metrics across products, we can analyze performance trends and forecast future capabilities. We are currently collecting the remaining ~280,609 product entries focusing on emerging technologies crucial for defense, AI, and secure communications.

We have acquired datasets from key microelectronics trade organizations that track monthly net billings—shipments between semiconductor manufacturers and their end customers, authorized distributors, and subsidiaries. These billings, reported by customer shipment location, use actual sales prices or comparable market prices for internal transfers. By combining this production and usage data APTO: Syntropy Mid-Year Progress Report (January 2025 with our capabilities data from product factsheets, we have built the foundation for predictive models that assess trends in production, capabilities, and downstream adoption across the microelectronics sector.

To achieve our second objective, we are aligning product classifications across distributor sites and trade organizations to connect capabilities with production data. We have developed two methods to extract patent and intellectual property information from product factsheets. The first method uses advanced embeddings and metadata extraction to map relationships between products and patents, creating factsheet embeddings that identify each manufacturer’s most relevant patents. The second method applies prompt engineering to factsheets to uncover embedded IP. Together, these approaches will build a comprehensive product-to-patent database that shows how government-funded research leads to commercial applications. This linked dataset powers predictive models that forecast production, capabilities, and usage trends in microelectronics.

Moving forward, we will focus on two priorities: expanding our database with the remaining product factsheets and enhancing our product-to-patent connections. We plan to refine our predictive models to deliver detailed insights into production and adoption trends, publish our initial findings, and extend this analytical framework to other critical technologies.

Introduction

We are approximately 9 months into the NSF-APTO program at the University of Chicago. In these 9 months, we have made foundational progress, positioning our team for accelerated analysis and discovery over the duration of the project. Most critically, (1) we have developed an efficient and effective organizational structure between the project’s multiple arms, (2) we have begun assembly of an extensive database that links technology production, capability, and use to upstream scientific progress, economic change, and policy impacts, and (3) we have begun preliminary analyses into forecasting and steering technological advance. As we transition into large-scale analysis, a current priority the development of quantitative performance metrics by which we can meaningfully assess the accuracy and reliability of our predictive models. In this memo, we overview our team’s organization into operational “thrusts”, we describe each thrust’s activities and objectives, and then outline in detail the performance metrics we are establishing to confirm the utility and predictive power of our models.

Our discussion of performance metrics was strengthened and refined at our Performance Metrics Summit, which was held on March 26, 2025. In this conference, the principal investigators from our partnered institutions gathered to discuss work developing quantitative metrics to clearly measure the success of their predictive models against rigorous benchmarks. Kicking off the summit, Dr. Rebecca Chmiel from the NSF provided valuable guidance and perspective on the importance of these performance metrics for assessing research outcomes. Following that introduction, the team shared a series of presentations, each accompanied by discussion of critical metrics that would link our progress in year one with our overarching goals across all five years and with other work across the NSF-APTO program.
Group Organization: Five Primary Thrusts

To structure our initiative and maximize operational efficiency, we have organized research activities into five distinct but integrated operational thrusts. Each thrust is led by one of the program’s co-principal investigators and focuses its effort on a core feature of the project. Coordination between the five thrusts is maintained through weekly meetings. During these regular meetings, team members discuss recent efforts, report progress updates, exchange information, and ignite the generation of new ideas. Members of other thrusts have an open invitation to attend the meetings of neighboring thrusts to stay updated on the other groups’ activities. In this way, we have successfully managed the program’s operations in an efficient, cross-disciplinary manner, resonant with the matrix organizational structure of effective corporate research organizations.

Thrust 1 - Large Language Models Thrust Leader: Dr. Doug Downey, Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence

The Large Language Models group seeks to build predictive models capable of forecasting critical technology outcomes. This work involves assembling relevant scientific and technology documents, building models chronologically to avoid data leakage, experimenting with complementary objectives to regularize models for improved performance, and finally, assessing model performance against held-out data sets. The group is also developing benchmarks against which the community of researchers can be mobilized to make progress on important technological performance prediction.
Thrust 2 - Embedding Representations Thrust Leader: Professor Yong-Yeol Ahn, Indiana University

The Embedding Representations group uses deep learning models, in combination with theoretically-inspired constraints, to generate information-rich representations of the global science and technology system. Analyzing the internal representations generated by powerful, predictive AI systems, this group applies novel methodologies to derive mechanistic and interpretable insights into the process and trajectory of technological advance.

Thrust 3 - Innovation Policy Thrust Leader: Professor Ufuk Akcigit, University of Chicago.
The Innovation Policy group seeks to discover and design science and technology policies that maximize US technological leadership. Their analyses combine the predictive power of Large Language Models and the causal power of structural statistical models and experiments to forecast likely outcomes and identify levers to control and accelerate technological progress.
Thrust 4 - Data Structures Thrust Leader: Professor Dashun Wang, Kellogg School of Management of Northwestern University and Ian Foster, University of Chicago

The Data Structures group seeks to build a corpus that links data on technology capabilities, production, and use (e.g. from product specification sheets, sales, news mentions, etc.), back through technology designs (e.g. technology patents), scientific and technical concepts (e.g., from scientific articles), people (e.g., scientists, engineers, and workers), and capital (e.g., research grants, start-up funding).

Thrust 5 - Complex Computations Thrust Leader: Professor James Evans, University of Chicago
The Complex Computation group seeks to supply the computational frameworks and resources necessary to integrate data across the five groups and train powerful predictive models of technology capability, production and use.

Thrust 1- Large Language Models

In year 1, this thrust has focused on two key areas: predicting scientific and technical advances and developing collective resources to extend our work by engaging the scientific community on these problems. For scientific prediction, we are creating datasets, benchmarks, and models to forecast research directions, collaborations, and impact. For resource development, we are processing patent documents to capture technological and scientific advances essential for predictive discovery.

Our 2025-2026 metrics include:
1. Predictive model quality: Assessing performance on tasks like predicting combined works, collaborations, advance (future) content, and citation velocity using standard metrics and comparing against baselines.
2. Reliability of automated metrics: Measuring how well our automated assessments correlate with human judgments when evaluating scientific and technological predictions.

3. Patent corpus quality: Evaluating coverage volume, update frequency, extraction accuracy, and knowledge graph integration.
4. Community engagement: Tracking adoption
through platform engagement metrics, benchmark submissions, leaderboard performance, and usage of our resources for LLM development.
Our ultimate goal is facilitating breakthroughs in scientific and technological prediction through the widespread adoption of our benchmarks, and corpus of papers, patents, and ultimately products.

Thrust 4 - Data Structures

We are developing automated pipelines for extracting Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) from scientific literature, technology patents, and product fact sheets, initially in domains including energy storage and AI, led by Co-PI Ian Foster and Ben Blaiszik. The system transforms unstructured text from research documents into structured, analyzable data through a four-stage process: data acquisition, LLM-based extraction, metadata storage, and analysis.

Our measurement framework tracks progress through quantifiable metrics:
1. Domain Coverage: Currently supporting 2 domains (energy storage, AI) with targeted expansion to microelectronics and quantum computing
2. Expert Validation: number of KPIs currently validated by external experts
3. Data Source Integration: sources operational (ArXiv API and local PDF directories), with patents and product fact sheets to come (currently 2)
4. Extraction Efficiency: Processing cost (now approximately $0.02 per document)

Year 2 metrics will include extraction accuracy versus human annotation, percentage of domain- relevant documents processed, emergence tracking of new performance metrics in literature, and automated analysis pipeline development. Initial prototype testing has demonstrated promising results on hundreds of papers with performance comparable to human annotators on polymer property extraction, though further validation is required in Year 2.

A second part of this thrust involves gathering the data required to do the extraction listed above. Syntropy.AI has been a core partner in this, with a sub-project that focuses on building comprehensive datasets linking technological products to upstream patents and R&D outcomes. Their measurement framework encompasses six key metric categories:
1. Data Scale Metrics
a. Product Corpus Size: Total count of unique, structured product entries (219,391 current,
500,000 target)

b. Product Category Distribution: Breakdown across 22 primary categories and 30+ subtypes
(e.g., 86,142 microcontrollers, 52,287 memory devices)
2. Metadata Quality Metrics
a. Ontology Depth: Percentage of products with full metadata (≥5 structured fields extracted)
b. Extraction Completeness: Coverage of critical specifications across product categories
3. Patent and IP Linkage Metrics
a. Linkage Density: Average number of distinct IP assets identified per product

b. Linking Success Rate: Percentage of factsheets successfully linked to ≥1 IP entity
4. Historical Trends Analysis

a. Price-Performance Trajectories: Year-over-year ASP trends by subcategory
b. Supply Chain Correlation: Mapping of price trends against manufacturing milestones
5. R&D Investment Traceability
a. Funding Traceability: Percentage of products with matched upstream grant or funding
document

b. Public Investment Impact: Connections between government funding and commercial
outcomes
6. Extraction Accuracy Benchmarking
a. Capability Extraction Precision: F1-score measuring extraction accuracy against expert
annotations
b. Quality Control Standards: Benchmark metrics for validating future capability datasets

c. This framework enables quantifiable tracking of progress while supporting predictive modeling across Capabilities, Production, and Use domains, with validation using statistical measures like KL divergence and log-loss.
The third and final part of this thrust project will focus on measuring the impact of artificial intelligence on scientific research and tracking researcher transitions into AI fields, led by Co-PI Dashun Wang. The measurement framework for this sub-thrust encompasses:

1. Dataset Development and Analysis
a. Dataset Creation: Number of specialized datasets tracking AI technology impact
b. Publication Output: Published papers documenting methodologies and findings
2. Impact Measurement Metrics
a. AI Technology Identification: Curated keyword lists for AI research classification
b. Direct Impact Quantification: Calculated weighted average fraction of papers utilizing AI
technologies across scientific fields

c. Cross-Disciplinary Penetration: Applied NLP techniques to extract AI-related terms from
publication and patent titles
3. Researcher Adaptation Analysis
a. Scientist Identification: Created synthetic CVs for researchers transitioning into AI fields
through name disambiguation
b. Research Interest Tracking: Developed dual-timeframe methodologies (5-year recent and
career-long) for quantifying research interest shifts

c. Transition Timing: Mapped temporal patterns of researcher migration into AI fields based
on publication metadata
This framework provides quantitative measurements of both the technology impact landscape and the human capital adaptation within the rapidly evolving AI ecosystem.
Thrust 5 - Complex Computations

For this part of the projects, we seek to (1) develop methods for predicting emerging critical technology areas from existing technologies; (2) establish that distances between technologies in our associated embeddings are proportional to the differences between levels of technological

capacity and performance for critical technologies; and ultimately (3) demonstrate the power of analyzing across vs. within technology areas for predicting technological advance.
1. Metrics for Predicting Emerging Critical Technology Areas
a. Early Signal Detection Rate: Percentage of correctly identified emerging technologies
detected X years before their exponential growth phase begins
b. False Discovery Rate: Ratio of incorrectly predicted "emerging" technologies to total
predictions made

c. Technology Ancestry Score: Quantification of how accurately the system identifies
technological lineages and inheritance patterns
d. Cross-Domain Innovation Index: Measurement of early technology combinations across
previously separate domains
e. Prediction Lead Time: Average time between prediction of emergence and actual
breakthrough/adoption milestones
f. Patent-to-Product Timeline Compression: Detection of acceleration in the time between
patent filing and commercial product release

2. Metrics for Embedding Distance-Performance Correlation
a. Technology Performance-Distance Correlation: Pearson correlation between embedding
distance and quantifiable performance differentials
b. Embedding-Based Forecasting Accuracy: Mean squared error between predicted
performance improvements and actual outcomes based on embedding trajectories
c.
Isoperformance Curve Consistency: Statistical consistency of embedding distances for technologies with equivalent performance metrics

d. Capability Transfer Prediction: Accuracy in predicting which performance attributes
transfer between technologies based on embedding proximity
e. Dimensional Significance Analysis: Identification of which embedding dimensions most
strongly correlate with specific performance metrics
3. Metrics for Cross-Domain vs. Within-Domain Prediction Power
a. Cross-Domain Breakthrough Rate: Frequency of major advances originating from cross-
domain knowledge transfer versus within-domain refinement

b. Knowledge Recombination Potency: Quantitative measure of innovation impact from
cross-domain versus within-domain knowledge recombination
c. Transfer Learning Efficacy: Success rate of applying models trained in one domain to
prediction tasks in other domains
d. Domain Boundary Permeability: Measurement of the rate of citation and terminology flow
across domain boundaries
e. Interdisciplinary Collaboration Impact: Citation impact differential between single-domain

and cross-domain research teams
f. Technology Convergence Forecasting Precision: Accuracy in predicting technology
convergence events and their timing based on cross-domain indicators
These metrics provide a comprehensive framework for evaluating progress on our three goals.

Broader Impacts Initiative

This grant has helped support The Summer Institutes in Computational Social Science (SICSS), which expands computational training with emphasis on LLMs at a wide variety of institutions. In Year 1, sites were established at University of Florida, Clark Atlanta University, with upcoming locations at Gustavus Adolphus College and University of Rochester. Program development included cultivating relationships with new sites and curriculum enhancement.
Our robust measurement framework includes:

1. Program evaluation by a dedicated evaluator tracking the efficacy of existing content and new LLM-based materials
2. Participant success tracking (completion rates, outcomes)
3. Engagement metrics for open-source curricula
4. Application pool analysis (institutional variety, participant backgrounds)
5. Career outcome follow-ups with alumni
6. Publication tracking of SICSS-initiated projects (articles and software)
7. Network expansion monitoring

The new SICSS-Saturdays online series launching this fall will feature advanced LLM methods and contemporary approaches, providing additional metrics for network growth and engagement with cutting-edge computational social science techniques.
Summary
We are approximately 9 months into the NSF-APTO program at the University of Chicago.
We have made substantial progress during this time on all fronts of the project.

We have successfully formed a cohesive unified cross-disciplinary team and we have advanced towards achieving our goals and objectives.
We have established well-defined quantitative metrics which we use to measure our progress.
This short report, with a focus on measurement, is an abstract and a preview to the full progress report which we will present on May 2, 2025 to the NSF management team as part of our 9-month review process.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Chief Executive Officer approve a grant of up to DKK 1,499,750 to the Kellogg School of Management and McCormick School of Engineering at Northwestern University for funding the “International Conference on the Science of Science and Innovation 2025” (ICSSI) led by Professor and Director Dashun Wang. The project period is 1 July 2024 to 30 July 2025.
The total budget for the conference is DKK 2,999,500, and ICSSI has obtained positive support from several Danish funders about co-funding the remaining cost.

The ICSSI is a critical part of the effort to continue to grow the science of science community, advancing the field of science of science and expanding science’s benefits to society. The purpose is to provide a unique platform for scientists to share research and ideas, build new connections, and collaborate with other academics in the emerging field of the science of science, as well as with policymakers, funders, and other stakeholders. Hence, the project is in alignment with the NNF strategy to build and disseminate knowledge about the societal impact of research.

Background
Based on a recommendation from the CEO meeting on 5 February 2024, the ICSSI has received positive support from three other Danish foundations (Leo Foundation, Villum Foundation, and Carlsberg Foundation) with a total commitment of DKK 1,499,750.

The ICSSI would be the fourth annual conference. Bringing the ICSSI to Europe and having a global presence will enhance the original goals of the conference to reach out at an international level, foster more international collaboration, integrate a greater number of European scientists, and achieve a more comprehensive scientific understanding.
Key elements of the recommendation

The focus of the ICSSI is to accelerate the development of the emerging, multidisciplinary field of the science of science. It will offer a platform for both producers (i.e., academic and industry scientists) and consumers/influencers (i.e., policymakers, publishers, funders, administrators, etc.) of the field to access funding, collaboration, idea exchange, and recognition. The aims are to support and cultivate the Science of Science community by institutionalizing this important feedback loop between producers and consumers/influencers in the field for years to come while advancing research and its application on the science of science and innovation and maximizing science’s benefits for human society.

Main applicant Dashun Wang has organized several conferences that delve deeply into the science of science. In 2016, he held his first international science of science conference at the Library of Congress. This gathering was instrumental in fostering a sense of shared identity among a diverse community of researchers and decision-makers, highlighting their common interest in pursuing scientific knowledge. Hosting this conference in Copenhagen in 2025 will represent a significant step toward efforts to reach out at a global level, foster international collaboration, and integrate more tightly with the EU representation in the science of science community. The budget primarily covers salary expenses for project team and event fee for the conference that expect to have 400 participants.

Memo: International Conference on the Science of Science and Innovation 2025
Introduction

Worldwide, interest is intensifying in how research is funded, practiced, and evaluated and in how research cultures and systems can be made more efficient, open, inclusive, and impactful. However, the research field of science of science still lacks forums/institutions or associations that bring together all interested parties. Despite the growing interest in researching and thinking about the multidisciplinary field of the science of science, only a few initiatives have taken place to initiate a forum for researchers working in this space to get together to present research papers, get feedback from top specialists in the field, learn about new data sources, and develop common research projects. Hence, there is a vast demand for cultivating the Science of Science community by institutionalizing the exchange of feedback between producers and consumers/influencers in the field, which is the International Conference on the Science of Science and Innovation (ICSSI) 2025 goal.

The PI, Professor Dashun Wang has organized several conferences that delve deeply into the science of science. In 2016, he held his first international science of science conference at the Library of Congress. This gathering was instrumental in fostering a sense of shared identity among a diverse community of researchers and decision-makers, highlighting their common interest in pursuing scientific knowledge. Building on this experience, the organizing team executed the inaugural ICSSI in 2022, followed by the second ICSSI in 2023. The 2022 conference was held at the National Academy of Sciences, and the 2023 conference was hosted by the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University. These interdisciplinary, in-person only events included panel discussions, keynote addresses, contributed research talks, poster sessions, and networking opportunities. In addition to these formal events for scholarly exchange, both conferences offered catered breaks, lunches, and a cocktail hour to foster informal interaction, networking, and community building within the field. The 2023 ICSSI also offered several concurrent sessions, a banquet, a pop-up art gallery, and a post-event hackathon. The conferences showcased the incredible diversity of research and innovation, featuring more than 30 internationally recognized speakers who represented academia, science funders, policymakers, and other consumers of the science of science research. The ICSSI will return to Washington, DC, in the summer of 2024.

The ICSSI is a critical part of the effort to continue to grow the science of science community, advance scientific research, and maximize science’s benefits to society. The ICSSI provides a unique platform for scientists studying scientific discovery to share research and ideas, build new connections, access funding, and collaborate with other academics in the emerging field of the science of science, as well as with policymakers, funders, publishers, administrators, and other stakeholders who support, use, and influence scientific research. Specifically, researchers at the conference discuss advanced techniques, algorithms, and tools for analyzing complex data sets and share insights and best practices across a wide range of research topics, including the lifecycle of scientific creativity, successful collaborations, innovative idea dissemination, and the factors influencing scientific productivity. Policymakers, funders, and other stakeholders glean a better understanding of the emerging field of science of science and its potential to impact scientific advancement and society more broadly. These insights can inform policies and strategies to enhance scientific outcomes and promote innovation, understanding, and collaboration.

Hosting ICSSI 2025 in Copenhagen will represent a significant step toward efforts to reach out at a global level, foster international collaboration, and integrate more tightly with the EU representation in the science of science community. A global presence may also enhance the ability of the conference to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of scientific advancements and to promote more cross-cultural collaboration and discovery.
Relevance to NNF’s strategy

Awarding this grant to the ICSSI 2025 aligns with NNF strategy by supporting and disseminating knowledge about the societal impact of research. The grant will support L.2, Enabling research infrastructure and technologies and L.3, Translational capacity and societal impact to build and disseminate knowledge about the societal impact of research. This ICSSI will facilitate collaboration among attendees, more international scientific collaboration, more influence on policy formulation and decision-making processes, advance the scientific knowledge, and develop new leaders in the science of science field. Research funders can get access to the latest research in the field.
Description of the initiative

This project aims to accelerate the development of the emerging, multidisciplinary field of the science of science. It will offer a platform for both producers (i.e., academic and industry scientists) and consumers/influencers (i.e., policymakers, publishers, funders, administrators, etc.) of the field to access funding, collaboration, idea exchange, and recognition. Through the establishment of annual conferences and the formalization of a professional society, we will cultivate the Science of Science community by institutionalising this important feedback loop between producers and consumers/influencers in the field for years to come while advancing research and its application on the science of science and innovation and maximise science’s benefits for human society.

This vibrant, three-day conference will include panel discussions, networking events, research poster sessions, award presentations, workshops, and events to recognize and express appreciation for outstanding contributions to the science of science.
Based on a recommendation from the CEO meeting on 5 February 2024, the ICSSI has received positive support from three other Danish foundations (Leo Foundation, Villum Foundation, and Carlsberg Foundation) with a total commitment of DKK 1,499,750.
Expected impact, success criteria and evaluation process

The ICSSI will cultivate a strongly connected community of researchers and consumers with newly funded research and new collaborations focused on identifying solutions for the world’s toughest scientific problems. The ICSSI will support the Science of Science Society and build an online presence for conferences aggregating published work and videos and the Science of Science social media accounts with active followers, contributors, and connections.

The ICSSI stands out among similar conferences because it provides a distinctive and inclusive platform that bridges diverse perspectives within the realm of scientific knowledge production and consumption. The ICSSI convenes scientists from industry and academia and policymakers, publishers, funders, and administrators, fostering a multi-channel dialogue that extends beyond traditional academic boundaries. This inclusive model contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the science of science, making it particularly relevant for global policies and communities. The ICSSI also seeks to encourage participation from students and early-career scientists from underrepresented backgrounds; travel grants for these attendees were provided in 2022 and 2023 to offset the high conference costs.

The ICSSI results in thought-provoking conference sessions, compelling papers, new research partnerships, and collaborative research initiatives among scientists, policymakers, and science funders. Being hosted in Europe, the 2025 ICSSI may also lead to more international scientific collaboration. Beyond the conference, the ICSSI has a dedicated website and social media accounts that allow for ongoing communication and collaboration between attendees. At a high level, the ICSSI advances scientific knowledge, influences policy formulation and decision-making processes, and fosters innovation on a global scale.

Beyond establishing the ICSSI for the field and the professional society, this grant could ultimately help develop a flourishing, multidisciplinary community that will expand global understanding of the drivers and mechanisms of innovation, which can be applied to reap more positive global societal change.
Next steps
Initiative a project planning group of the collaborating Co-funders, NNF and ICSSI.

The ICSSI 2025 will further develop the Science of Science Association as a professional association that can institutionalize the important producer/consumer feedback loop in the field for many years to come.

The next step for the Science of Science Society would be to open avenues of future research for the entire community to understand the challenges and needs of policy-makers and funders, which could impact the field beyond the lifetime of the project. The long-term impact on this research field could lead to improved use of resources for research and more accurate decisions, with large benefits for the advancement of science, the progress of science, and the well-being of human society.

1 Introduction: Augmented Innovation with Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI2) for
Material Discovery: Why and how

Research in many areas of materials science, and more broadly across physical and biological science and engineering is hampered by enormous design spaces that overwhelm researchers’ ability to evaluate the full range of potentially valuable candidate designs by simulation or experiment. Here we propose a software system that harnesses recent advances in data science, the science of science, and AI to reduce that search space by producing a stream of intelligent hypotheses that can accelerate and punctuate scientiﬁc advance, initially for materials discovery, but later for several other domains.

The success of modern artiﬁcial intelligence and machine learning applications has been driven by the increasing availability of large-scale data. In the context of science and technology, data-driven models fed with published scientiﬁc results and the results of prior experiments have been used to create powerful prediction engines, as the discovery of established and novel, designed materials with desirable properties or the targeted construction of new therapies. Such approaches have been designed in one-off experimental efforts. Because such efforts have been developed by domain scientists, they have never taken into account increasingly powerful insights from the science of science that could inform the range of information that can be harvested and exploited to improve scientiﬁc search. For example, these AI approaches have ignored insights regarding the wisdom of scientiﬁc crowds and the speciﬁc distribution of human researchers, who continuously alter the landscape of discovery and invention. As a result, AI algorithms often intentionally compete with human experts, failing to complement them in accelerating or punctuating collective advance. As we will demonstrate below, own experiments demonstrate that incorporating knowledge of experts and expertise can increase predictions of future discoveries by more than 100% over AI methods that ignore them.

More importantly, AI systems for hypothesis generation, regardless of sophistication, have never been developed into general purpose cyber-infrastructure that can be readily adapted for wide usage and scien- tiﬁc beneﬁt. Here we propose to develop and scale a high-throughput hypothesis generation engine that consumes datasets of facts from the literature and metadata on scientists and collaborations, hyperlinking them to produce intelligent, actionable and promising experiments. By programmatically incorporating in- formation on the evolving distribution of expertise, our system will enable a balance of exploitation and exploration in experimental search that will 1) accelerate discoveries predicted to appear in future, but also 2) punctuate advance by identifying promising experiments unlikely to be pursued within our system’s inter- vention. We will pilot a system that augments innovation with artiﬁcial intelligence to drive experiments in material science (AI2-MS), with an effort to scale it much more broadly across the physical and biological sciences. We will work with materials scientists to apply, evaluate, and reﬁne this system in the context of electrolytes, solar materials (e.g., photovoltaics, and other energy generating and storing materials (e.g., thermoelectricity, ferroelectricity). Such a system must not only serve up potential relationships, but show how it can respond to feedback from simulated and material experiments performed by our experimental partners.

Our approach is summarised by Figure 1. Our piloted experiment begins with a Fact Extract stage that takes as input the streaming research literature, encompassing both data—the content of the research arti- cles themselves—and meta-data on article authors, institutions, journals, and precise time published. The output of this stage for our material science case include (a) materials, alongside (b) material properties and their uses, but also (c) scientists and their high-dimensional contexts, and (d) time. Materials would include chemicals, compounds, mixtures, and composites. Properties comprise desirable and undesirable attributes of these materials, which may be quite general, like porosity, or more speciﬁc, such as whether a material can act as a semiconductor photocatalyst to promote water splitting and sacriﬁcially produce both hydrogen and oxygen. Overview: Identification of the research and issues

The “No Free Lunch” (NFL) theorems prove that no machine learning algorithm is better than any other across all possible problems (and all possible worlds)1,2. This suggests that rather than avoid bias, the task of machine intelligence is to assemble biases that correspond to the world. At the limit, this involves the creation of artificial agents (“digital twins”) to perceptually replicate that world. Consider how the human sensorium has evolved over millions of years. Since the scientific revolution, we have expanded our sensorium with prosthetics3,4 like telescopes that enable us to accomplish tasks ranging from probing the cosmos to enhancing national security. An emerging focus in cognitive science, dating to 19th-century physicist von Helmholz, centers on identifying the generative capacity underlying these sensors. In a famous 1995 paper, “The Helmholz Machine,” computer scientists built a successful generative model of sensory functions that enabled the statistical inference of their causal source and significance in the world5.

In Helmholz’s conception, the violation of generative models draws special attention to unexpected sensory inputs6. In this way, the phenomena of attention as driven by expectation violation lies at the root of human sensory experience and modern deep neural networks7. 19th Century polymath Charles Peirce argued that neither the logics of deduction nor induction alone could characterize reasoning, but rather their collision in a process he termed abduction. Abduction begins as expectations born of experience, tradition, or theory become disrupted by unexpected surprises8. When our models are violated by sensory input, we become surprised and shift attention to the unexpected, which spurs new understandings to make the surprising unsurprising. But how do these new understandings emerge and in a robust, accurate form?

To explore this, consider abduction beyond the context of an individual human perceiver, but occurring across the global, collaborative system of scientific discovery. One account for where new hypotheses emerge is serendipity, or making the most of surprising encounters9,10; as per Pasteur’s oft-quoted maxim “chance favors only the prepared mind”11. But this poses a paradox. The successful scientific mind must simultaneously know enough within a scientific context to be surprised, and enough outside to imagine why it should not be surprising. Surprising successes systematically emerge across, rather than within, researchers; most commonly when those in one field surprisingly publish problem-solving results to audiences in a distant other12. This suggests the importance for multi-modal, artificial intelligent agents not merely to have a single model of the world, but many models—a society of mind13—such that when a dominant model is surprised, others may engage through conversation, and become repurposed and rebuilt to resolve that surprise. The activation space underlying large, multi-modal foundation models can similarly generate text, images, sound, and video that mirror the diverse styles of content represented among their training data14–16. Recent work demonstrates how inference in these models optimizes plausible outcomes by unleashing a within-model process of gradient descent for error minimization akin to the process of fine-tuning a model from external data17,18. If we conceive of the high-dimensional foundation model space as a space of cognitive world models, we may conceive of perception as abduction, which opens new opportunities to understand and optimize it. This recommends that we understand these models as simultaneously unlocking insights into and learning lessons from individual cognition and collective culture.

In the context of multi-modal sensation, alternative sensors are often redundant and surprise one another. One can identify a jet aircraft by sight, sound, touch, or smell, but sensory data does not always reduce to a simple, singular picture of the world. When sensors are well-calibrated and reliable, then the surprise associated with their conflict can be trusted as an indication of critical surprise. In science, the experimentally reliable distinction between wave and particle
representations of light garnered confidence in new understandings about quantum phenomena, just as surprising sensors in a field of conflict are central for unveiling a strategic deception.

Technical approach Our proposed project will explore and expand the sensory capacity of multi-modal foundation models in the following four ways. We will (1) evaluate a theory of perception as abduction across the complex cognitive space underlying multi-modal models. Such an approach will exploit surprising deviations within and between vector-based “perspectives” identified within and across layers of these models19. This will draw upon innovations by our team members and others to align representations across model layers through placing and following tracers20, and deploying theory and methods from both neurocognitive (e.g. fMRI techniques)21–24 and dynamics in social networks25–27. We will examine, trace, and align such representations within and across sensory modalities to identify redundancies and distinctive biases among them.
We will also (2) develop methods to robustly evaluate the accuracy of foundation model

generations by expanding our view of these models from cognition to culture in order to effectively preserve uncertainty and perspective conflict. Large language and multi-modal models are currently less entropic than human individuals and populations over time. We will explicitly articulate, model, and enhance the capacity for foundation models to preserve sensory and model diversity. We propose a variety of architectural approaches that delay convergence, then calibrate and deploy these diverse computational perspectives to improve our reliable causal estimation of significant, surprising events from sensory data.

Next, we will (3) investigate the distillation of models for specific application scenarios by exploring differences between the intrinsic geometry and dimensionality between efficient (a) model learnability and (b) model representation. Overparameterized models have evolved in both brains and machines to enable flexible, context-sensitive learning.28 We will explore the number, topological architecture, and intrinsic geometry of model parameters needed to learn models, update models, and store and deploy “fixed” models. This will allow us to use and experiment with distilled systems as digital twins of their larger counterparts within dynamic contexts (such as security settings) that can benefit from lean, special-purpose intelligence.

Finally, (4) we will develop mathematical methods to predict the performance of perception systems by designing a range of novel behavioral tasks for which multi-modal perception is critical. This will allow us to examine when language is not enough (e.g., when it insufficiently captures bias)—when it must be expanded with sensory capacity in other modalities from cognition and culture to perform. We will harness three core methods from our prior work: (i) mathematical modeling of perceptual functions, (ii) controlled psychophysical behavioral and fMRI experiments for comparing the perceptual experience across machine learning models and humans, and (iii) interactive social network experiments that involve agents’ coordinating perceptual models, learning abductively from coordination surprises, and eventually establishing shared descriptions of the world. Consider the following example from our prior work and our proposed extension for how we will integrate these three components in a novel paradigm.

The study of cultural intelligence—among humans and robots29,30—often evokes a simple game that requires agents to coordinate their perceptual models through the use of language. In prior work, our team examined how human populations develop shared vocabulary systems when completing this kind of game online. Participants were tasked with sending each other single words of their choice for the purpose of directing each other to click on ambiguous, novel shapes within a complex environment of many such shapes.27 We found that small populations arrived at highly idiosyncratic categories for these shapes—i.e., divergent perceptual models of

the same artificial world. Yet, separate large populations independently converged on highly similar perceptual models of these same shapes. Our theory explains that in small populations, social influence allows individuals’ idiosyncratic views to take hold. However, in a large marketplace of ideas, weak cognitive biases conserved across the population pressure agents to converge on the options that reflect their shared, embodied common ground, leading to replicable evolutionary trajectories in the emergence of a collective world model.
We aim to extend this work by (i) simulating this experiment with artificial agents (“digital

twins”) to examine the different world models that emerge under varying conditions of perception and social interaction, and (ii) modifying the extent to which multimodal translations are required for coordination among agents in this language game. Imagine an analog of this game in which, rather than exchanging linguistic labels to coordinate, agents exchange images or sounds as they develop a multimodal pairing system for coordinating on the selection of stimuli from either the same or a different modality. This paradigm makes it possible to grow different multimodal interfaces through the coordination process. We can then apply methods of model interpretability to characterize the information architecture that artificial agents develop when converting signals between modalities during the coordination game. We can further use information-theoretic measures (e.g., Shannon entropy and compression) to characterize which modality conversions (e.g., color to word, sound to image) exhibit the greatest efficiency and stability. The goal is not only to study the emergence of multimodal interfaces as a function of social coordination, but also to characterize their stability in terms of cognitive and social biases, and ultimately to make robust predictions about the emergence of multimodal models in human populations examined through the same experimental infrastructure.
As part of this process, we will develop behavioral paradigms to compare the world models

formed by populations of artificial and human agents. Our team has a strong track record of innovation in this area23, using both mathematical, behavioral, and fMRI techniques31–34. For example, our team developed novel computational and mathematical paradigms for identifying the models of color perception latent in a range of computer vision algorithms as well as humans. We use wavelet transformers to outperform extant machine learning approaches in emulating human color perception. This is promising since wavelets have been shown to capture a variety of computational problems (e.g., compression) and likely capture perceptual representations across modalities. We also developed a behavioral sorting task that allowed direct comparisons of how human perceptions of color similarity relate to those produced by any vision algorithm. This involved the creation of validated psychophysical stimuli (such as controlled color tiles and gratings and composite images with controlled color distributions) which allowed for controlled elicitation and observation of the perceptual models latent in both artificial and human agents. Our proposal to incorporate psychophysical validation paradigms into socially interactive experiments will make a critical advance not only in the interpretability of the perceptual features in foundation models, but also in how such models aggregate via interacting agents into shared world models via communication dynamics (which ultimately mediate the abductive processes of world-formation as agents learn from the surprises that arise as they attempt to coordinate). Our team has the unique expertise capable of combining these simulation experiments with association behavioral and fMRI analyses for identifying, benchmarking, and augmenting the perceptual representations that underlie foundation models and their interactions.

Impact on DoD capabilities Improved sensory modeling and multi-modal capacity integrated within artificial intelligence has profound implications for national defense and security, particularly in terms of preparing for

and responding to systemic and unexpected shocks at both small and large scales. Our proposal to study foundation models in the context of socially networked experiments is especially relevant concerning the ability to simulate the conditions under which agents are more or less likely to successfully integrate their world models for the purpose of group coordination and problem solving. Our proposed paradigm offers the potential to simulate ways of improving the ability of agents to integrate their world models—or to sustain coordination despite differences in world models—as a function of individual-level modifications to learning algorithms, as well as collective-level modifications to network structures and interaction patterns. This is useful for (1) validating sensory inferences from existing multi-modal models in fluid, high-risk security settings where individual and group-level adaptive reasoning is essential; (2) integrating novel sensory capacities into existing large multi-modal models for expanding the integrated intelligence capacity of surprising adversaries and avoiding surprise by them; and (3) projecting “minimal” models into lean representations for special-purpose individual and autonomous deployment in flexible settings, e.g. in human-AI hybrid collective intelligence systems.

Research team and management plan We have assembled a team of experts equipped with the necessary knowledge to implement this proposal—i.e., experts in deep transformer-based multi-modal foundation models from the perspective of neural networks, social networks, cognition, culture, and arbitrary artificial and physical systems. The team will be led by PI James A. Evans, Max Palevsky Professor of Sociology and Data Science, University of Chicago and Santa Fe Institute, who studies the sensory and knowledge capacity of large multi-modal models to simulate cognition and culture; Co-PI Brice Ménard, Professor of Physics and cognitive science, Johns Hopkins University who studies the properties of neural networks in artificial and biological systems; Co-PI Douglas Guilbeault, assistant professor in Organizational Behavior, Graduate School of Business, Stanford University who studies computational models of cognition and culture; Co-PI Lisa Aziz-Zadeh, assistant professor at the Brain and Creativity Institute and Psychology, University of Southern California (USC) who studies the correspondence between brains and AI models; and Co-PI Ethan Nadler incoming assistant professor of astrophysics at UCSD, who studies cosmology and the mathematics of perception. Evans will convene bi-weekly meetings with the research teams across institutions to coordinate the analytical, simulation, and empirical work. The team has extensive experience working together and integrating diverse research modalities.

Summary of estimated costs We propose a budget of $1.5M/year, which will support a postdoctoral research associate for each (Co-)PI for each of the 5 years. We note that multiple investigators have deep collaborations with AI-based companies, institutes, and agencies (e.g., Google, Anthropic, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, the Department of Energy’s Trillion Parameter Consortium) that will give us unique access to large-scale models that supersede the costs of our budget.

A. Personal Statement
For this proposal, I bring over 20 years of experience conducting brain-imaging and behavioral

studies on cognitive neuroscience in humans. I am currently the director of the Center for the Neuroscience of Embodied Cognition (CeNEC) and a professor at Brain and Creativity Institute (BCI), Department of Psychology, and Division of Occupational Science and Occupational Therapy, at the University of Southern California (USC). My research has focused on understanding how sensorimotor and emotion related brain circuits underlie higher cognition, such as empathy, compassion, social understanding, and communication. A large part of my work has focused on social cognition, including working with both typically developing populations as well as clinical populations (congenital amputees, autism spectrum disorder, developmental coordination disorder). I have served as Principal Investigator (PI) on numerous studies from the NIH, DoD, Google Research Grants, and other foundations. Thus I have 15 years of experience leading and participating in interdisciplinary collaborative projects. I look forward to applying this expertise to the current proposal, Modeling perception as abduction to explore, expand, and enrich the sensorium of large multi-modal models. In particular, I have a history of collaboration with Doug Guilbeault and Ethan Nadler, and look forward to continuing to collaborate with them and other colleagues in this important project.

C. Contributions to Science

1. The neural basis of social and empathic processing. How do we understand and empathize with other people, especially those dissimilar to us? In a series of MRI/fMRI experiments and theory papers, I have explored this topic from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective. We have looked at understanding other people’s actions and intentions, empathizing with their experiences, as well as how these processes are modulated by having differences between the self and other. We have studied both typically developing people as well as clinical cases to deepen our understanding of this topic. I have had a Google Research grant, an NIH R01 and R03 grant as well as private foundation grants, and I have served as the PI on all projects. brain activity in regions associated with physical pain and reward. 4. Embodied semantics. Embodied semantics is a linguistic theory that posits that sensorimotor regions involved in the experience of a concept are also involved in the semantic representation of the concept. For example, embodied semantics would predict that the phrase “kick the ball” would be processed by motor regions involved in kicking actions. My group has been among the first to investigate neural support for this theory. We have conducted a number of studies on this topic, and I have been part of a large multisite Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity (IARPA) grant (W911NF-12-C-0022), where I was the PI of the brain imaging experiments. Our data revealed that language does indeed activate sensorimotor brain regions involved in the experience associated with the meaning of the linguistic phrase. We have found support for this in motor regions, in visual processing regions, and in emotion related brain regions. We have also found that context and individual difference can modulate these effects. b. Landau, A.N., Aziz-Zadeh, L., & Ivry, R.B. (2010).
