Abstract. The notion of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) that computationally mimics human intelligence has dominated computational intelligence designs, but is tuned to replace humanity rather than augment its capacity. We argue that AI should be designed to complement individual and collective human capacity, avoid humanity’s blind spots, and overcome cognitive and cultural limitations. In this research initiative, we aim to conceptualize the nature and character of complementary AI, and advance ambitious research and technology designs that target human-AI complementarity. We will conduct research in the following pathways towards human-AI complementary: AI coordinators to divide and conquer with fixed human and AI capabilities in the present; AI coaches to help humans to better unleash AI capabilities and compensate for its limitations; AI collaborators to complement human strengths and weaknesses; AI controllers to survey, audit, and regulate other AIs to ensure human benefit; and to promote beneficial human-AI co-evolution over the long run towards healthy human-AI ecosystems that enable expanded collective capacity and flourishing in society. This initiative will advance data and AI science by raising novel, complex questions regarding how to train models without targeting. It will require increased integration with social and behavioral sciences to model and monitor evolving individual and collective human limitations. It will draw on business and economics expertise to measure and model human-AI productivity; legal and policy expertise to propose models of AI co-regulation; and expertise across sciences, engineering, arts, and humanities to explore and experiment with expanding human-AI capacity and imagination regarding the greatest challenges facing humanity.

Complementary AI
James Evans, Sociology and Data Science
Chenhao Tan, Computer Science and Data Science, Harris School of Public Policy

Research Initiative Description. “Artificial Intelligence” (AI) was initially coined1 to canonize Alan Turing’s “imitation game” approach to computationally mimic human intelligence2. This notion of AI dominated computational intelligence designs for more than half a century, it is tuned to replicate and replace humanity, but not augment our capacity to face our greatest challenges. Alternatively, we argue that AI should be designed to complement individual and collective human capacity, avoid humanity’s blind spots, and overcome cognitive and cultural limitations. In this research initiative, we aim to conceptualize the nature and character of complementary AI, and advance ambitious research and technology designs that target human-AI complementarity. We will conduct research in the following pathways towards human-AI complementary: AI coordinators to divide and conquer with fixed human and AI capabilities in the present; AI coaches to help humans to better unleash AI capabilities and compensate for its limitations; AI collaborators to complement human strengths and weaknesses; AI controllers to survey, audit, and regulate other AIs to ensure human benefit; and to promote beneficial human-AI co-evolution over the long run towards healthy human-AI ecosystems that enable expanded collective capacity and flourishing in society.

This initiative will advance the fields of data science and artificial intelligence by addressing complex and novel questions regarding data generation and training without human performance templates. It will involve the construction of digital doubles of individual and collective humans to model AI complementarity. Moreover, it will require increased integration with social and behavioral sciences to identify and monitor evolving individual and collective human limitations. The initiative will draw on business and economics expertise to measure and model human-AI productivity; legal and policy expertise to propose models of AI co-regulation; and expertise across sciences, engineering, arts, and humanities to explore and experiment with expanding human-AI capacity and imagination regarding the greatest challenges facing humanity.

PI qualifications and prior work. PI Evans has done pathbreaking research in the creation of AI “digital doubles” of humans and human systems3,4, but also in creating human-aware AI systems that complement human systems, especially in the context of scientific discovery, technology innovation, and new venture creation5–8. He has been a leader in the computational social science and science of science and innovation communities, founding and recurrently running the international conference on the latter, with a special focus on how to build AI that complements science, social science, and innovation5,9–12. PI Tan has done pioneering research in human-centered AI, especially in developing human-centered explanations that aim to achieve complementarity in human-AI decision making, including a theoretical framework to understand the role of human intuitions13, model-driven tutorials14, human-compatible case-based explanations15, evaluation of the utility of explanations16,17. He has also worked on delegability18 and novel paradigms of human-AI interaction19.

Moreover, Evans and Tan have worked together in organizing and running conferences, and engaging in collaborative research. They were recently invited to write a perspective on Complementary AI for the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

Societal impact. An important side outcome of the AGI vision is that it leads to siloed communities where AI researchers focus on realizing AGI, while the rest of the world focuses on criticizing AI and bracing for new AI to come. We believe that it is critical to promote collective discussion regarding the best route for human-AI complementarity and set complementary AI as the ultimate vision, competing with and (hopefully) displacing AGI. This proposal invites researchers across the UChicago campus community to engage with interdisciplinary efforts to advance the frontier and the ecosystem of complementary AI.
Community Building, Outreach, Broadening Participation, and Partnerships.

The research initiative will actively seek to involve and incorporate students, postdoctoral scholars and junior faculty in both its convening activities (e.g., reading groups, workshops, conferences) that set the agenda for the initiative, and also in realizing that agenda through research and design. We involve faculty, researchers, staff, and students from groups historically underrepresented in data science in a special sub-initiative on identifying the diversity of human values against which AI should complement, and how complementing the capacities of some humans and human groups can constrain others. We will also seek out partnerships with institutions for which AI can create expanded capacity, ranging from local prisoner rehabilitation and technology training to national scientific and innovation investment and defense.

Advancing DSI’s and the University’s Strategic Mission. This research initiative leverages the strengths of social sciences at the University of Chicago and complements the existing AI and Science research initiative. It promotes an alternative vision to artificial general intelligence and can potentially contribute a new school of thought in AI. PIs will develop related courses that can be integrated into the PhD and masters programs.

Funding and Sustainability. We believe that this initiative will attract substantial funding interest from government and philanthropic funders. Evans and a CS colleague from UIUC (Lav Varshney) just received a DARPA grant to build an AI-based approach to evaluate the creative complementarity of research hypotheses and findings generated by AI. We have learned of other approximately aligned funding initiatives from across the US Department of Defense (e.g., DOD headquarters, DARPA, AFOSR, ONR, Army), and related interest from the Moore, Open Philanthropies, Templeton, Sloan, Novo Nordisk, and Allen Institute for AI foundations. We believe that this initiative could speciate funding opportunities in specific areas of complementarity (e.g., AI self-governance, AI creativity augmentation, etc.) that could lead to new funded initiatives. We will actively seek DSI support to target existing initiatives and to help inspire and guide new initiatives in this domain.

Project plan. We will consider the following efforts in the next four years:
We will build a framework for dissecting jobs, tasks, and cases for coordinating the current distribution of capabilities across human and AI. We will propose new algorithms to perform the coordination between human and AI and build new datasets to benchmark the capabilities of human and AI. This effort will last from year 1 until year 4.

We will build novel explanation algorithms and assistance to coach humans about AI capabilities and desirable ways to use AI in a human-centered way. This requires better modeling of human intuitions. This effort will last from year 1 until year 4.

We will advance algorithms to improve AI models so that they can be better collaborators for humans, including building robust and controllable AI, aligning AI with human values and decision making mechanisms, and advancing the understanding of human-AI collaboration. This effort will last from year 1 until year 4.
Exploring novel theories and perspectives to advance our understanding of human-AI co-evolution. This effort will start from year 2.

We will work with the broader research community at the University of Chicago to explore opportunities to improve human-AI collaboration with ideas from complementary AI, ranging from healthcare to scientific research.
Partnerships and collaboration. The PI of this project will be James Evans and Chenhao Tan. We will have the following people as external advisors:
Leadership and governance.

What success will look like? The key measures of success are twofold. First, the University of Chicago is recognized as the thought leader in the space of complementary AI. Second, there are dynamic communities and efforts across different parts of the campus that build complementary AI and leverage complementary AI to improve human endeavor. 
In 3-4 years, we will hopefully be well positioned to apply for substantial funding either from NSF or from foundations.

We propose the development of an innovative data-driven, model-based system to comprehensively evaluate and predict the scientific and societal impacts of research funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF). This evaluation will occur across the universe of relevant research, including possible research they could fund in future and could have funded in the past. This system will provide NNF with situational awareness to strategically lead, rather than follow, global scientific trends, particularly in the domains of health, environment, and biological science. By leveraging advanced AI techniques and network science, the proposed system will map the complex landscape of scientific content and contexts, creating a powerful “digital double” of scientific attention and impact over time. This dynamic model will further facilitate informed decision-making by simulating the potential consequences of various scientific developments, allowing NNF decision-makers to actively predict and shape the trajectory of science and technology advancement. The project’s multidimensional metrics will assess contributions to emerging and established areas of research, the prescience of science and technology outputs, and the disruptive nature of innovations. If successful, this pioneering approach holds the promise of transforming how foundations and organizations worldwide assess, evaluate, and drive scientific and societal progress.

The Novo Nordisk Foundation represents the leading global foundation for scientific research and societal impact. This places them in the unique position not to follow, but lead scientific efforts with the potential to impact the health and prosperity of the planet with a special commitment to substantial investments in the science of health, environment and biological science. In the Novo Nordisk Foundation’s 2022 Societal Impact report, the foundation details a powerful commitment to social impacts across nine distinctive areas: fostering diverse talent and stimulating equity-inducing collaboration, supporting organizations and infrastructure, promoting excellence and innovation in research, developing innovative products and solutions for society, creating jobs and growth, developing new technologies that impact global health, and raising the bar on global education. Each of these commitments is paired with metrics to assess Novo Nordisk’s impact. Here we propose the development of a data-driven, model-based system by which the foundation can assess scientific and societal impacts in an integrated way, but also predict future ones, allowing it to maximize its leadership potential to improve global health and environment, alongside institutional impacts to improve access and participation in future generations of science. Specifically, our system will allow the foundation to simultaneously consider and simulate the consequences of a range of possible investment decisions, which will empower reasoned selection, and the ability to causally influence science, scientific infrastructure, and science environments in powerful ways.

Science can be explored as a whole, leveraging increasingly widespread open-access data about science and the scientific process combined with powerful modeling advances from artificial intelligence (AI) and network science. The persistence (or inertia) and density (or overlaps) of people working on topics within the scientific system allow us to build a powerful “digital double” of scientific attention, impact, and investment over time, which we can project into the future. AI in the form of deep neural networks provides novel representation learning techniques that allow us to map the scientific content of scientific fields across tens of millions of papers, concepts, and claims onto continuous distributions of points in high-dimensional vector spaces (embeddings). Similarly, they allow us to map the scientific context of regional and national innovation systems (e.g., the EU and member countries) across all participating institutions, authors, and diverse identities projected onto the same space. This allows us to link funded identities and institutions (contexts) with their scientific output (content) and its implications for technology, scientific capacity, and benefit to humanity. Such techno-scientific maps allow us to directly measure the geometric distances between scientific items as semantic and scientific similarities. Moreover, contents and contexts have a discrete graph representation, where one may explore items that have a realized relationship, along with the strength of that relation. This generates citation networks of papers, collaboration networks of authors, and discrete knowledge bases of scientific claims. Together, one can view these discrete representations as scientific facts that occur; and the continuous AI-learned manifolds as the probability of scientific events likely to occur in future.

Longitudinal analyses of embeddings and networks allow us to determine how science evolves, with a special focus on the disciplines of the Novo Nordisk Foundation: the sciences of health, environment, and underlying biology. Specifically, we propose two approaches that can identify gaps in the knowledge space and new links across the space where cross-fertilization is most likely, and where they would be most surprising and impactful to science, technology, and human benefit. This would allow the Novo Nordisk Foundation to identify contributions where it would lead rather than follow global scientific activity like a few of the other strategic foundations, including the Gates Foundation in the U.S. and the Wellcome Trust in the UK. Furthermore, modeling the scientific system as a whole would allow us to simulate the causal impact of its investments before it makes them in order to evaluate multiple investments ahead of time. This would allow the foundation to not only passively react to proposals that come in, but more directly target and catalyze new work with the greatest potential to punctuate advances in life-enhancing science and technology. In this way, we propose to create a system that can recommend how to strategically expand the frontier of knowledge in the Foundation’s core topics.

As we propose below, we will initially generate three classes of model-based metrics that assess Novo Nordisk Foundation-funded science and technology in the context of global, European, and Danish scientific development. The first relates to the Novo Nordisk Foundation’s contribution to emerging versus established areas of research. The second relates to their production of prescient vs. predictable science and technology. The third examines the degree to which these novelties have been received and acknowledged as disruptive new directions to science and technology or developing established directions. We will compare these funded projects with unfunded projects, research that did not seek funding and research that was not performed, but could have been catalyzed.

We will also prospectively assess the first two measures (the third is ex post), on new applications as a pilot of a grant recommendation system, which could be used as the basis for funding experiments that demonstrate the causal impact of model-based investing. Our model would propose investments of various risk profiles, and predict impacts on scientific, technological, and human systems that could be compared in micro- and meso-scale investments. Corrections from these experiments could be incorporated into our “surrogate” model of the scientific system. We will also seek to incorporate additional measures and evaluations that capture other NNF goals in an integrated way, highlighting overlapping opportunities as well as trade-offs between them with respect to investments. This model-based approach would allow the Novo Nordisk Foundation to more powerfully design investments that satisfy their values for impact, but also to demonstrate the future impact of those plans and evaluate realized outcomes with greater coherence and visibility.

Benefits to the Novo Nordisk Foundation

Our project will allow us to help the NNF evaluate: (1) proposals for research funding and the amount and character of their projected impact; (2) individual researchers, as a function of their prior work and trajectory, along with the amount and character of their impact; (3) research institutions (e.g., proposed institutes), as a function of their portfolio of prior projects and distribution of personnel; (4) calls for proposals in terms of their risk and ripeness for potential discovery. We will evaluate each of these products, people, and institutions the fulsome context of existing competitors, but also counterfactuals we can generate and evaluate through simulation.

We will work closely with Novo Nordisk Foundation evaluation staff, and especially the Impacts department, as a collaborator, with a commitment to implement the resulting system across NNF interests. Specifically, we will evaluate potential science investments to explore scaling up the system to incorporate additional impact metrics and work with the Impact department and other NNF granting staff to trace the potential for follow-up experiments that unequivocally demonstrate causal impacts. If successful, we would seek a deeper partnership with the Novo Nordisk Foundation to incorporate designed capacities into NNF procedures. Success would enable the Novo Nordisk Foundation to emerge as the global leader in science-based impact investing, which could be followed by foundations and governments around the world. We also hope that engagement with Novo Nordisk Foundation staff would allow us to perform follow-on projects that explore the nature of downstream implications.

The NNF will benefit from this project on both short and long-term time scales. On the short term, we will provide the NNF with an engine for the evaluation of grants, requests for proposals, people, and research institutions in terms of risk and benefit to the NNF, science, and society. Over the longer term, we will build a system of scientific simulation that will allow the prospecting of new opportunities that maximize the impact and visibility of the foundation. We will also explore and build new systems to facilitate the integration of emerging AI models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs) as detailed below. Moreover, we will expand our evaluations beyond NNF proposals and grants to include Novo Holdings life science company investments (e.g., seed, venture and growth investments), Novo Nordisk’s therapeutic developments (e.g., Diabetes, Obesity, etc.), and Novozymes’ industrial biological applications (e.g., industrial enzymes and microoranisms). On the shorter term, this will enable us provide an evaluation of investment strategies across a range of areas. On the longer term, it will facilitate the identification of natural and quasi-experiment statistical experiments, and also stage controlled funding “experiments” in collaboration with NNF and member companies.

From our findings, we will generate a series of technological dashboards to provide NNF and associated companies with the situational awareness required to improve the quality and diversification of their technology development portfolios. These dashboards will be powered by APIs that link them flexibly with publication, patent, and product databases, as well as our digital doubles of the scientific system to allow expansion and reconfiguration for a wide range of uses. 
Data
The main features of Novo Nordisk Foundation data we will use for our project include:

Context. The Novo Nordisk Foundation database has dedicated fields for the main components of each proposal: problem statement, purpose, research question, hypothesis, project partners, past experience of the team in the topic (project history), state of the art, project components, and project evaluation. From these fields, we will be able to project these proposed and funded projects within an evolving knowledge space where these projects can be situated and identified as leading, lagging, or less relevant for ongoing scientific and technical progress.

Content. We will link this with content data from all of the dominant databases cover the broader universe of scientific research. These include OpenAlex, the open source descendent of the Microsoft Academic Graph; Clarivate’s Web of Science; and Springer Nature’s Dimensions database. From these data, we will model titles, abstracts, and article full-text where possible. We will richly annotate these databases with structured meta-data, including funding data from acknowledgments linked with the online databases of national funding, the demography of investigators, and research organizations.

Output. The Novo Nordisk data also includes publications produced by the project. From them we will extract text information to position them in the evolving knowledge space, as well as citation information, to assess impact, disruptiveness versus development, as well as novelty and prescience in the unfolding evolution science and society-enhancing technologies.
Three Complementary Approaches

Scientific and technological development are fundamentally global, collective phenomena: New ideas and tools accumulate and diffuse around the world as public goods, replacing prior approaches in long waves of creative destruction.1,2 In this project, we seek to explore the leadership role that the Novo Nordisk Foundation is playing in global, European, and Danish science and technology. Analysis of recent shifts in global scientific leadership has reduced the phenomenon to metrics such as research articles produced, authors who produce them, and the citation attention they garner across the global system of science. These indicators trace scientific and technological leadership in the past, but not the future. Here we propose construction of novel families of model-based measurements, estimated across global scientific activity from 2000, which effectively capture leadership in terms of science and technology that is globally and regionally on the rise.

In order to identify distinct dimensions of leadership, we take three complementary approaches that evaluate national contributions to unfolding global scientific and technological advance across all areas and within critical strategic areas including artificial intelligence, biotechnology, energy, and semiconductors. Our first approach identifies the leadership of each sample of science within emerging versus established or dissolving areas of science and technology by building a model that embeds more and less probable research pathways through an evolving hypergraph of research ideas and scientists.3,4 In prior work, we showed that simulating plausible research pathways with this model enabled highly accurate predictions of future discoveries and the discoverers who will make them in areas across the physical and biological sciences.5 This model reveals gradual “tectonic shifts” among scientific concepts and can predict the eruption of new areas as their component ideas and techniques move toward catalysis. It also directly predicts which scientists and funders are poised to lead in these emerging areas. In this part of the project, we will also explore deep network transformer models that build upon the technologies underlying Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 and its contemporaries (see final section for details).

Our second approach builds a distinctive model to capture the global prescience versus predictability or irrelevance of scientific contributions by building a model of the probability of each combination of concepts through their projection within an embedding of scientific work that evolves over time. In prior work, we showed that papers that are surprising in the year they are published are more likely to become high-citation or hit papers.6 Here we extend that insight to show the degree to which Novo Nordisk and comparable foundations and governments produce “prescient” papers that start surprising when published, but become the norm for research in the future. Insofar as our first approach identifies leadership in areas predicted to emerge based on existing currents in science and technology; our second identifies leadership in areas that pivot science and technology toward new, unexpected directions that violate existing currents. In this part of the project, we will also explore extensions of the model. This may include explicitly building on the LLM architecture underlying modern interactive chatbots, but training those models chronologically (and causally), year-by-year, to identify proposed and funded projects that defy not only the unstructured composition (e.g., as more or less surprising bags of concepts), but their structured composition, introducing a new syntax of scientific and technical claims (see final section).

Our third approach identifies the degree to which emergent and prescient work becomes recognized as disruptive by the broader research community. Innovation is unequally rewarded, and prior work demonstrates that scientific novelty does not always translate into recognition7. We model the scientific community’s response and recognition for emerging or prescient published research using citation patterns. Citations indicate the importance of a work, signaling the substantive source of ideas or potentially a symbolic gesture that others do (or ought to) recognize a work as important. Rather than trace raw research attention, we adopt the citation-based ‘disruption index’8–11 to quantify the extent to which a new publication displaces by eclipsing prior work in the network of citations (Fig. 3a). Based upon scholars’ tendency to cite a work instead of versus alongside the sources it draws on, the disruption index characterizes how the novelty of a current work has become appreciated by the scientific community. Unlike the other two approaches, which look prospectively at work that leads toward new science and technology advancements, this approach retrospectively identifies work attributed downstream for new directions responsible for pivots in the pattern of scientific attention.

Detailed Methods 
Data
We will use the Dimensions database from Digital Science, the Web of Science, and Open Alex. Digital Science is a synthetic database linking 136M global research papers, 154M global patents, 7M grants, 252M Altmetric data points reflecting public engagement, 787K clinical trials, and 933K policy documents.

We replicate these analyses on the Web of Science (WoS) Core Collection database of academic publications, citations, and authors for our modeling. We focus most of our analyses on the years 2000-2021. Author-based analyses begin in 2008, a year when WoS indexing and metadata linkage for authors dramatically improved, and ends with the most recent year for which we have full data. We further narrowed our analyses to exclude review articles and articles not in English. We use a very conservative author disambiguation strategy relying on names and email addresses to ensure that matched authors really are the same, although this will mean that some authors have multiple records and our overall count of authors is likely to be an overcount. We will ensure the robustness of our conclusion by demonstrating their robustness to this and all other relevant operational decisions.

We will replicate these analyses with OpenAlex 12, an open access database similar to the WoS, but with broader coverage of publication venues, especially including conferences where leading AI research is published. 
Modeling Prescience

We model the emergence of inferred techno-scientific connections collectively and cognitively accessible to scientists by constructing a hypergraph over research publications. A hypergraph is a generalized graph where an edge connects a set of nodes rather than a node pair. Our research hypergraph is mixed, containing nodes corresponding not only to techno-scientific keywords contributed by the authors (Web of Science) or directly inferred from article title and text (OpenAlex and Dimensions), but also the alternatively funded and situated researchers who investigate them. Following construction of this research hypergraph, we identify cognitively accessible inferences by generating random walk sequences over it. These walks suggest paths of inference available to active human scientists. If one scientific concept representing a scientific phenomenon (e.g., COVID-19) is investigated by a scientist who, in prior research, worked with another concept (e.g., a therapeutic drug), that scientist is more likely to consider whether those two concepts meaningfully combine within a valuable discovery or invention than a scientist without the research experience. If that scientist later coauthors with another who has previously worked with another concept (e.g., a vaccine) that scientist is more likely to imagine whether the putative vaccine has the property of COVID-19 prevention through conversation than a scientist without the personal connection.5 In this way, the density of random walks over our research hypergraph is proportional to the density of cognitively plausible and conversationally attainable inferences. For a pair of techno-scientific literatures that share many authoring scientists, a random walk over our hypergraph will frequently bridge them, just as a researcher will rarely consider connecting a property valued only in one community with a material understood only in a disjoint one. It has been identified that topics with high human expert density around them proffer an informative signal regarding near-future discoveries. These topics might be located far from one another in terms of the number of steps required to travel between them in the hypergraph, but a random walker—and the collective scientific mind—can easily travel between them if intermediate steps are socially dense, facilitating conversation and collaboration.

To generate each random walk sequence, our model (i) initiates the walk with one techno-scientific concept as first node in the sequence, (ii) randomly selects an article (hyperedge) having mentioned that concept, (iii) randomly selects another concept or author from that article as next node (end of first step), then starts the second step by randomly selecting another article with the newly selected concept or author, and repeats this Markov process 3,13 a pre-specified number of times (see Supplementary Information for more details). Each random walk step can be viewed as a simulation of human action: an author-author step mimics networking or conversation between two expert collaborators; an author-concept step represents how an author is deeply familiar with the selected concept they have studied and published on; finally, a concept-concept step captures the potential for the transition to be realized by scientists through reading a collection of scientific articles. From the collaborative character of science, author nodes in our hypergraph outnumber concepts. To compensate for this imbalance, we use a non-uniform sampling distribution parameterized by 𝛼, which roughly determines the fraction of concept to author nodes in resulting sequences. We follow the parameter that maximizes the likelihood of predicting discovery, 𝛼=1, such that scientists and concepts are equally likely to be chosen.

Random walks over the mixed hypergraph induce meaningful proximities between nodes. The proximity of two authors suggests they share similar research interests and experiences. The proximity of a concept to a scientist assesses the likelihood she is or will become familiar with that concept through research experience, related reading, or social interaction. The proximity of concepts to one another suggests that they may be substitutes, complements or share another more subtle relationship such as interaction or comparison. Finally, the proximity of concepts to one another suggests the likelihood that they are meaningfully related, but also that a scientist will discover and publish that. In this way, our hypergraph-induced proximities incorporate physical properties latent within literature, but also the distribution of human scientists, which enables us to anticipate inferences by those country-situated scientists and predict who will make what upcoming discoveries. The distribution of human scientists is a factor available to and naturally “read” by other competitive scientists when they attend conferences and survey their fields for promising new directions.

In order to foresee the potential discovery of connections between concepts, we utilize random walk-induced node similarity metrics to capture the relevance between them. These metrics, evaluated between pairs of concepts, reflect the human-inferrable relatedness of corresponding nodes. Our metric is based on a popular, unsupervised neural network-based embedding algorithm called DeepWalk14, estimated over the random walks we generate. Like previous content-only methods15, this method also entails construction of a word embedding model15. Instead of abstract sentences as input, we construct our embedding over our hypergraph, considering every random walk sequence a “sentence” that links scientists and scientific concepts. This metric exceeds the prediction performance of transition probability that a random walker travels from the author node to a concept through intermediate author and concept nodes within a fixed number of steps, calculated with Bayesian rules5.

Whereas a text-based embedding captures semantic relevance among words, our approach obtains word vectors while preserving hypergraph proximities among all nodes and therefore can be used to measure the human cognitive accessibility of each material with respect to a targeted property. Cosine similarity between techno-scientific concepts and researchers within the resulting embedding space can be used as a relevance metric. We use our relevance metric based on deepwalk similarities, as criteria for selecting concept pairs most likely to emerge as next discoveries. Deeper graph convolutional neural networks confirm the pattern of results obtained from deepwalk.5 In this grant project, we will also work to develop comparable deep models that improve on these results by accounting for varying layers of network context (see bottom section).

To identify research areas with increasing relevance, we will compute the momentum of embedding distance between concept pairs, i.e., the difference of embedding distance between current and previous year. This captures the dynamic likelihood of concept collocations in scientific articles, where having a negative momentum means two concepts are moving closer to each other and are more likely to be connected in near future. Concepts close to each other—within 0.1 (9°) cosine distance—and continuously converging define emerging fields in techno-scientific discovery and invention. Therefore, we compute a concept distance matrix for the current year, as well as a ratio of the distance velocity for each concept pair. Then, we identify the hierarchical agglomerative cluster using average concept keyword distance, and stopping cluster merging with average distances greater than 0.1. Because authors and concepts are mapped to the same embedding space, the identified clusters allow us to query authors closest to the epicenter, defined as the k-medoid, of each emerging field. By attributing each author to her host funding source and region, we can analyze the presence and dominance of the Novo Nordisk Foundation and other supporters in these emerging fields. Specifically, we measure (1) the per capita probability of the Novo Nordisk Foundation and comparable funders’ scientists being among the closest 100 to the epicenter (k-medoid), (2) the share of emerging fields with meaningful presence, at least 5 of top 100 scientists; and (3) the global share of scientists within the top 100 of all emerging fields. We will explore the robustness of all of these choices, and seek to extend them with deeper transformer-based models to natively capture career context-sensitivity. We will also explore the comparable embedding of properties, materials and authors via metapath2vec16. Longitudinal study of these dynamics will enable us to predict improved future connections between authors, properties and materials based on their proximity in the embedding.
Modeling Prescience

A new combination of research contents may surprise because it has never succeeded before, despite having been considered and attempted17–20; or because it has never been imagined—representing a combination of ideas inaccessible within disciplinary conversation. Our model articulates a simple mental process: Scientists and inventors combine things together that are (1) scientifically or technologically close and (2) cognitively salient. While formally simple, this model is more effective than those from the literature and even advanced deep learning models in capturing novelty and impact. As we model contents and contexts separately—a paper is simultaneously a combination of contents (e.g., keywords) and a combination of contexts (e.g., referenced journals), we also measure the content and context novelty of a paper separately corresponding to the novelty of its content combination and its context combination, respectively.

We measure the prescience of a paper by the decrease in its surprisal between when it was published and two years later, in order to identify work that was initially surprising, but became the norm through leadership or luck. As the hypergraph embedding model described above is dynamic and the underlying embedding space varies by year, we compute two surprise scores for each paper: one using the embeddings from the year when it was published and the other using the embeddings from two years later. This allows us to measure the prescience of that paper as the difference between the two surprise scores: papers that were surprising initially but become much less so later on are papers that were prescient or ‘ahead of their time,’ unusual at their publication date but not later on.

This model was fit using the top 262,000 keywords used in publications, thus excluding infrequent keywords. Only articles with keywords were used to calculate the prescience results we present. This allows us to assess the degree to which Novo Nordisk-funded and considered researchers are making prescient versus predictable contributions to the scientific frontier.
Modeling Disruption

To measure how the innovativeness of papers are recognized by the scientific community, we calculate the disruption index8,9,11 of scientific publications based on citation networks. The disruption index D, which characterizes to what extent the focal paper destabilizes or consolidates prior science, can be computed as

where nf is the number of subsequent papers citing only the focal paper and none of its references, nb is the number of subsequent papers citing both the focal paper and its references, and nr is the number of subsequent papers citing only the references of the focal paper. Varying between -1 and 1, the disruption index portrays the degree to which the focal paper disrupts or develops science. If a work completely overshadows prior work by garnering all subsequent attention to itself while its inspirations lie forgotten, then the measure equals 1. If a work is always cited alongside its inspirations and visa versa, then the work can be understood to broadcast the importance of prior work and the measure equals -1.  For example, IBM’s 1982 U.S. patent for a Scanning Tunneling Microscope and Cetus’ 1987 U.S. patent for a “Process for Amplifying Nucleic Acid Sequences” or the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), were both associated with Nobel Prizes, and both post a disruptiveness score of 1, while Amazon’s successful One-Click patent for online purchasing is much less than one, and amplifies prior e-commerce innovations.8 A larger disruption index implies the focal paper is more likely to disrupt existing ideas and its innovativeness is more favorably appreciated by the scientific community; while a smaller one reveals the focal paper tends to develop or consolidate prior knowledge. To make the comparisons fair, we compute disruption scores only for papers with both references and citing papers. Similar to existing literature8,9,11, we define disruptive papers as the ones with D>0. We further replicate our results with the CD5 index, i.e., the disruption index with 5-year time windows where only papers published within 5 years from the focal paper’s publication are considered in the calculation of nf, nb, and nr. This will explore the degree to which emerging and prescience work funded or considered by the Novo Nordisk Foundation is credited with disruptive impact across the scientific system.
Complex Prediction Associated with Impacts

In addition to our models that seek to promote excellence and innovation in research, develop innovative products and solutions for society that impact global health, as detailed above, we will also implement metrics and models tuned to other valued NNF outcomes. These include fostering diverse talent, stimulating equity-inducing collaboration, supporting organizations and infrastructure, creating jobs and growth. and raising the bar on global education. We will begin with the quantification of bias in existing indicators and models, as well as others that currently emerging or dominant.
Quantifying bias across indicators and models

Scientific data is intrinsically intertwined with biases, manifesting in diverse aspects of research dissemination and collaboration in ways that can inadvertently limit the pool for diverse talent. For example, given equal performance, women tend to receive fewer citations than their male counterparts26,27—including from themselves28); minorities often form isolated clusters within networks29,30); researchers tend to cite work from colleagues of the same nationality31,32, and native English speakers usually face fewer obstacles in publishing within high-impact journals33.
Some of these biases are naturally part of the scientific landscape, other might stem from discriminatory scientific cultures or mechanisms that have nothing to do with scientific quality.34

Acknowledging this, we plan to audit our existing indicators, models, and results, as also those we develop across gender and nationality (initially utilizing country of first affiliation as a proxy). This endeavor is not merely diagnostic but also mitigative, as we intend to explore and implement scenarios to alleviate identified biases35, thereby contributing to a equitable and fair measures and predictions consistent with NNF values. Consider the following exemplary analyses:
Modeling Emergence & Prescience

Here, we will focus on the role of potential biases in maximizing a paper’s emergence and prescience, defined as its domain’s predicted growth and the decrease in its surprisal between publication and the years that follow, respectively. The intuition behind these measures are as follows: papers erupt at the confluence of concepts in embedding space, and papers that were surprising initially become much less so later when those papers were prescient or ‘ahead of their time’. Nevertheless, the process of becoming less surprising might may be entwined with biases related to gender or nationality, as novelty is often shaped by author characteristics (Yang et al. 2022). Under some circumstances, however, betting on novelty may reward gender and minority status as persons with these identities have been demonstrated to disproportionately engage in scientific and technological risk-taking7. First, we will measuring empirically the probability of prescience conditional on gender and nationality. Then, using a shapley values approach36, we will quantify the importance of various variables, including gender and nationality, to provide the prescience prediction. A systematic difference found in the distribution of prescience conditional to gender and nationality would indicate a perception bias of what is novel. These results will be tested in controlled experiments where we will ask scientists to quantify novelty, varying on different attributes. The result will allow NNF to sponsor cutting-edge work with the potential to transform the scientific field while simultaneously growing a diverse scientific workforce. A similar approach will be used to evaluate other NNF values beyond equitable and diverse participation (e.g., maximizing downstream environmental or population health benefits).
Modeling disruption

Citations, on which the disruption measure is based, are themselves biased. Citations are affected by homophily, meaning that a citation is more likely given to someone that shares similar features, such as gender or nationality30. Given that gender and nationality are heavily imbalanced classes, the coupling of homophily and class imbalance can distort the interpretation of any citation-based score, including disruption. We will study disruption and its evolution conditional to these attributes, and propose corrected measures conditional on the gender and nationality of authors on the focal paper. As above, we will apply this logic to other NNF values (e.g., environmental flourishing and population health) to anticipate the consequences following from various granting criteria on those values and elucidate critical foundation trade-offs.
Modeling institutional change

We will further predict other developments in science relevant to core NNF priorities, including  the development of a dynamic multi-disciplinary system, robust and innovative institutions, and downstream applications. Along the way, we will seek to better predict and guide successful future collaborations via multilayer embeddings. Here the nodes are authors, and layers include (1) citations between authors; (2) collaborations between authors; (3) semantic similarity/proximity in the language embeddings of authors’ titles and abstracts; and (4) similarity in the space of functions and their associated values (e.g., more and less environmental impact). The result will comprise a single embedding of authors combining information from the four layers. Our approach will yield an extension of the graph-embedding node2vec algorithm37,  with a switching probability between layers. A short term goal will involve identifying the impact associated with pairs of authors who have not yet collaborated, or pairs of author backgrounds and new topics, from which basis we can explore the impact of institutional and collaborative investments on the structure, integration, and sustained health of the Danish and European science relative to the rest of the world.

Relevant to all considerations of scientific investment, we will calibrate the growth and decline of micro- and macro-scale fields of scientific and technological investigation. Investments in fields producing decreasing benefits for science, health and environment will underperform those yielding increasing benefits. As a first operationalization, we conjecture that a field declines when the average number of citations to (new) papers, patents, and (indirectly) products, is lower than the average number of citations to their references—the foundational work on which they build. Longitudinal analysis of the percentiles of papers with net positive citation gains reveals field trajectories, highlying inflection points. This approach will allow us to identify which fields are on the rise and deserve attention and support, and which fields are plateauing or declining and warrant fewer incentives. This is an example of feature that shapes the results of scientific investment above and beyond the particular research project. We have actively explored these and related dynamics and structures in the past—including the influence of fields38, teams9,39, careers40, awards41–43, and diverse other institutions across the science of science and innovation, in which the PIs have made consistent leading contributions44–48.
The Future: Exploring the limits of working with LLMs for prediction

In just the last year, LLMs have emerged to approach or exceed human-level speech production and language prediction. Throughout this project, we will explore whether, when, and how the transformer technology on which they are built can improve them. Because production-quality models have almost universally been constructed outside of universities and demand extensive (and expensive) engineering expertise, we cannot do this on the budget provided, but are seeking alternative funds (e.g., NSF APTO program). If successful, we could port the results from those experiments to these models, their predictions, and science policy simulations in the short term. In the longer terms, we could explore future NNF projects that take advantage of building and adapting LLMs for scientific simulation and prediction as sketched below.

In complementary work, we have proposed to build a data-driven “digital double” of the global techno-scientific system with deep-learned, chronologically-trained, context-sensitive large language models (LLMs), where funded awards, articles, patents, products, and related news are embedded and mapped to quantitative metrics of technology capability, production, and use. LLMs will capture changes in our metrics as corresponding distances and trajectories within their embedding spaces and to function as 1) large-scale observatories for science funding, capacity, production, and use; and 2) platforms for virtual experimentation that guide 3) precise causal estimation of the relationship between science policy levers (funding, organizational, immigration) in order to drive leadership in technological advancement in core NNF areas. By representing the complex global scientific and technological system, LLMs and associated embeddings will also function as an unprecedented platform for prediction and virtual experimentation, enabling us to anticipate results from much more expensive policy experiments (e.g., funding, competition, immigration), and guiding search for mechanistic models that causally identify the impact of policy levers. This may allow us to explore new opportunities that accelerate the co-evolution of data-driven AI with causal models of global science and technology capability. Our research will also enable specific advances in computational science and modeling, including the geometry of embedding representations that maximize prediction, causality, and human understanding; transformers that translate scientific structures into technical functions; and chronological training of LLMs to unleash their capacity for technology prediction and the instantaneous recognition of disruptive technological advance.

We propose that purpose-built LLMs could better characterize and predict the global system of scientific and technological development to understand and shape NNF technological capabilities, production, and use. This approach would enable exploration in a holistic way by building a large language model (LLM) atop precise data on global technology funding, research, intellectual property, products, and their mentions, linked by the people, regions, and organizations producing and consuming them to dynamically account for complex and emergent interdependencies between diverse technological domains. Our proposed LLM will suggest structural models to causally identify the impact of funding on interlocking discoveries, overlapping supply chains, global networks of skilled labor, and industrial organizations that drive or impede international technology leadership. Consider the enabling relationship between computing and data for artificial intelligence (AI); energy storage for mobile communication; and AI for robotics, materials, and biology. Expanding on our (i.e., Evans’) work directing research associated with the U.S. National Network of Critical Technology Assessment and building insight about global and domestic situational awareness for the U.S. government, we believe that constructing such a model could allow us to better model, measure, simulate, and causally estimate emergent relationships between NNF-focal areas and others that intermediate them to more refined global observatory and virtual laboratory for scientific and technological advancement. These experiments will be driven by seven initial hypotheses about how this approach might improve our ability to understand the complex systems that constitute science and anticipate the effects of investment.

Our first hypothesis is that LLMs must be chronologically trained to assist technology prediction. Contemporary LLMs, including Open AI’s GPT-4 and Google’s BARD, are trained indiscriminately on large tranches of temporally unlabeled text, including the Common Crawl and Wikipedia, but this limits their development as engines of science and technology prediction by obscuring their ability to predict any particular technological artifact (e.g., a patent, article, or product) from the past. We will explore the potential for chronologically training LLMs to tune their ability to contextually predict past technological advances without the shadow of the future, poising them to anticipate global technological futures from the present. Our second hypothesis is that we can construct generative LLMs and associated embeddings in which the distance between technologies of distinct performance levels is proportional to the difference between levels of outcome impact and performance (e.g., as for environmental or health outcomes). This potential is anticipated by recent work demonstrating the historical relationship between technological advances anticipated by formulations like Wright’s Law, Moore’s Law, and Huang’s Law and successive shifts in technical approach required to achieve continued improvement in semiconductor transistor or GPU density and performance over time.

Our third hypothesis is that LLMs and their underlying embeddings can be meaningfully combined and tuned with policy-relevant data on the position and distribution of innovation funding and innovating people to facilitate a digital double of the technology development system that enables effective policy evaluation and simulation. Our fourth hypothesis is that by taking a holistic approach to technology capacity, production, and use that crosses technology areas, we can perform much better than we could perform by modeling each in isolation.

Our fifth hypothesis is that our LLM can drive development of prescient structural models for causal identification of the influence of technology inputs on outputs. Structural models serve as indispensable tools for operationalizing data for causal identification of the policy levers that drive technological development. Our sixth and final hypothesis is that these structural models will allow us to recursively tune our LLMs. As we build our system to evaluate NNF current and future scientific investments, our exploration of rapidly improving LLMs may complement and, in some cases, substitute for specific components of our system to in order to maximize the precision and recall of NNF funding outlays that increase NNF successes and decrease missed opportunities. Full development of such a system lies beyond the scope of this proposal, but the validation of the hypotheses sketched above will clarify the benefits and limitations of LLMs and the transformer neural network architectures on which they are built.

Conclusion
In summary, we propose to develop an innovative data-driven, model-based system to comprehensively evaluate and predict the scientific and societal impacts of research funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF). The system will provide NNF with situational awareness to strategically lead global scientific trends in health, environment, and biological science.

Specifically, the project will allow us to help the NNF evaluate: (1) proposals for research; (2) individual researchers; (3) research institutions (e.g., proposed institutes); and (4) calls for proposals in terms of their risk and ripeness for potential discovery. By leveraging advanced AI techniques and network science, the proposed system will form a powerful “digital double” of scientific attention and impact over time. Along the way, we will explore the prospects of emerging AI techniques (e.g., LLMs) to enhance the components of the system. If successful, our pioneering approach holds the promise of transforming how foundations and organizations worldwide assess, evaluate, and drive scientific and societal progress.

The NSF-APTO Program

Introduction The National Science Foundation (NSF) has launched The NSF-APTO Program to enhance the national capacity to assess and predict outcomes of research and development in critical technology areas�

The NSF-APTO Program will help decision makers identify specific investments and policies that enable the United States to accelerate the development of critical technologies essential for the long-term national security and the economic prosperity of the country. The program received funding in August of 2024 and work began in earnest in Q4 of 2024. The two primary grant awardees are The University of Chicago and Northwestern University�

The NSF-APTO Program comprises of many scientists and engineers from The University of Chicago, Northwestern University, Indiana University, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, corporate partners, and participants from the Argonne National Laboratory�

To catalyze collaborations between these participants and to kick-off the program, The University of Chicago organized a two-day workshop, during November 1 and 2 of 2024, in which researchers across our partner institutions came together, gave lectures, engaged in focused discussions and forged effective working relationships.

Following the event, we organized regular weekly meetings for each of these teams to exchange ideas, share progress updates, and preserve the momentum generated by the kickoff workshop.

The Group Organization and the Five Primary Thrusts

To give more structure to our organization and to increase productivity and maximize our operational efficiency, we have organized ourselves into five distinct but fully integrated cross-disciplinary operational thrusts�

Each thrust will work on core, cross-integrated aspects of the program� Each thrust is led by a thrust leader who is a co-principal investigator of the program. We have organized weekly meetings for each of these thrusts. During these weekly meetings team members gather to discuss recent efforts, to report progress updates, to exchange information and to ignite the generation of new ideas. Members of other thrusts have an open invitation to attend the group meetings of the neighboring thrusts in order to learn about activities in which other groups are engaged. In this way, we seek to manage the operations of the program in an efficient, cross-disciplinary manner resonant with the matrix organizational structure of efficient corporate research organizations.
The Five Thrusts and the Thrust Leaders

THRUST 1 Large Language Models Thrust Leader: Dr. Doug Downey The Large Language Models (LLM) group seeks to build models to enable technology prediction through integrating relevant technology documents, building models chronologically to avoid data leakage, and generating complementary objectives to regularize models for improved performance. We hold weekly virtual meetings and the weekly meetings for this thrust occur on Wednesdays at 11 AM CST. We held a lengthy discussion of these topics at the workshop. The notes are encapsulated here.

THRUST 2 Embedding Everything Thrust Leader: Professor Yong-Yeol Ahn The Embedding Everything (EE) group seeks to construct data representations, often in the context of generating LLMs, with theoretically-inspired constraints and complementary data that enable mechanistic, interpretable prediction of technology advance. We hold weekly virtual meetings that occur on Wednesdays at 12 Noon CST. We held a lengthy discussion of these topics at the workshop. The notes are encapsulated here.

THRUST 3 Innovation Policies Thrust Leader: Professor Ufuk Akcigit The Innovation Policy (IP) group seeks to discover and design science and technology policies that maximize US technology leadership through their simulation with LLMs and embeddings, and their evaluation with structural statistical models and experiments. We hold weekly hybrid meetings. The meetings for this thrust are on Fridays at 12 Noon CST. We held a lengthy discussion of these topics at the workshop. The notes are encapsulated here.

THRUST 4 Data Structures Thrust Leader: Professor Dashun Wang The Data Structures (Data) group seeks to build a corpus of linked data that moves from data on technology capabilities, production, and use (e.g. from product specification sheets, sales, news mentions, etc.), back through technology designs (e.g., technology patents), principles (e.g., scientific articles), people (e.g., scientists, engineers, and workers), and capital (e.g., start-up funding). We hold monthly mini-conferences, alternating between Northwestern University and The University of Chicago. We held a lengthy discussion of these topics at the workshop. The notes are encapsulated here.

THRUST 5 Complex Computations Thrust Leader: Professor James Evans The Complex Computation (CC) group seeks to integrate data and computation across the prior four teams in order to enable powerful predictive models of technology capability, production and use. We hold weekly, in-person meetings for this thrust. The meetings for this thrust are on Tuesdays at 12 Noon CST.

Education and Teaching

As a result of the new faculty interactions catalyzed by the new NSF-APTO grant, Principal Investigator Professor James Evans and Co-Principal Investigator Professor Ufuk Akcigit have developed a new course for undergraduate and graduate students at The University of Chicago� The new course title is “Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth�”

The focus of this new course is on technological innovation, which alongside economic growth, are among the most compelling, critical and challenging phenomena to understand, predict and manage in modern society. Innovation has always been associated with unleashing transformative growth in art, science, and the economy, and in this new course, we explore these issues in the context of the contemporary emergence of the Artificial Intelligence (AI).

AI represents a novel source of innovation in economy and society. It is also a powerful tool for understanding, modeling, and steering technological innovation in new ways. The primary purpose of this course is to enable the students to understand innovation and growth in the age of AI. Students learn about AI related tools, and how theoretical frameworks and methods from economics, sociology, evolution, and complex systems may be used to understand processes of technological innovation.

This new course is designed to provide students with a background in dynamic analysis, data analysis, and modern AI, requisite for studying innovation in the modern age. They will also learn about compelling theoretical and empirical challenges, ranging from the paradox of institutionalizing innovation to inequalities that emerging AI capacities could create or remove, to advances AI could unleash in science and technology, to the spread of misinformation, to consequences of AI tools and “agents” in all domains of modern life, to existential risks associated with AI. In this course, we cover theories and models at an abstract and advanced level. Students attending this course are required to have the degree of mathematical maturity associated with advance calculus, optimization, matrix algebra, basic statistics, and basic programming. The course will involve a technical mid-term and a final group project involving theoretical and data analysis that explore innovation and growth in the age of Artificial Intelligence.

Corporate Partnerships

An important aspect of our work involves forming and fostering corporate partnerships with high-tech corporations working in the fields of Product Analytics, Innovation Analytics, and Artificial Intelligence�

About the picture on the cover

The image on the cover symbolizes our innovation policy initiatives and efforts related to scientific planning for science policy. The CHIPS and Science Act, along with related national regional and commercial efforts of 2022, seeks to build a foundational scientific understanding of the policy levers that will drive sustained technology science and leadership in an increasingly competitive global environment. The Innovation Policy Lab initiative in collaboration with our Global Science & Tech Observatory will construct a virtual laboratory to establish causal linkages between specific government philanthropic and corporate policy levers and S&T leadership. Through this initiative, we are designing AI systems to simulate outcomes of S&T to policy perturbation, including targeted funding educational competition and organizational policies. We seek to use these policy simulations to support the estimation of structural models that causally identify the impact of funding on interlocking discoveries, overlapping supply chains, global networks of skilled labor, and industrial organizations that drive or impede international technology leadership.

Introduction

The National Science Foundation (NSF) launched the NSF-APTO Program to enhance national capacity to assess and predict outcomes of research and development in critical technology areas. This Program will help decision makers identify specific investments and policies that enable the United States to accelerate development of critical technologies essential for long-term national security and economic prosperity. The program received funding in August of 2024 and work began in Q4 of 2024.

The University of Chicago NSF-APTO Program comprises scientists and engineers from the University of Chicago, Northwestern University, Indiana University, the Allen Intelligence, various corporate Institute for Artificial partners, and participants from Argonne National Laboratory. To catalyze collaborations between these participants and to kick-off the program, the University of Chicago organized a two-day workshop, on November 1 and 2 of 2024. During this two-day workshop, researchers across our partner institutions came together, gave lectures, engaged in focused discussions and forged effective working relationships. View the workshop newsletter here.

We have also developed a new course for undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Chicago, entitled “Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth”, designed as a new collaboration between the two Principal Investigators James Evans and Ufuk Akcigit. We have also begun a new weekly seminar on AI, Innovation and Growth at the intersection of the social and computational sciences with weekly visitors from around the world. Our Principal Investigators, postdocs, and students will interact with these research leaders to gain novel insights on our ongoing projects.

To provide structure to our organization, increase productivity, and maximize operational efficiency, we have organized ourselves into five distinct but fully integrated cross-disciplinary operational thrusts. Each thrust will work on core, cross-integrated aspects of the program and is led by a thrust leader who is also a co-principal investigator. We have organized regular weekly meetings for these thrusts. During these weekly meetings, team members gather to discuss recent efforts, report progress updates, exchange information and ignite the generation of new ideas relevant to our overall goal.

An important aspect of our work involves forming and fostering corporate partnerships with high-tech corporations working in the fields of Product Analytics, Innovation Analytics, and Artificial Intelligence. We have already engaged a number of commercial corporations, and we will continue to build relationships with new, relevant partners, including the companies supported by the NSF-APTO initiative and product giants like Amazon. We will form new partnerships with other commercial high-tech companies having access to unique product capability, production and use data and powerful analytics.

To integrate our program and facilitate collaboration between our multiple institutions, we recently hired an experienced business director for the NSF-APTO Program at the University of Chicago who now serves as a facilitator. His primary function is to bring people together and form coherent cross-disciplinary collaborations that work towards achieving our shared goals and objectives. He will also build strategic alliances between universities and corporations as we bring product data into the project, and share models, results, and insights out from it.

We have also recently hired a number of new graduate students, post-doctoral associates, and researchers to work on the NSF-APTO Program.
We are also in the process of exploring and analyzing the various action items we can take in order to enhance the project’s Broader Impact. Some of these initiatives are already in execution, with others in the planning stage.

Our biggest accomplishments of the past six months have involved: 1) hiring relevant staff, postdoctoral associates, PhD and master’s students; 2) guiding our component teams to focus on the overall NSF-APTO goals of gathering data on relevant technology capability, production, and use; and 3) beginning to build powerful technologies to model and produce policy-relevant inferences to more effectively guide it. We have managed to successfully organize a unified cross-disciplinary initiative in which everyone is working in close and active collaboration toward our project goals.

Overview and Importance of LLMs and Related LLM Applications

A “large language model” (LLM) is a form of artificial intelligence that uses deep learning algorithms to process and generate human-like text by analyzing massive amounts of (i.e., webscale) text data, allowing it to perform tasks like translation, summarization, question answering, creative writing, and drafting code, essentially mimicking human language and underlying reasoning patterns through a complex multi-layer neural network architecture called a “transformer.” The transformer architecture excels at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them.
molecular structures and properties to accelerate drug discovery and materials science development.

In the context of the NSF-APTO Program, and the mission of accomplishing the strategic objectives of the NSF’s Technology and Innovation Partnerships (TIP) directorate, LLMs are powerful because they can be trained with large- scale science, technology, and product data. This will enable us to predict and steer future technology advance, ensuring continued U.S. leadership in global technology advancement relevant to greater security and prosperity.

In addition to teaching human languages to artificial intelligence (AI) applications, language models (LLMs) can also be trained to perform a variety of tasks like understanding protein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease. Like the human brain, large language models must be pre- trained and then fine-tuned so that they can solve a widening range of practical, business, and scientific problems. Large language models have large numbers of parameters, which represent the model’s complex knowledge bank. Their problem-solving capabilities are being applied to fields like entertainment, finance, and healthcare.

Our proposed technology LLMs will yield three key model outputs, and one key data output. First, LLMs natively produce interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as a global observatory of the techno-scientific system they encode, signposting how the U.S. can navigate toward greater global leadership. Second, our LLMs are generative models that function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of government and industrial policies to facilitate U.S. leadership. Third, our LLMs will propose and support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of government policies that drive or impede international technology leadership. Finally, our models will improve the extraction of product-level data that, in turn, will improve the success of the models themselves and the science of technology advance that they support.

MID-YEAR PROGRESS UPDATE - JANUARY 2025
1:
Construct an initial version of a science prediction benchmark, capable of assessing existing AI models’ capacity for predicting content of future scientific papers, technology patents, and products.

Predictive models of science could accelerate the identification of breakthroughs, help funding organizations prioritize investments, and begin to automate certain scientific workflows, but broad-coverage benchmarks for evaluating such models do not exist. In the past six months, we have built an initial version of a science prediction benchmark for LLMs and other science-domain models, consisting of 6 tasks (3 generation + 3 classification/regression), covering open computer-science-domain literature from Semantic Scholar’s paper corpus. These tasks include:

1)
Follow-up proposal prediction: Given a set of existing literature, predict the proposal of a paper that will cite this set.
2) Author collaboration prediction: Given a set of authors’ publication histories, predict the proposal of a paper that
they will go on to collaborate on.
3) Experiment prediction: Given a paper proposal and summaries of papers it cites, predict the list of experiments that
will be conducted to test/verify the proposal.
4)

Impact prediction: Given a paper proposal and summaries of the papers it cites, predict its citation velocity upon successful publication.
5)
Co-citation prediction: Given a set of existing papers, predict whether all of them will ever be simultaneously cited by a future paper.
6) Author Interest prediction: Given an author’s publication history and a new paper, predict if the author will go on
to cite the paper.

While the classification/regression tasks can be evaluated straightforwardly using accuracy and correlation metrics, the generation tasks pose a more difficult challenge for evaluation, since (a) many possible correct answers exist and (b) accurately measuring the extent to which an output paper proposal covers the essence of a given paper is challenging. We are exploring the use of multiple evaluation strategies for these tasks, including a novel retrieval-based metric, and other established LLM-based metrics/frameworks (BERTScore, RAGChecker, IdeaMatcher, etc). Our results so far indicate that these evaluation metrics are only mildly correlated with each other. We intend to collect human annotations to determine which of them correlate the best with human judgements and use that metric for the generation tasks in our benchmark.

2. Develop an early-stage chronologically-trained scientific language model, on scientific text. We have also been exploring ways to develop a science-domain language model that has been trained in a chronology- and/or citation-structure-aware manner, because we hypothesize that models trained this way would be better-equipped to perform science prediction tasks. Specifically, we have experimented with continually pretraining public 8B-scale LLaMA models on sets of scientific literature that have been serialized in different ways (BFS, DFS, publication date, by clustering semantically related papers together, etc.) to capture chronology and citation-structure. The models we train in this manner can then be further fine-tuned for use on downstream prediction tasks from our benchmark. Our efforts on this front have not yet yielded promising results. The models we have developed this way are often outperformed by non-science-domain LLMs like GPT4o and even by similarly sized LLaMA models fine-tuned directly on our benchmark tasks (without any additional pretraining). We believe that this may be because the highly-trained instruction-tuned LLaMA models that we work with undergo catastrophic forgetting and lose their robust instruction-following abilities during our continued pretraining phase. We intend to explore more training strategies and architectural choices for science-domain models after we finalize and release our science prediction benchmark.
