MID-YEAR PROGRESS UPDATE - JANUARY 2025

In the initial phase of our work, we developed an integrated approach designed to provide clear guidance on structuring and optimizing science funding across a range of high-impact research areas to promote technological leadership, general welfare and sustained economic growth.
1:

Construct an array of dynamic general equilibrium models to capture the behaviors of scientists and firms underfunded and unfunded scenarios as revealed in our LLMs, explicitly formulating the optimization problem faced by individual researchers.

One of our primary achievements was the development of a dynamic general equilibrium (DGE) model that spans multiple sectors, incorporates endogenous firm innovation processes, and captures knowledge spillovers from both basic science and academic publications. We have also embedded input-output linkages to reveal how advancements in one sector can cascade through the broader economy, impacting output across diverse industries. By detailing how researchers and firms optimize their innovation strategies and benefit from exogenous technological spillovers from outside of their fields, this flexible framework enables us to evaluate the heterogeneous macroeconomic impact of various government- funded research programs on both welfare and growth. As a theoretical laboratory, the model generates counterfactual predictions on the effectiveness of government funding given to different scientific and technology fields, highlighting the importance of cross-sectoral interactions and spillovers. Validating these predictions, however, requires precise estimation of key parameters—an endeavor that hinges on high-quality datasets capturing researchers, institutions, and product-level details, which we turn to in the following section.

We seek to use these policy simulations to support the estimation of structural models that causally identify the impact of funding on interlocking discoveries, overlapping supply chains, global networks of skilled labor, and industrial organizations that drive or impede international technology leadership.

One critical aspect of constructing high-quality datasets is curating the most recent and comprehensive records of publications and patents, which serve as the foundation for our measurement of knowledge spillovers among researchers and across technological fields. Accurate disambiguation of authors and institutions is paramount to capturing the pathways through which ideas diffuse. In this regard, support from partners such as AI2 is invaluable. Only reliably disambiguated publication and patent datasets allow us to minimize the bias in measuring spillover flows between researchers, institutions, and sectors. Building on our existing data infrastructure, we have updated our publication and patent repositories by incorporating the SemanticScholar dataset from AI2 and the latest version of the OpenAlex database. These updates are complemented by rigorous validation procedures, including the examination of key distributions such as annual publication counts, document classifications, and the detection of author lumping, where multiple publications are erroneously assigned to a single author. These evaluations allow us to assess the conservativeness of disambiguation algorithms provided to us and ensure the robustness of the datasets for downstream econometric and computational analyses.

A parallel component of our data acquisition strategy focuses on product- and firm-level data, particularly in strategic high-tech industries. This enables the precise estimation of production functions and elasticity parameters within the DGE-network model introduced earlier. These elasticity parameters guide how technological and scientific advancements ripple through the economy by shaping supplier-customer relationships and influencing input substitution patterns across sectors. By integrating firm-level data with aggregate input-output tables from the BEA, we aim to capture both upstream and downstream effects of technical change with unprecedented granularity. Our collaboration with contractor Syntropy ensures the acquisition of these highly detailed product-level datasets and their alignment with our modeling framework. Once integrated and combined with our existing data sources, this information will facilitate the estimation and calibration of the model, laying the groundwork for robust policy analysis.

3:

In summary, we have made considerable progress in developing our dynamic general equilibrium framework and establishing a solid foundation for comprehensive data collection that incorporates robust name disambiguation and firm- and product-level details. Building on these achievements, our next steps will focus on estimating the model’s key parameters (goal 3), performing counterfactual innovation and science policy analyses, including embedding LLM- based forecasts of scientific progress to evaluate their potential economic outcomes. As we advance, we are committed to strengthening collaborations with partners and stakeholders, refining our findings, and delivering a comprehensive blueprint for effective and impactful science and innovation policy.

For generative modeling of grants and products, which can be pivotal for predictive modeling and causal inference of funding impact, we have finalized a preliminary study on a generative model of scientific citation systems. This approach models the evolution of the entire citation system, rather than individual publications, to more accurately predict future citation trajectories. Our model includes two components: (1) a publication generation model, currently a zero-knowledge null model that positions each new paper near a randomly chosen existing paper in the embedding space, and (2) an embedding-based citation model that generates new citations based on embedding distance (“relevance”), existing citations (preferential attachment), and fitness (“quality”). In evaluations of predicting future prominence (e.g., inclusion in the top x% of cited papers), this whole system-level approach outperforms traditional paper-level models. We aim to extend this foundation to develop generative models that also account for grants, patents, and products, enabling more comprehensive insights into the interplay between funding and scientific outcomes.

2. Build and deliver an initial dump (~500k products) of product factsheets data for critical technology areas (e.g. Microelectronics and High-Performance Computing).

To date, we have collected and integrated over 219,000 product factsheets, representing 43.9% of our target. Our dataset includes comprehensive product documentation (some documents spanning 300 pages) with detailed metadata for essential microelectronics products: microcontrollers, memory chips, FPGAs, and RF transceivers. The data, sourced from major distributors like DigiKey and Mouser as well as directly from microelectronics vendors, provides valuable insights into product capabilities and their evolution. Through tracking technical metrics across products, we can analyze performance trends and forecast future capabilities. We are currently collecting the remaining ~280,609 product entries focusing on emerging technologies crucial for defense, AI, and secure communications.

We have acquired datasets from key microelectronics trade organizations that track monthly net billings—shipments between semiconductor manufacturers and their end customers, authorized distributors, and subsidiaries. These billings, reported by customer shipment location, use actual sales prices or comparable market prices for internal transfers. By combining this production and usage data APTO: Syntropy Mid-Year Progress Report (January 2025 with our capabilities data from product factsheets, we have built the foundation for predictive models that assess trends in production, capabilities, and downstream adoption across the microelectronics sector.

To achieve our second objective, we are aligning product classifications across distributor sites and trade organizations to connect capabilities with production data. We have developed two methods to extract patent and intellectual property information from product factsheets. The first method uses advanced embeddings and metadata extraction to map relationships between products and patents, creating factsheet embeddings that identify each manufacturer’s most relevant patents. The second method applies prompt engineering to factsheets to uncover embedded IP. Together, these approaches will build a comprehensive product-to-patent database that shows how government-funded research leads to commercial applications. This linked dataset powers predictive models that forecast production, capabilities, and usage trends in microelectronics.

Moving forward, we will focus on two priorities: expanding our database with the remaining product factsheets and enhancing our product-to-patent connections. We plan to refine our predictive models to deliver detailed insights into production and adoption trends, publish our initial findings, and extend this analytical framework to other critical technologies.

Introduction

The National Science Foundation (NSF) launched the NSF-APTO Program to enhance national capacity to assess and predict outcomes of research and development in critical technology areas. This Program will help decision makers identify specific investments and policies that enable the United States to accelerate development of critical technologies essential for long-term national security and economic prosperity. The program received funding in August of 2024 and work began in earnest in Q4 of 2024.

The University of Chicago NSF-APTO Program comprises of scientists and engineers from the University of Chicago, Northwestern University, Indiana University, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, various corporate partners, and participants from Argonne National Laboratory. To catalyze collaborations between these participants and to kick-off the program, the University of Chicago organized a two-day workshop, on November 1 and 2 of 2024. During this two-day workshop, researchers across our partner institutions came together, gave lectures, engaged in focused discussions and forged effective working relationships.

To provide structure to our organization, increase productivity, and maximize operational efficiency, we have organized ourselves into five distinct but fully integrated cross- disciplinary operational thrusts. Each thrust will work on core, cross-integrated aspects of the program and is led by a thrust leader who is also a co-principal investigator of the program. We have organized regular weekly meetings for these thrusts. During these weekly meetings, team members gather to discuss recent efforts, report progress updates, exchange information and ignite the generation of new ideas relevant to our overall goal.

To integrate our program and facilitate collaboration between our multiple institutions, we recently hired an experienced business director for the NSF-APTO Program at the University of Chicago who now serves as a facilitator of the program. His primary function is to bring people together and form coherent cross-disciplinary collaborations that work towards achieving our shared goals and objectives. He will also build strategic alliances between universities and corporations as we bring product data into the project, and share models, results, and insights out from it.
We have also recently hired a number of new graduate students, post-doctoral associates, and researchers to work on the NSF-APTO Program.

We have also developed a new course for undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Chicago, entitled “Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth”, designed as new collaboration between the two Principal Investigators James Evans and Ufuk Akcigit. We have also begun a new weekly seminar on AI, Innovation and Growth at the intersection of the social and computational sciences with weekly visitors from around the world. Our Principal Investigators, postdocs, and students will interact with these research leaders to gain novel insights on our ongoing projects.

Overview and Importance of LLMs and Related LLM Applications

A "large language model" (LLM) is a form of artificial intelligence that uses deep learning algorithms to process and generate human-like text by analyzing massive amounts of (i.e., webscale) text data, allowing it to perform tasks like translation, summarization, question answering, creative writing, and drafting code, essentially mimicking human language and underlying reasoning patterns through a complex multi-layer neural network architecture called a "transformer." The transformer architecture excels at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them.

In addition to teaching human languages to artificial intelligence (AI) applications, large language models (LLMs) can also be trained to perform a variety of tasks like understanding protein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease. Like the human brain, large language models must be pre- trained and then fine-tuned so that they can solve a widening range of practical, business, and scientific problems. Large language models have large numbers of parameters, which represent the model's complex knowledge bank. Their problem-solving capabilities are being applied to fields like entertainment, finance, and healthcare.

In the context of the NSF-APTO Program, and the mission of accomplishing the strategic objectives of the NSF’s Technology and Innovation Partnerships (TIP) directorate, LLM’s are powerful because they can be trained with large-scale science, technology, and product data. This will enable us to predict and steer future technology advance ensuring continued U.S. leadership in global technology advancement relevant to greater security and prosperity.

Our proposed technology LLMs will yield three key model outputs, and one key data output. First, LLMs natively produce interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as a global observatory of the techno-scientific system they encode, signposting how the U.S. can navigate toward greater global leadership. Second, our LLMs are generative models that function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of government and industrial policies to facilitate U.S. leadership. Third, our LLMs will propose and support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of government policies that drive or impede international technology leadership. Finally, our models will improve the extraction of product-level data that, in turn, will improve the success of the models themselves and the science of technology advance that they support.

Year 1 Goals:
1. Construct an initial version of a science prediction benchmark, capable of assessing existing AI models’ capacity for predicting content of future scientific papers, technology patents, and products.

Mid-Year Progress Update - January 2025
1: Construct an initial version of a science prediction benchmark, capable of assessing existing AI models’ capacity for predicting content of future scientific papers, technology patents, and products.

Predictive models of science could accelerate the identification of breakthroughs, help funding organizations prioritize investments, and begin to automate certain scientific workflows, but broad-coverage benchmarks for evaluating such models do not exist. In the past six months, we have built an initial version of a science prediction benchmark for LLMs and other science-domain models, consisting of 6 tasks (3 generation + 3 from classification/regression), covering open computer-science-domain Semantic Scholar’s paper corpus. These tasks include:

literature
1) Follow-up proposal prediction: Given a set of existing literature, predict the proposal of a paper that will cite this set.
2) Author collaboration prediction: Given a set of authors' publication histories, predict the proposal of a paper that they will go on to collaborate on.
3) Experiment prediction: Given a paper proposal and summaries of papers it cites, predict the list of experiments that will be conducted to test/verify the proposal.

4) Impact prediction: Given a paper proposal and summaries of the papers it cites, predict its citation velocity upon successful publication.
5) Co-citation prediction: Given a set of existing papers, predict whether all of them will ever be simultaneously cited by a future paper.
6) Author Interest prediction: Given an author's publication history and a new paper, predict if the author will go on to cite the paper.

While the classification/regression tasks can be evaluated straightforwardly using accuracy and correlation metrics, the generation tasks pose a more difficult challenge for evaluation, since (a) many possible correct answers exist and (b) accurately measuring the extent to which an output paper proposal covers the essence of a given paper is challenging. We are exploring the use of multiple evaluation strategies for these tasks, retrieval-based metric, and other established LLM-based including a novel

9
metrics/frameworks (BERTScore, RAGChecker, IdeaMatcher, etc). Our results so far indicate that these evaluation metrics are only mildly correlated with each other. We intend to collect human annotations to determine which of them correlate the best with human judgements and use that metric for the generation tasks in our benchmark.
2. Develop an early-stage chronologically-trained scientific language model, on scientific text.

We have also been exploring ways to develop a science-domain language model that has been trained in a chronology- and/or citation-structure-aware manner, because we hypothesize that models trained this way would be better-equipped to perform science prediction tasks. Specifically, we have experimented with continually pretraining public 8B-scale LLaMA models on sets of scientific literature that have been serialized in different ways (BFS, DFS, publication date, by clustering semantically related papers together, etc.) to capture chronology and citation-structure. The models we train in this manner can then be further fine-tuned for use on downstream prediction tasks from our benchmark. Our efforts on this front have not yet yielded promising results. The models we have developed this way are often outperformed by non-science-domain LLMs like GPT4o and even by similarly sized LLaMA models fine-tuned directly on our benchmark tasks (without any additional pretraining). We believe that this may be because the highly- trained instruction-tuned LLaMA models that we work with undergo catastrophic forgetting and lose their robust instruction-following abilities during our continued pretraining phase. We intend to explore more training strategies and architectural choices for science- domain models after we finalize and release our science prediction benchmark.

3. Incorporate patent data and meta-data into the dataset.
Our patent data ingestion begins with Semantic Scholar, which has a mature paper- ingestion pipeline that has powered the Semantic Scholar website for many years but has never addressed patent data. We have developed design documents that define data models and tools for ingesting and represent patents. The documents aim at two primary goals, in order of priority:

a. Regularly ingesting patent data and storing it in a manner that it can be integrated into other knowledge graphs (including Semantic Scholar's KG of papers) and output in a normalized format for language model training as in Ai2's pes2o dataset.
b. Connecting patents to the Semantic Scholar KG of papers, by identifying matching authors and citations.

We have developed two different design documents, one that builds directly on the Semantic Scholar pipeline, and another that is more independent. We expect to make a decision between the alternative designs in the next two weeks and believe we are on track to release an initial patent dataset to the community in 2025. This will poise us to connect technology design data with capabilities, production, and use in the years to come.

Mid-Year Progress Update - January 2025

In the initial phase of our work, we developed an integrated approach designed to provide clear guidance on structuring and optimizing science funding across a range of high- impact research areas to promote technological leadership, general welfare and sustained economic growth.

1: Construct an array of dynamic general equilibrium models to capture the behaviors of scientists and firms underfunded and unfunded scenarios as revealed in our LLMs, explicitly formulating the optimization problem faced by individual researchers.

One of our primary achievements was the development of a dynamic general equilibrium (DGE) model that spans multiple sectors, incorporates endogenous firm innovation processes, and captures knowledge spillovers from both basic science and academic publications. We have also embedded input-output linkages to reveal how advancements in one sector can cascade through the broader economy, impacting output across diverse industries. By detailing how researchers and firms optimize their innovation strategies and benefit from exogenous technological spillovers from outside of their fields, this flexible framework enables us to evaluate the heterogeneous macroeconomic impact of various government-funded research programs on both welfare and growth. As a theoretical laboratory, the model generates counterfactual predictions on the effectiveness of government funding given to different scientific and technology fields, highlighting the importance of cross-sectoral interactions and spillovers. Validating these predictions, however, requires precise estimation of key parameters—an endeavor that hinges on

11
high-quality datasets capturing researchers, institutions, and product-level details, which we turn to in the following section.
2: Pilot development of dynamic data on technology usage from the presence and LLM-coded character of product mentions in business and popular press, the web and social media. Validate and complement product mentions with Nielsen-Kilts scanner data housed at UChicago, obtained from retail point-of-sale systems, which will enhance our metrics of production and use.

One critical aspect of constructing high-quality datasets is curating the most recent and comprehensive records of publications and patents, which serve as the foundation for our measurement of knowledge spillovers among researchers and across technological fields. Accurate disambiguation of authors and institutions is paramount to capturing the pathways through which ideas diffuse. In this regard, support from partners such as AI2 is invaluable. Only reliably disambiguated publication and patent datasets allow us to minimize the bias in measuring spillover flows between researchers, institutions, and sectors. Building on our existing data infrastructure, we have updated our publication and patent repositories by incorporating the SemanticScholar dataset from AI2 and the latest version of the OpenAlex database. These updates are complemented by rigorous validation procedures, including the examination of key distributions such as annual publication counts, document classifications, and the detection of author lumping, where multiple publications are erroneously assigned to a single author. These evaluations allow us to assess the conservativeness of disambiguation algorithms provided to us and ensure the robustness of the datasets for downstream econometric and computational analyses.

A parallel component of our data acquisition strategy focuses on product- and firm-level data, particularly in strategic high-tech industries. This enables the precise estimation of production functions and elasticity parameters within the DGE-network model introduced earlier. These elasticity parameters guide how technological and scientific advancements ripple through the economy by shaping supplier-customer relationships and influencing input substitution patterns across sectors. By integrating firm-level data with aggregate input-output tables from the BEA, we aim to capture both upstream and downstream effects of technical change with unprecedented granularity. Our collaboration with contractor Syntropy ensures the acquisition of these highly detailed product-level datasets and their alignment with our modeling framework. Once integrated and combined with our existing data sources, this information will facilitate the estimation and calibration of the model, laying the groundwork for robust policy analysis.

3: Pilot linking our model to data on the size, organizational structure, and industrial or field position of sponsored universities and businesses in targeted technical advance to predict how changes in strategic funding, training, and inter- country alliances will shape strategic technologies.
In summary, we have made considerable progress in developing our dynamic general equilibrium framework and establishing a solid foundation for comprehensive data

collection that incorporates robust name disambiguation and firm- and product-level details. Building on these achievements, our next steps will focus on estimating the model’s key parameters (goal 3), performing counterfactual innovation and science policy analyses, including embedding LLM-based forecasts of scientific progress to evaluate their potential economic outcomes. As we advance, we are committed to strengthening collaborations with partners and stakeholders, refining our findings, and delivering a comprehensive blueprint for effective and impactful science and innovation policy.

For generative modeling of grants and products, which can be pivotal for predictive modeling and causal inference of funding impact, we have finalized a preliminary study on a generative model of scientific citation systems. This approach models the evolution of the entire citation system, rather than individual publications, to more accurately predict future citation trajectories. Our model includes two components: (1) a publication generation model, currently a zero-knowledge null model that positions each new paper near a randomly chosen existing paper in the embedding space, and (2) an embedding- based citation model that generates new citations based on embedding distance (“relevance”), existing citations (preferential attachment), and fitness (“quality”). We aim to extend this foundation to develop generative models that also account for grants, patents, and products, enabling more comprehensive insights into the interplay between funding and scientific outcomes.

Year 1 focused on cultivating relationships with new SICSS sites and auditing the SICSS curriculum to see how it could expand its integration of research from the proposal.

Two sites were successfully launched in the latter part of the summer of 2024, SICSS Florida and SICSS Atlanta. SICSS Florida (July 1 – July 12) ran as a co-sponsored institute between the University of Florida and Florida Atlantic University, physically taking place in the ATLAS Lab, an AI-driven digital media analysis lab at the University of Florida. Speakers came from academia and industry across the country and participants came from universities across the state to learn computational social science skills and develop novel projects. SICSS Atlanta (July 22 – August 2) ran for the 3rd year, but for the first time at one of Atlanta’s HBCU’s. In partnership with faculty at Clark Atlanta University and the AUC Data Science Initiative, SICSS Atlanta invited PhD students, postdoctoral researchers, and faculty from across Georgia and the world to skill-build and develop novel projects. Both SICSS Florida and SICSS Atlanta featured custom-created complete curricula for all instruction.

After the conclusion of these SICSS sites, Albrecht brought on a postdoctoral researcher and a program evaluator to help work on an audit of SICSS materials and existing LLM curricula. This work will facilitate information sharing with other investigators on this grant for the upcoming season of SICSS institutes in the summer of 2025. We have also
23
planned a series of meetings across the investigator team to more directly integrate the results and ongoing research from Year 1 into the next flight of SICSS sites.

Significant effort was put forth in building networks to establish new and continuing sites for SICSS upcoming set of summer institutes, including attending conferences and conducting preliminary conversations with potentially interested groups. Following the SICSS site application process, where applications were due from potentially interested sites on December 1, 2024, 4 sites were selected for funding this upcoming year. SICSS Atlanta will return at Georgia State University, the only Predominantly Black Institution in the United States. SICSS Tuskegee will take place for the first time at Tuskegee University, an HBCU in Alabama. SICSS Minnesota will take place for the first time at Gustavus Adolphus College, a liberal arts college in Minnesota. SICSS Rochester will return at University of Rochester, a small university in New York. Albrecht will be on site for SICSS Atlanta, SICSS Tuskegee, and SICSS Minnesota. All of these sites were chosen for their potential to build community and broaden participation in computational science. Each of these universities serves a community that is under-resourced and historically under-participates in computational social science. At the same time, each of these locations is optimally geographically positioned with strong local organizers.

Mid-Year Progress Update - January 2025
Vision and Mission

Our “Broader Impact” vision is to have a positive influence on our community in the greater Chicago area, and to extend the reach and accessibility of AI-related research tools to various groups across the US, and to turn insights and technologies gained from our research into national capabilities providing local opportunity.

First, and foremost, we seek to have a positive influence on our immediate community. Within a few miles of the University of Chicago there are numerous high-schools, colleges and other institutions that could benefit from being engaged with members of our NSF- APTO group. As part of our mission, we will seek to positively influence the lives of young people who attend high-schools and colleges within the immediate proximity to the University of Chicago through educational, internship, and employment opportunities.
1: Collaboration and Knowledge Transfer

Our work on building models, predictions, and interfaces to serve insights to government and science policy stake holders will begin in year 2, once we have piloted more of these designs for evaluation. It will commence in collaboration with the University of Illinois at Chicago’s Electronic Visualization Lab, and with domain experts from key US government agencies, committees and directorates that support government functions including strategic planning and funding prioritization, technical horizon scanning, skilled talent availability and utilization analysis, partnership and alliance cultivation, research protection and counter-party risk analysis, and supply chain analysis.

2: Advancing Science and Technology
We are currently in the early stages of exploring the possibility of creating a new commercial entity in the Chicago area. This new commercial entity would be a new
for
27
company. This new company could potentially create new high-tech jobs for the recent graduates of colleges and universities within the Chicago metropolitan area.

Creating new high-tech jobs for people in the Chicago area could have a marked impact on their lives and the lives of their families. The creation of a new commercial high-tech company requires preparing and submitting SBIR-STTR grant proposals to government agencies. With the SBIR-STTR grant money we could run a commercial program at the new company and hire selected employees or interns from local academic institutions, including various colleges and community colleges within the Chicago area.

Dr. Kamran Mobarhan, our business director, will function as our “entrepreneur in residence” and he will help with the efforts related to the creation of a new company and consequently the creation of new jobs for the communities on the south side of Chicago.

The primary function of this new company will be to take scientific concepts and innovations from participating universities (e.g., The University of Chicago’s Knowledge Lab) and transform these scientific concepts into commercial products that could generate sales revenue. With financial funding generated in this manner we will be in a position to support the academic advancement and the professional career development of local students in the Chicago metropolitan area.
3: Broadening Participation of Underrepresented Groups: Integrating Education and Research

As part of the Broader Impact goals of this proposal, we are in close working collaboration with Professor Kat Albrecht from the Georgia State University who has committed to running sites of the Summer Institutes in Computational Social Science aimed at broadening training in LLM’s and computational sciences. We hope to have one of these future Summer Institute events take place at the University of Chicago, potentially in collaboration with the Chicago State University.

4: Education and Next Generation Workforce Development for Underrepresented Groups
We are in the early stages of exploring the possibility of creating a community-based internship program for high school students and undergraduate students from various high-schools, community colleges and colleges in the Chicago area.

Potentially, in these internships, half a dozen talented high-school students and half a dozen talented under-graduate students from local colleges such as for example the Chicago State University will be paired up with mentors at the University of Chicago for a period of 6 to 8 weeks during the summer time. The mentors would be graduate university students, or undergraduate university students, from the groups of investigators who are working on the NSF-APTO program. During these 6 or 8 weeks, the interns will work closely with the mentors and the interns will get a taste of what it means to be a graduate student or an undergraduate student at the University of Chicago.

28
If the initial phase of our experimental summer internship program is successful then we will explore expanding the above internship program to cover other partner universities in the NSF-APTO program, and potentially even some of our corporate partners.
5: Public Engagement with Science and Technology [and Outreach]

The NSF-APTO Program includes collaboration with universities, national laboratories and cultural institutions, including for example the Kellogg School of Management, the Warton School of Business, and the Art Institute of Chicago. These are all part of our effort to establish the University of Chicago, through the NSF-APTO program, as a cross- disciplinary focal point of science, business and art related to technology advancement.

We are in the early stages of planning public lectures with the Art Institute of Chicago. Professor Evans and Professor Akcigit are launching a new seminar series on innovation and growth at the University of Chicago. Moreover, Professor Ufuk Akcigit runs the Growth Academy, a two-week summer institute in collaboration between the University of Chicago and the World Bank for bureaucrats from middle-income countries to advance their understanding of the relationship between technological innovation and growth. These are a few examples of the public engagement programs which we are planning.

Junsol Kim

Multi-Agent Diversity in Reasoning Language Models
Abstract

How do people update beliefs from feedback, and what functional form governs those updates? Leading models often assume linear change, which obscures mechanisms, can mislead inference, and can amplify researcher bias through speciﬁcation choices. I address these gaps with equation discovery algorithms. In this talk, I will introduce the SINDy (Sparse Identiﬁcation of Nonlinear Dynamics) algorithm, which searches a library of candidate functions and selects a set that best explains trajectories, yielding interpretable equations rather than black box ﬁts. Applied to reinforcement learning (Case #1), this approach identiﬁes a nonlinear probability-weighting rule in two new studies and validates it against prior work. The model generalizes to eight of nine existing datasets and outperforms canonical alternatives. In re-analyses, it revises previously published conclusions, aligning results more closely with the original authors’ hypotheses. Using the same lens for emotion (Case #2), I use SINDy to integrate two parallel literatures by combining affect dynamics and reinforcement learning into a uniﬁed model of happiness dynamics. The identiﬁed hybrid model improves prediction over exogenous-only accounts in a large-scale dataset (N > 16,000), reveals a tradeoff between internal persistence and the duration of external impacts, and provides evidence for multiple attractor basins. Together, these ﬁndings advance nonlinear updating as a shared mechanism for belief formation and affective change. More broadly, this program of research demonstrates how AI for scientiﬁc discovery can be used to accelerate theory building across the social sciences. Future work extends to prospect-theory contexts and to making SINDy more accessible to social scientists by conditioning feature selection on inferential statistics. Large language models (LLMs) with enhanced reasoning capabilities, ﬁrst deployed in OpenAI’s o1 and popularized by DeepSeek-r1, have demonstrated superior performance across a range of complex questions and cognitive tasks, but the reasoning mechanisms behind these improvements remain poorly understood. Our analysis reveals that deep reasoning models systematically diversify their internal thinking process by effectively simulating debate between agents with multiple perspectives. Through quantitative methods including linear probes that detect personality traits and occupational expertise embedded in model

activations, we demonstrate that reasoning-optimized LLMs exhibit signiﬁcantly higher perspective diversity than their baseline counterparts. This multi-agent diversity correlates with improved veriﬁcation behaviors and problem-solving strategies. The ﬁndings suggest that sophisticated reasoning emerges not from singular expert thinking but from orchestrated cognitive plurality—a computational parallel to collective intelligence in human groups where diversity enables superior problem-solving performance.

Scientiﬁc breakthroughs typically emerge through the surprising violation of established research ideas, yet quantifying surprise has remained elusive because it requires a coherent model of all contemporary scientiﬁc worldviews. Deep neural networks like large language models (LLMs) are arbitrary function approximators tuned to consistently expect the expressions and ideas on which they were trained and those semantically nearby. This suggests that as LLMs improve at generating plausible text, so the perplexity or improbability a text sequence would be generated by them should come to better predict scientiﬁc surprise and disruptive importance. Current AI systems minimize risk by enforcing ideological neutrality, yet this may introduce automation bias by suppressing cognitive engagement in human decision-making. We conducted randomized trials with 2,500 participants to test whether culturally biased AI enhances human decision-making. Participants interacted with politically diverse GPT-4o variants on information evaluation tasks. Partisan AI assistants enhanced human performance, increased engagement, and reduced evaluative bias compared to non-biased counterparts, with ampliﬁed beneﬁts when participants encountered opposing views. These gains carried a trust penalty: participants underappreciated biased AI and overcredited neutral systems. Exposing participants to two AIs whose biases ﬂanked human perspectives closed the perception-performance gap. These ﬁndings complicate conventional wisdom about AI neutrality, suggesting that strategic integration of diverse cultural biases may foster improved and resilient human decision-making.

AI Interpretability research is an ideal case for early efforts in automating science: all necessary data can be generated in silico, there is still a lot of low-hanging fruit, and interpretability research needs to accelerate if it is to keep pace with the rapid progress in AI capabilities. To this end, I introduce AutoInterp, an LLM-based

system for end-to-end automated interpretability research. The user inputs a topic or question, and from there the system implements a chain of API calls to (i) turn the user’s prompt into an empirical research question, (ii) turn that question into a set of analyses, (iii) execute those analyses, (iv) interpret results, and (v) write up a report. In this talk, I will overview how AutoInterp works, share some of its research ﬁndings, and encourage the audience to contribute to this open-source, community-driven project!

talk will discuss a system designed to predict the impacts of newly published research. Given a paper, what will be discovered, invented, and produced? To answer these questions, the system (1) predicts whether a paper will be highly impactful; (2) predicts which scientiﬁc/technological/market categories the paper will be impactful in; (3) predicts which conceptual combinations and discoveries will be reported by citing works. This talk covers system design and three sets of experiments from my ﬁrst month of work, focusing on making predictions about science from part (3) of the system. Context experiments ask how much information about a paper is necessary for good predictions, and what the cost-quality tradeoff looks like. _Perplexity and perspective experiments_ ask whether scientiﬁc surprise has epistemic structure: how do predictions vary across topical vantage points, and how does conditional perplexity—the surprise of one concept given another—relate to semantic distance? *Pattern experiments* compare the predictions of omniscient agents against decentralized perspectives, and explores how to use perplexity and semantic distance to build diverse panels of reviewers and improve prediction quality.

Many people now trust AI to build software, make important decisions, and provide emotional support. The effective design of social technology requires thinking beyond the simplistic framing of “artiﬁcial intelligence,” a term coined 70 years ago. In this talk, I will present studies characterizing modern AI as “digital minds,” general-purpose agents that appear to think and feel. I argue that we can ground discussion of transformative AI in real-world data. In surveys, we show how the public sees minds in machines and how perceptions changed from 2021 to 2025. Then, by interviewing heavy users of the ChatGPT and Replika chatbots, we characterize the rise of “digital companionship,” including both its potential beneﬁts and risks to mental health. Finally, we show that the complex social impacts of digital minds, such as supporting or reducing human agency, can be measured by reﬂexively leveraging AI-powered simulation to evaluate AI systems. By studying human and AI behavior in tandem and building human-in-the-loop tools, we can constructively shape the future of human-computer interaction.

Computational Creativity
Can algorithms be truly creative?
Can algorithms be truly creative?
The recent proliferation of generative AI in science art and literature has brought a

central question to the forefront of public debate – is AI truly creative? On one hand
AI systems are clearly capable of generating novel texts images and songs that are
not mere replicas of existing content. But critics maintain that AI creativity is limited
to interpolation and extrapolation outputting mixtures and mashups of existing
content without ever generating something fundamentally new. Our research
engages with this timely question on both a theoretical and empirical level. We

analytically clarify the different meanings and forms of creativity we assess the
capabilities of models to meet these standards and we put forth methods for
augmenting AI creativity when they fall short. We also explore the relationship
between individual creativity and 'creative' environments that engender innovative
activity using them to explore ecologies of innovation-generating AIs. By clarifying
and augmenting the creative potential of AI models we reimagine the role of artificial

intelligence in creative processes while probing the age-old question of what it
means to have a 'new idea.'

AI Societies

Analyzing self-organizing AI collectives
Today’s AI agents can act and interact much like humans and when multiple AIs are

put into conversation they can even 'program' each other through textual
communication. The capability of AI agents to influence each other through direct
and indirect interactions much like peer influence and cultural diffusion paves the
way towards the emergence of AI societies. While some research has examined
meticulously designed and controlled AI collectives the fate and outcomes of fully
autonomous AI societies with minimal human oversight remain largely unexplored.

Will these societies mirror the trajectory of human civilization evolve into entirely
different silicon-based collectives or face inevitable collapse due to AI’s nonhuman
nature? Investigating these organic AI societies may not only deepen our
understanding of AI but could also shed light on emergent patterns of human social
behavior. Moreover as AI societies gain greater autonomy they may transcend the
boundaries of human imagination sparking innovations that go beyond our current

comprehension. Harnessing artificial collective intelligence will present both
significant value and considerable challenges and the AI Societies initiative seeks to
chart a path into this emerging domain.

How do AI systems understand the social world?

A foundational principle of the machine learning paradigm is that models can build
their own detailed knowledge bases from training data without having it explicitly
coded by engineers. Through exposure to ever larger collections of texts images
audio and videos today’s AI models are constructing increasingly sophisticated
representations of the social world. These models compress their extensive
knowledge of culture and identity science and history as well the pragmatics of

language and interaction into a few gigabytes by identifying and exploiting the
underlying patterns of social life. Reverse engineering a model’s internal
representations could therefore offer profound and novel insights not only into the
AI systems themselves but into human culture language and interaction. What can
we learn about ourselves by examining what AI systems have learned about us?

Existential Epistemology
In order to anticipate and ensure humanity’s flourishing and long future, what new forms of knowledge will we need to explore?
Asking questions of an uncertain future
With civilization facing unprecedented global threats ranging from nuclear
devastation climate change and superintelligent AI to engineered pandemics hyper-
stratification and critical resource depletion we may be at a pivotal point in human

history. As the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists’ Doomsday Clock at the University of
Chicago seeks to remind us humanity’s potential for self-inflicted catastrophe has
dramatically increased over the last century. Unlike other scientific frontiers however
in which replication and causal inference may be essential for robust understanding
we have only a single planet and a single future for human society. In this singular
global experiment we must build models of the future and act on them without

deeper epistemic assurances for human health and safety. This initiative seeks to
explore and advance new standards for the partial and even speculative knowledge
required to engage with issues on a planetary scale and to use this knowledge to
direct the global collective action and innovation that our survival may demand.
